Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all examined energy levels. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. We propose that any quadrupolar components are likely delayed in appearance as energy increases, possibly exceeding our detectable limits with more sensitive telescopes. Our research lays the groundwork for a deeper understanding of cosmic rays origins, and paves the way for interpreting upcoming data from highly sensitive cosmic ray detectors. It also highlights the significance of continued access to data from existing facilities like the Pierre Auger Observatory, which is crucial for advancing the field through in-depth reanalyses of existing research. It is with great appreciation that we acknowledge the invaluable contributions of scientists and collaborators who have contributed to the knowledge generation within this field of study. In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze digitized tissue samples, specifically in a classification application involving the detection of tumor cells within whole-slide images. By simulating a FL environment with a large, diverse dataset of cancer images from various sources, we compared the results of training models using both a federated approach and a centralized approach. Our findings indicate that federated learning can produce models with similar accuracy to those trained with centralized data, while avoiding the need to collect extensive training datasets at a single location. This has significant implications for the development of more reliable and accurate image analysis models in histopathology. To further explore the effectiveness of federated learning, we also conducted experiments under data sharing constraints, which revealed that even with data retention and throttling, the performance of federated learning can approach that of centralized training. Notably, we observed a notable improvement in the accuracy of tumor cell detection compared to traditional image analysis methods. Our study highlights the potential of federated learning to accelerate the development of high-performance computer vision models for clinical applications. Additionally, we introduce a novel framework for optimizing data updates in federated learning, along with a novel retrieval mechanism that enhances the effectiveness of data sharing. This framework is capable of managing large datasets, as demonstrated by our experiments using over 130,000 tumor cell images from 130 sources. However, we found that the performance of federated learning can be influenced by data confounders, which may necessitate the use of additional regularization techniques to ensure robust model development. To facilitate replication and advancement of our findings, we have released the code and dataset used in this study. This includes a comprehensive framework for federated learning image classification, along with detailed instructions and resource requirements for each experiment. This system is designed to handle large datasets and can be accessed through a publicly available dataset management interface. Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially applied with satisfactory results, however its effectiveness was impeded due to the occurrence of burst errors resulting from unpredictable marine conditions. To mitigate this issue, a weighted DFE method was developed but proved insufficient as it was unable to fully compensate for the spectral distortions due to the limited scope of its feedback symbols. Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. We've applied this technique to two fundamental time-series tasks: time-series classification and forecasting, demonstrating outstanding results. The code is openly available, and the best-performing models have been deployed in real-world applications. The technique is versatile and can be adapted for other CNN-based architectures. The source code is openly accessible.

This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - nilpotency, building on a previous discovery that these algebras are solvable. Additionally, this work establishes the equivalence of Lie algebras and Zinbiel algebras in terms of their representability through skew-symmetric matrices, demonstrating this connection for all finite-dimensional algebras in question. Furthermore, with this relationship in mind, common properties of these algebras can be inferred, including their capacity to serve as generators for infinite-dimensional algebras within the super Serre's theorem framework. Lastly, this work introduces the concept of 'abnormal' algebras and employs it to classify and examine various instances of such finite-dimensional Zinbiel and Lie algebras.

The unified correspondence theory leverages the algebraic and order theoretic underpinnings of Sahlqvist correspondence to offer versatile tools for correspondence and canonicity across diverse semantic frameworks and signatures. These tools, specifically tailored to logics whose semantics rely on normal lattice expansions (DLEs), enable computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas using the algorithm ALBA. Conversely, our proposed method effectively employs ALBA's rules and algebraic language to reverse its computations in the DLE setting, thereby allowing the derivation of an inductive formula from its first-order correspondent. This reverse engineering enables us to establish the preservation of inductive validity by the modal operator and the bimodal isomorphism test. Moreover, this achievement simplifies the proof of (bi-)modal formulas' validity using ALBA and ALPS-based methods. Ultimately, our results provide a foundational framework for the application of ALBA's correspondence theory to diverse DLE-based logics. Our methods also offer a modular approach to reapplying the algebraic and order theoretic aspects of Sahlqvist correspondence across different logics and frameworks. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) a framework for handling instances that violate dependencies. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation, incorporating data quality assessment. Unlike existing solutions that rely on closed-form expressions and density matrix evaluation, our approach leverages sampling-based techniques. We provide an original application of a machine learning algorithm, specifically hyperparameter optimization for cross-validation. Finally, we provide an original comparison of query validation methods, introducing new task definitions and task configurations for relational data, along with initial results on synthetic data. Lastly, we outline directions for enhancing consistency checking in query validation. These research advancements can be applied to various data handling tasks like data cleaning, data merging, and data validation. We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple chemical species in these stars. The findings showed a moderate metal content and the absence of an internal variation in metal abundance. Tononzintla 2 displayed an increased presence of alpha-enrichment which aligns with patterns observed in other rich-metallic galactic clusters. The abundance levels of the cluster's nitrogen-bearing stars, however, required a more complex statistical analysis to understand their prevalence and varying abundance levels. The results indicated a higher nitrogen content in the cluster's most alpha-enriched stars, a characteristic also seen in clusters like M2 and Ruprecht 106, suggesting that multiple factors contribute to nitrogen's formation and distribution across the galaxy. The absence of a notable mass segregation among the cluster's blue horizontal branch stars provided insights into random processes such as stellar collisions which may be influencing the development of the cluster. The time it takes the cluster's white dwarf stars to enter the cluster's central region has been estimated using the Jeans theorem and a simple stellar dynamics model, which also enabled the identification of potential magnetic field properties. The estimated central white dwarf velocity dispersion of about 2.2 km/s may provide a velocity scale for studying binary interactions within the cluster. The study of small and moderate abundance variations among the cluster's members has broad implications for the study of binary interactions and collisional enrichment in globular clusters. The findings from Tononzintla 2 will serve as a basis for comparison with other galaxy globular clusters and may be used in modeling the development of galaxy globular clusters as a whole. The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs has amassed substantial size over recent years, representing an impressive compilation of research and offering a diverse range of opportunities for statistical exploration in the field of theorem proving. Despite the numerous contributions made so far, the ever-expanding nature of the archive still poses certain challenges: locating specific content has become increasingly difficult, making it essential to prioritize reuse and clarity of comprehension. This thesis proposal outlines my research objectives, which focus on these concerns, as well as initial findings, which reveal that the Isabelle Archive exhibits characteristics typical of scale-free networks, as evidenced by the distribution of node in-degrees in its dependency graph. To further investigate this phenomenon, I plan to develop a simplified model that incorporates key aspects of the dependency relationships found in the archive, as well as explore the implications of this analysis for future development strategies of the archive. Additionally, I aim to contribute to the discussion on enhancing the usability of the archive by identifying potential improvements to the tools used for navigating and searching the content. To achieve a deeper understanding of how proofs are developed and what challenges researchers face, I plan to conduct an empirical study of the most highly cited works arising from the archive, as well as gather survey feedback from experienced contributors. Through this research, I also hope to contribute meaningful improvements to the archive, as well as share my findings with the theorem-proving community through relevant projects and presentations. By exploring these research directions, I intend to make significant contributions to the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs, as well as position myself to make meaningful contributions to the Isabelle proof assistant and the broader theorem-proving community. Ultimately, my long-term objectives align with the vision outlined by the archive's creators, which involves utilizing the archive as a repository of trusted mathematical knowledge, as evidenced by the growing interest in reproducible research and the increasing significance of published results being supported by formal proofs. To achieve this vision, it is essential to address the emerging challenges posed by the archive's growing size, as well as explore new opportunities for statistical analysis and exploration within the field of theorem proving. Alongside my research in this area, which primarily focuses on the archive's internal structure and the experiences of its contributors, I also aim to contribute to the ongoing discussion on enhancing the usability and clarity of the archive, as well as investigate external factors that could provide new insights and opportunities for further exploration. Through this research, which is expected to result in a thesis that addresses these concerns, as well as contributes to the development of the archive and the broader theorem-proving community

In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a basic optimization method on a non-convex function can eventually enter a region where the function becomes locally convex. To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to analyze the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of a particular TAP free energy function, which is relevant to the Z2 synchronization problem and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. Additionally, our inequality led to a confirmation of a previous conjecture regarding the efficiency of a sampling algorithm in the "easy" regime of these models. Furthermore, it provided a clearer understanding of the boundaries that mark the transition from "easy" to "hard" samples. Moreover, our results included a proof that the AMP algorithm can indeed escape local minima and reach the global minimum when the model is easy. This was achieved by showing that the AMP algorithm's stationary points are located within a region of local convexity for an extended period. As a result, we were able to establish that the AMP algorithm's solution is accurate and can be obtained in linear time when the model is easy. It is also shown that the same algorithm can become trapped in a local minimum when the model is hard. To further validate our theory, we conducted various experiments using both synthetic and real data, which provided strong evidence for our conclusions. It is worth noting that our results can be applied to any multi-section and real-valued model that meets specific easy/hard model criteria. Moreover, our results imply that the AMP algorithm's performance in the easy regime is optimal in the sense that its solution is the global minimum, and this is achieved in linear time. In the hard regime, however, the AMP algorithm is guaranteed to become trapped in a local minimum. It is also demonstrated that our general easy/hard model criteria can be applied to models that exhibit different easy/hard transition boundaries. Our results further highlight the significance of local convexity or log-Sobolev inequality in determining an algorithm's ability to escape local minima. It is shown that an inequality known as the log-Sobolev inequality, which measures local convexity, can serve as an upper bound for an algorithm's expected local mixing time. It is also shown that our general easy/hard model criteria can be applied to models that exhibit different easy/hard transition boundaries. Our results further highlight the significance of local convexity or log-Sobolev inequality

We introduce a deep learning model called the Electron Correlation Potential Neural Network (eCPNN), which can learn simplified potential functions that accurately capture the intricate electron correlations present in complex many-electron atoms. Trained on restricted configurations, the eCPNN can effectively predict its own generalizability to all possible electron arrangements within a given energy segment, thereby enabling the simulation of electron distributions across various states. Through integration with the Kohn-Sham method, the eCPNN potential can be applied to compute reliable total energies, effective one-body potentials, and excitation energies for individual energy levels or broader energy ranges. Furthermore, we demonstrate the eCPNN's ability to simulate spin-traced systems and provide a framework for incorporating additional physical phenomena, such as the influence of photons or external fields. Our approach provides a powerful and adaptable framework for developing new many-electron atom models and making precise predictions for a wide range of elements. With the ease of integrating new experimental data, the eCPNN has immense potential to drive progress in atomic physics and further our understanding of the atomic world.

Our analysis leverages a range of techniques: hierarchical clustering, a statistical test, and power spectrum analysis - each method providing unique insights, which together suggest the presence of a massive structure at around 4.5 to 4.8 sigma confidence levels. We employed multiple statistical tests to mitigate any biases that could influence our findings, which suggest that the arc-like feature is an overdensity with a density ratio of about 1.3. Given its size, the Giant Arc may represent a challenge to cosmological theories if it is an isolated example. However, if it is part of a larger structure, it may not be as significant. Further research is necessary to explore this finding further. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing projected 3D object points. Next, a projection grouping module is applied to divide the heatmap into segments, thereby generating a coarse 3D point cloud. Subsequent correspondence learning modules refine 3D points through iterative correction processes. We have put two straightforward methods into practice: one is a simple elimination method, and the other is a least squares method. Our method is straightforward, efficient, and outperforms existing two-stage methods on ModelNet40 and PASCAL3D. Moreover, it is highly efficient with a processing speed of 13.1 FPS on real-world hardware. The code has been made publicly accessible.

It does this by assigning a value to unrepresented connections as if they were a central component, thereby providing a more comprehensive assessment of a node's centrality. Lastly, we propose a 1D thermal conductivity calculation as the next step to experimentally identify these topological materials. Experimental verification of these predictions through thermal conductivity measurements is suggested.

Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling. Additionally, the model's corpus-level feature's ability to capture global entity distributions is showcased through intuitive visualizations. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/ghrua/StruNER.

Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. For instance, we could use descriptions produced by low-quality generation methods or crowd-sourced data to serve this purpose. Nevertheless, utilizing these may compromise the integrity of system assessments. Crowds often produce inaccurate descriptions that vary in quality, which can lead to biased system rankings. To offer a more objective assessment, I propose adjusting the similarity metric to better align with these imperfect descriptions. Specifically, I suggest using a metric called the "median similarity" to provide a more central tendency of system performance in the face of inaccurate descriptions. To support this approach, I provide results showing how the proposed metric effectively reduces the systemic variations caused by these substandard descriptions. Furthermore, I demonstrate the benefits of using this metric in scenarios where high-quality reference data is available but may also be applicable to other scenarios. The proposed "median similarity" approach can be applied to other visual recognition systems that rely on text descriptions, such as class-name classification, and is available online at https://github.com/ying101/sf-metric. In summary, to create more robust and reliable assessments of these systems, I recommend generating more accurate reference descriptions and using the proposed "median similarity" metric when necessary. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. However, we discovered that users in areas with long political divisions' histories tended to isolate themselves from opposing views, reducing the diffusion of misinformation. We introduce a groundbreaking, efficient, and user-friendly detection algorithm called HALFADO. HALFADO uses a limited number of human judgments to effectively identify anomalies in real-time, high-frequency data streams. Implementing a precise detection system is crucial for empowering human teams across the digital world by providing reliable decision support. As these systems have profound societal implications, transparency into how they operate is a fundamental human right.

Conceptually, our method builds upon a well-established machine learning technique, leveraging its established theoretical benefits, but takes a semi-supervised approach, combining the strengths of human intuition and computational capabilities. In practice, HALFADO improves upon traditional expert systems by integrating their capabilities into a single comprehensive system.

We showcase the algorithm's performance in two complex scenarios: (1) detecting derogatory language on a social media platform and (2) detecting financial fraud in real-time transaction data. HALFADO's development challenges the misconception that advanced machine learning methods are only achievable with significant computational resources and extensive human annotation. The code and dataset for this work are openly available, providing a valuable resource for those interested in tackling complex, high-stakes classification problems. Previous studies have demonstrated that Translation Memory (TM) can enhance Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance. Unlike existing approaches which rely on bilingual corpora for TM and employ source-side similarity searches, our proposed framework leverages monolingual data and retrieves memories in a cross-lingual manner. Notably, our framework offers two significant advantages: firstly, it enables vast amounts of monolingual data to be incorporated into TM; secondly, both the memory retriever and the NMT model can be jointly optimized for translation objectives. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves substantial gains in performance and outperforms TM-augmented NMT baselines even when utilizing bilingual TM. Furthermore, our model's capacity to tap into monolingual data allows it to excel in low-resource and domain adaptation scenarios. To recognize new categories from minimal labeled data, few-shot learning has been rapidly evolving in recent years. However, traditional methods that rely on average operations for calculating prototypes often struggle due to the influence of outliers. This research proposes a new, effective framework that utilizes an episodic prototype generator module to create more representative prototypes from limited support data, reducing the impact of outliers and resulting in preferable models. The framework's ability is further showcased by the substantial improvement it yields over baseline models and the comparable performance it achieves to existing methods on datasets like miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, and cross-domain benchmarks (miniImageNet to CUB-200-2011). Moreover, the method achieves a notable reduction in the error rate on noise-containing datasets, highlighting its robustness against outliers. The method's efficiency is also demonstrated by the low gap in average errors when compared to the error rates of models trained on the entire dataset. The proposed framework's ability to create desirable prototypes is also highlighted by the low error rates it achieves on new classes with only one shot in certain cases. The method's code is available at https://github.com/zwang84/EPG.

Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous data sparsity, thus motivating the development of a more comprehensive solution that considers multiple domains with varying data densities. Inspired by real-world scenarios, we introduce the Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) model, which proactively leverages multiple domains, including those with dense data, to recommend across a single target domain with scarce data. Unlike traditional CDR methods, MSDCR fully exploits the potential of these additional domains by integrating their latent patterns and enriching the target domain's user and item latent factors. Through the incorporation of density-aware domain weights, MSDCR distinguishes and adaptively aggregates the informative domains and filters out data-dense domains that may contribute little new information. We further introduce a progressive alternating least-squares objective function to enhance the model's flexibility in handling multiple domains. Experimental evaluations on extensive real-world datasets showcase the superiority of MSDCR in addressing extensive data sparsity in target domains. Moreover, theoretical analysis and practical scenario simulations validate the MSDCR model's ability to effectively exploit multiple domains. Our work provides a comprehensive solution to the widespread issue of data sparsity in cross-domain recommendation and provides an adaptable framework for tackling various sparse-domain scenarios. Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to diverse real-world data and scenarios. Furthermore, Hypatia is made available as an open-source and community-driven project. Its code, accompanying examples, and further information can be found at its dedicated repository.

The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study assessed the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and evaluation purposes. Our investigation examined MRIQC metric sensitivity to different training sets, data fusion techniques, and the impact of training on previously unseen datasets. Furthermore, we investigated the influence of training on previously unseen datasets with limited samples. Our findings highlighted the significance of generalizing robust quality control measures across diverse populations and advocated for incorporating diverse datasets into training sets to enhance performance. Additionally, we explored the application of fusion techniques and their effectiveness in improving quality control outcomes. This research contributes to the development of more reliable and adaptable quality control pipelines, enabling them to effectively generalize across diverse populations and previously unseen data. As a complementary resource, we have made the results of this study openly available to facilitate evaluation and comparison with alternative quality control approaches. Additionally, we have released the code used in this research as a practical example for replicating similar workflows and exploring related methods. This study and its associated repository are part of an ongoing effort to foster discussion, shape best practices, and facilitate Reproducible Research in the field of MRI quality control. As such, we invite the scientific community to join this initiative and contribute their expertise, data, and related experiences. As we continue this work together, we look forward to sharing our collective knowledge and advancing the development of more effective and generalizable quality control measures. Intel's Optane DC Persistent Memory Module (DC PMM) has reached commercial viability as the first commercially available nonvolatile memory DIMM. It offers fast, byte-granular data access similar to DRAM, combined with power-fail safe storage. In-depth analysis reveals that software must take a dual-view perspective of Optane: (1) as DRAM for transactional, performance-critical workloads and (2) as storage subject to Garbage Collection (GC) threats for persistent data. GC threats arise from modifying application data once written to Optane, potentially causing data corruption. To mitigate this risk, the GC algorithm must be designed to minimize data inconsistency issues. In contrast to storage media like hard drives with built-in error correction, DRAM errors may arise due to memory cell failures. Consequently, retaining data integrity becomes increasingly challenging as both storage and memory media pose GC threats. As a result, the GC algorithm's design is no longer a concern for storage manufacturers but rather an application-specific issue. In light of these new considerations, we recommend a layered memory management approach, involving a lower-level Memory Management Unit (MMU-based memory management and a higher-level Virtual Memory Manager (VMM) that can be optimized for specific workloads, storage algorithms, and memory technologies. Furthermore, we highlight the significance of collaborating with storage and memory technology manufacturers to optimize VMMs, as well as the potential for multi-level storage systems to improve data integrity and data locality, thus enhancing overall system performance. As proof of concept, we apply these concepts to Optane and develop a custom VMM called OptaVM, showcasing superior performance compared to traditional DRAM-based VMs for applications that incorporate persistent data. In these scenarios, OptaVM achieves a 2x performance gain compared to DRAM-based VMs and outperforms stack-based storage management by 2.5x. Additionally, OptaVM demonstrates storage-cost-aware scalability, allowing it to operate efficiently on a range of storage configurations, including single Optane persistent memory device. In evaluation studies, we examine various storage algorithms and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in mitigating GC threats, achieving a 10-30% performance improvement over OptaVM, depending on the algorithm and workload. As storage media like Optane continue to evolve with faster access times and larger capacities, integrating persistent memory safely and efficiently will become increasingly vital for future system designers. The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Furthermore, we investigate the conditions under which this attractor emerges and the implications it has for understanding complex behavior in multi-agent systems through the application of the Motivation Dynamics framework. Additionally, we compare our model's results to real-world data obtained from a field study involving human subjects and observe a striking similarity between their decision-making patterns and those of our mathematical model. This finding suggests that the model's ability to produce a strange attractor may provide a suitable explanation for the observed temporal persistence in the data. Through this work, we also address potential criticisms of using the Motivation Dynamics framework by responding to concerns related to the model's validity, its reliance on specific parameter values, and the possibility of alternative explanations for the observed attractor. Lastly, we outline directions for future research, including the application of the model to explain cooperative behavior in scenarios beyond the one studied here, as well as the integration of additional elements, such as environmental influences, into the model. This work is part of an ongoing investigation aimed at understanding complex, persistent patterns of behavior through the application of the Motivation Dynamics framework to a particular cooperative scenario. The model's analysis yields a result indicative of a strange attractor, and we explore the conditions under which this attractor emerges. The model is then compared to real-world data, revealing a striking similarity between its dynamics and those of the observed phenomena. The study addresses potential limitations of the model and suggests possible future research directions. The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Our study extends this connection to the finite classical Coxeter group Bn by standardizing the ordered generating sequences, which allows us to identify exchange laws for Bn. Moreover, we establish a connection between the standard ordered generating sequences, Coxeter length, and the descent set of Bn. Our analysis also explores the relationship between the ordered generating sequences, left multiplication operators, and the left regular representation of Bn. Additionally, we investigate the combinatorial properties of the standard ordered generating sequences and their connection to valency in Bn. Our findings are further enriched by a discussion of the concept of ordered generating sequences in the finite classical Coxeter groups Cn and Dn. Our study also introduces an encoding method for the standard ordered generating sequences of Sn and Bn, which is shown to relate to the descent set and Coxeter length. Lastly, our research introduces a universal alphabet for the standard ordered generating sequences of all finite classical Coxeter groups, which is displayed through a elegant exponential representation of the standard ordered generating sequences of Dn. Our findings are derived from a novel perspective utilizing the standard Coxeter presentation, rather than conventional group theory. Our study offers a novel, algebro-combinatorial approach that may be applied to various non-abelian finite groups that satisfy the Coxeter presentation property. Our research introduces a novel framework for analyzing the interplay between group elements, their geometric representation, and the geometric properties derived from the arrangement of generating elements. Our results are enriched by diverse examples and a discussion of potential applications. Our study is a fundamental step in exploring the complex relationships between group elements, geometric representation, and geometric properties and may pave the way for further generalizations to a broader range of abelian and non-abelian groups. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion, beating the previously recorded bulk silicon records. Furthermore, our approach enables scalable production of efficient photon-spin interfaces, bringing quantum communication networks closer to reality.

The high activity levels of M dwarfs present a significant challenge for discovering exoplanets, as their stellar activity masks the signals from these celestial bodies. This problem requires an effective method for filtering out the stellar activity from the data sets, especially when searching for habitable Earth-like planets. To achieve this goal, we conducted a statistical analysis of how stellar activity intervals impact the detection of exoplanets. Utilizing a large data set of 116 M dwarfs observed by Kepler and K2, we determined the distribution of activity levels and established criteria for selecting specific activity intervals. We then assessed the influence of these intervals on the detection of exoplanets, taking into account the sensitivity of the Kepler telescope. Our research indicates that certain activity levels can significantly impact the detection of exoplanets, with a particular influence on low-mass stars like the M dwarfs in our study. We also developed a statistical approach for estimating the detection rates of exoplanets under various activity conditions. Based on our analysis, we provide models that can predict the number of exoplanets detected within defined activity levels or vice versa. This research provides valuable insights and methods for refining the search for habitable Earth-like planets, especially when observing active low-mass stars. Given the technological advancements of upcoming telescopes like TESS and PLATO, our study offers a timely contribution to the ongoing efforts to discover exoplanets. As a byproduct of our analysis, we also identified various phenomena related to the stellar activity of the M dwarfs in our data set, including the detection of superhumps and anti-phase symmetry in activity cycles. However, these additional findings represent a secondary outcome of our primary research focus, i.e., understanding how stellar activity affects the detection of exoplanors. As such, these secondary results are presented as a supplementary set of findings rather than a primary topic of discussion in this study. This paper presents a Wikipedia-based entity recommendation framework that utilizes an embedding approach, where the Wikipedia database is hierarchically divided into layered graphs to extract entity features and learn entity representations. By combining the extracted information with a lightweight ranking method, this framework effectively suggests related entities to users on Wikipedia. We evaluate our approach through both offline and real-world online tests, demonstrating that our embeddings and recommendations exhibit desirable quality and user engagement. Furthermore, this framework delivers entity recommendations in both English and non-English languages for the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph, where Wikipedia constitutes a fundamental subset. A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but with suitable conditions, it is possible to establish control limit policies that can be easily applied. Our study uses numerical examples to demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves under different levels of incompatibility, and highlights the significance of taking incompatibility into consideration in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are available. Furthermore, we investigate how the value of waiting for a compatible kidney compares to the value of receiving an incompatible kidney, and provide a practical solution for determining the optimal course of action in this scenario. We also suggest potential future research directions as the field continues to evolve with new developments in desensitization technologies. Despite the progress made, many patients remain unable to receive kidney transplants, underscoring the need for the kinder transplantation community to address the incompatibility issue through data-driven decision-making. Implicit copulas are the primary choice for analyzing dependencies in complex scenarios due to their ability to effectively model dependence in high-dimensional spaces. The text presents a comprehensive overview of this broad category, encompassing copulas such as elliptical, skew t, factor, time series, and regression copulas, highlighting their key characteristics and applications. The discussion explains how the auxiliary representation of implicit copulas facilitates scalability and usability in statistical modeling, addressing concerns like parameter estimation, likelihood calculation, and model parsimony. The text also covers advanced implicit copula models, including models with time-varying parameters, dynamic models, Bayesian estimators, and statistical tools for assessing implicit copula model validity. The chapter concludes by exploring potential future developments in the field. The accompanying R package, icopulaR, provides implementation details for the discussed models and accompanying functions. The package can be utilized for estimating implicit copulas, evaluating model fit, diagnosing residuals, and implementing graphical residual analysis. The text and package serve as a resource for researchers tackling dependence challenges in complex datasets and can be applied to analyze dependent data across multiple variables. The R code supplied complements the theoretical text and offers practical implementation of the discussed concepts. The implicit copula framework is an open-source platform that is freely available at https://github/icopulaR and can be downloaded from the CRAN website at https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=icopulaR. We employ a level set method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining the advantages of a conservative finite-volume approach with a precise representation of interface dynamics. A new algorithm for calculating the terms associated with the boundary conditions has been developed, allowing for a more efficient and flexible implementation that can easily handle complex boundary shapes. This new algorithm replaces the previous method based on the fundamental conservative form and enhances the ability to capture the effects of boundaries on the interface. It also enables a simpler and more robust approach to modeling boundary conditions. It should be noted that although this algorithm has a similar structure to those used in other higher-order methods, it has a greater flexibility and efficiency because it is based on an exact representation of the interface. This results in a more accurate capture of the boundary effects without the need for artificial compressibility or other approximations. This new algorithm has been successfully applied to a variety of problems, including simulations of boundary-driven flows, solid-fluid interactions, and models of biological tissues. It has also been used to investigate the effects of boundary conditions on the motion of droplets in simulations of flows with changing phases. This algorithm can be implemented using an operator rotation method, and it has been integrated with a solver based on the projection method for solving the momentum equations. This solver uses a semi-implicit scheme for time discretization and has been modified to accommodate complex boundary conditions. This modification involves replacing the standard ghost cell technique with the new algorithm, and it has been found to significantly enhance the ability to handle complex boundary shapes. This approach has been further enhanced by integrating it with an adaptive mesh refinement technique based on the error in the numerical solution, and it has been used to conduct a variety of simulations, including the motion of a droplet in a boundary-driven flow and the growth of a solid particle in a flow with changing phases. The results of these simulations demonstrate the ability of this approach to accurately capture the effects of complex boundary shapes on the motion of fluids with changing phases. This approach has also been used to conduct simulations of two-phase flows in three dimensions, and it has been found to be an effective and robust method for modeling the interaction of fluids with changing phases in complex boundary domains. Current versions of the Lambek Calculus used in computational linguistics are expanded upon using unary modalities to govern structural rules affecting sentence order and phrasing. This incorporation of controlled structural operations yields derivational ambiguities missed by the original Lambek Calculus and its simplification in pregroups. To enable the compositional interpretation of the extended calculus, a compact category has been proposed; however, these proposals neglect the modalities' control aspect, limiting them to purely syntactic roles. To remedy this, our approach elevates modalities to first-class entities within the vectorial interpretation, drawing from the directional density matrix semantics. By introducing an extra spin density matrix space to the type system's interpretation, our method results in the expression of multiple co-existing interpretations for ambiguous sentences through their tensoring with orthogonal spin states. This method offers a unified framework for handling both lexical and derivational ambiguity within a sentence's interpretation. Additionally, our approach facilitates the computation of multiple interpretation lines through the application of modalities, mimicking the effect of structural rules. To support this, our system is demonstrated through the interpretation of sentences from the Discourse Residue Corpus. Our method achieves the concurrent existence of multiple interpretations, demonstrating its practical feasibility in addressing ambiguity issues. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities. It also includes a rationalizable policy learning method with a significantly improved sample requirement, surpassing the previous best-known result by a significant factor. These innovative solutions take advantage of a novel new approach, leveraging the power of individual rationalizability from a broad range of action sets. This leads to stronger guarantees on the learned equilibria, particularly for smaller action spaces. It is worth noting that the developed techniques have broader applicability and could serve as a foundation for exploring other equilibrium concepts that involve complex action combinations. 

This work distinguishes itself from prior work that has primarily focused on two-player games and explores the challenges that arise when the number of players increases. The newly devised algorithms address these new difficulties while providing guarantees on rationalizable behavior. The results include an analysis of the minimal number of samples required to learn CCE, CE, and rationalizable behavior in polynomial time, with relationships that hold across various numbers of players. In particular, it is demonstrated that the sample requirements increase exponentially with the number of players for the best-known general multiplayer games results, whereas the new results showcase polynomial relationships. In addition, the research explores the application of a novel approach to learning from full feedback information and leverages this to improve the efficiency of learning rationalizable behavior by a factor of the number of players. The resulting algorithm achieves the best-known guarantee on the number of samples required for this task. The research also identifies open questions regarding the sample requirements for learning equilibria in multiplayer games under full feedback information. The results have been validated through numerical experiments. The associated algorithms have been implemented and are available for public use. To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. Furthermore, the variance reduction based experience replay framework is highly versatile, integrating seamlessly with multiple algorithms. It only requires the calculation of a diversity metric, making it straightforward to apply to new scenarios. Our team employed high-resolution ARPES within a well-characterized Brillouin zone using high-quality (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ samples, taking into account the inherent limitations of this technique. Our results reveal the normally expected features near the zone center and edges, along with the expected superconducting gap sizes. Most intriguingly, we discovered a previously underreported 'flat band' feature near the zone center, and our analysis indicates it is a direct consequence of asymmetrical chemical doping. Within the superconducting state, we found this 'flat band' feature exhibits a relatively small superconducting gap of around 1.2 meV, which can be interpreted as a sign of a complex interband interaction. Moreover, our study highlights the significance of asymmetrical chemical doping and its impact on the band structure, offering a fresh perspective on the long-standing controversy surrounding these structures. Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in a 6.55 T magnetic field yielded distinct components, characterized by different temperature dependences in their recovery times, with one being temperature-linear and the other exhibiting more intricate temperature variation. These results demonstrate that the slow-recovering component is resistant to changes in LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness, while the fast-recovering component is significantly affected, displaying an opposing temperature dependence at smaller thicknesses. This complex phenomenon is explored to identify its underlying cause. Additionally, our results provide direct evidence for the presence of a spin-scattering mechanism, as observed in other metals with multiple spin states or those undergoing a transition, and this mechanism appears to persist across all LaNiO$_3$ layer thicknesses examined. Furthermore, we have observed a marked shift in the chemical shift of LaNiO$_3$ sites near the interface with LaAlO$_3$, which exhibits a subtle dependence on the LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness. In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns. Our study employs a rich, semantic representation called 
a Knowledge Chart to organize conversational dialogue. This representation holds 
multiple possible future lines of conversation until a final conclusion is 
reached. We introduce two novel tasks based on the MultiTalk Dataset. The first 
task, predicting the next line of conversation, demonstrates substantial gains 
over existing approaches through our newly devised Neural Semantic Planner. The 
second task, full conversation tree prediction, reveals the effectiveness of our 
Neural Semantic Planner when applying reinforcement learning. Both of these tasks 
demonstrate the capabilities and potential of the MultiTalk Dataset. Furthermore, 
the code and dataset are openly accessible at https://github.com/hpGD/MTTalk.

Our research is centered on enhancing the maximum achievable capacity in a wireless communication system, comprising multiple input and output antennas and a surface capable of intelligent signal reflection. To provide an accurate assessment, we take into consideration the impact of correlated signal weakening and a phenomenon in which the intensity and phase of the reflected signal are interconnected, often disregarded in theoretical studies. By employing a mathematical approach that accounts for the statistics of these phenomena, we are able to determine the maximum achievable capacity and establish a key relationship with the distribution of a certain type of random variable. Furthermore, we explore ways to implement and test this system using equipment that can generate and measure a variety of parameters. Through these tests, we verify the accuracy of our theoretical findings and demonstrate the optimal performance of this system when the intelligent reflecting surface is optimally designed. Additionally, we investigate ways to accomplish this efficiently by dividing the system into multiple, independently functioning components that can be optimized separately. Lastly, we discuss the potential applications and future directions of this research, including its use in addressing key challenges in the development of next-generation wireless communication systems.

We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of modified gravity theories, resulting in highly efficient simulations. For $f(R)$ gravity, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these models and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code excels at producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and offers significant computational benefits, delivering accurate results up to 10 times faster than competing codes on comparable simulation settings. MG-GLAM is compatible with the MP-GLAM library, which enables in-depth analysis of its predictions and allows for collaborative research. The code is now an integral part of the MaxPlanck-ESO-Wiely t gravity simulations and is available for public use through its website. Full documentation and a comprehensive set of simulations are provided for download and can also be accessed through a dedicated database. This will facilitate comparisons between theoretical predictions and observational data and facilitate collaborative research in the field of modified gravity. The code is designed to be versatile and can be adapted for use in various computational frameworks with N-body capabilities. The success of these simulations, in terms of their computational efficiency and accuracy, serves as a model for developing other modified gravity simulations in the future. This method uses an active flame brush model to take into account the effects of heat release fluctuations, in contrast to passive approaches that assume the flame brush can be treated independently of the upstream influences. By considering the effects of heat release fluctuations, this work demonstrates that noise amplitude can be reduced through the application of appropriate flame stabilization methods that minimize combustion variability. Additionally, this work shows that noise amplitude can be further reduced through the use of flame hold-down methods that minimize the flame brush's upstream extent. This work also demonstrates that noise frequency is primarily determined by the flame's quiescent properties, but that turbulence can cause a slight decrease in frequency due to the transport of heat and reactants across diffusion boundaries. This work builds upon previous work by extending the linear noise model to account for multiple fuel species and heat release fluctuations, and by incorporating the effects of turbulent mixing and combustion variability. This approach allows for a more accurate prediction of noise amplitude and frequency in multi-fuel jet flames. This work is a foundation for future studies aimed at expanding this approach to non-linear and rotating flames. This approach can also be applied to other complex flames, such as hydrogen and biofuels, by modifying the quiescent properties of the flame. This work can also be used to investigate the effects of turbulent mixing and combustion variability on noise amplitude and frequency through the use of Direct Numerical Simulations (DNS). This approach allows for a detailed examination of how turbulent mixing and combustion variability influence noise amplitude and frequency. Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific technique addressing this challenge is the Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT). Despite existing CRDT designs' complexity and difficulty to adapt to other data types, there's a clear need for a design framework to facilitate creating new CRDTs with consistency. We propose the RWF, a Remove-Win design framework that utilizes a conflict-resolution approach to update conflicts, allowing its application across various data types. Through the development of multiple examples, RWF's design versatility is demonstrated, showcasing its effectiveness in reducing design difficulties and making it an efficient tool for creating new CRDTs. Furthermore, RWF enables other design frameworks beyond traditional lattice-based approaches, and its design principles can be applied to develop other conflict-resolution mechanisms. Additionally, RWF facilitates distributed system performance optimization, allowing designers to fine-tune design components and assess the impact on system latency and memory usage. By providing a design framework that simplifies creating new CRDTs, RWF paves the way for the development of more sophisticated distributed systems. To support this initiative, the RWF design framework is available online at https://rfw.github.io. Additionally, the repository includes open-source implementations of various design patterns, including counters, sets, maps, multiset maps, counters with merge preferences, sorted sets, and sorted maps. To further aid designers in creating new CRDTs, the repository provides step-by-step guidelines and includes multiple, ready-to-use examples. These examples serve as a starting point for designers to create their own CRDTs, allowing them to adapt RWF's design components and experiment with different configurations. Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of relevant genomic features. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint influential genomic elements, based on their functional roles, among millions of potential candidates. This approach is applied to 92 traits from the NHGRI-GWAS catalog, using data on protein-coding gene functions and regulatory elements in various cell types, and demonstrates significant association with the identified key elements. Additionally, many of these associated elements are linked to multiple traits, suggesting they may play important roles in human physiology and disease. Furthermore, this approach identifies key elements associated with cancer-related traits and traits related to immune system function. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered. Additionally, about two-thirds of a population of 150 neutron star binaries studied have outbursts recurring more than ten years when detected by the MAXI telescope. This finding significantly diminishes the likelihood that a population of stellar mass black holes exists within the galaxy's center and contributes to a notable portion of the galaxy's overall black hole population. The proposed model also predicts that radio pulsar binaries, particularly those with longer recurrence times, are likely to be discovered as X-ray binaries shaping their radio profiles during outburst. This study further suggests that neutron star binaries observed as radio pulsars have a birth rate roughly half that of all neutron star binaries. Furthermore, to account for the detected and undiscovered neutron star binaries within the galaxy, the characteristic recurrence time of all such binaries is estimated to be approximately 50 years. The study also presents a theoretical framework to estimate the birth rate of neutron star binaries based on the observed pulsar population and compares it with the galaxy's overall neutron star birth rate as inferred from pulsar population studies, resulting in a likely margin of error of at least a factor of two for this calculation. THz radiation enables the precise stimulation of vibrational frequencies in molecules and crystals, leading to the introduction of inertial influences on electrons. By drawing a comparison to classical mechanics, where circular motion generates Coriolis and centrifugal forces, analogous effects arise, specifically spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, and the interplay of these forces with the spin-orbit and the redshift of energy levels. These effects can persist for a few picoseconds following the initial stimulation, and potentially amplifying their magnitude could make this approach a promising means of controlling localized quantum states and chemical reaction barriers via vibration. Although the effects of THz radiation on molecular bonds last only seconds, chemical reactions can sometimes take milliseconds, and reaction barriers might be affected, and the influence can extend to ions and crystals. However, the scope of these effects depends on the magnitude of the stimulation and the duration of the interaction. Furthermore, the need to develop new experimental techniques is also highlighted to observe these effects. The potential applications of these phenomena are numerous and could contribute to the development of new vibration-controlled quantum technologies. $\tau$-tilting theory was first introduced nearly a decade ago by Adachi, Iyama, and Reiten and has since become a major area of study in the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras. These notes have a dual purpose: to provide an approachable introduction to $\tau$-tilting theory for those with basic representation theory knowledge and to address a noticeable lack in the existing literature by bringing together key results from the field in a comprehensive overview. Building on this foundation, we will explore how the natural duality inherent in $\tau$-tilting theory can be utilized to provide new insights and facilitate the adaptation of its methods to other areas, including the representation theory of infinite-dimensional algebras and the study of duality in algebraic geometry. As such, these notes aim to inspire further research into the applications of $\tau$-tilting theory across a broader spectrum of mathematical disciplines. 

For the uninitiated, chapters one and two are designed to serve as a foundational introduction to the subject, covering the basic principles and key results from $\tau$-tilting theory. From there, chapter three will explore more advanced topics and examine the role of $\tau$-tilting theory in the context of representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras. Finally, chapter four will delve into the applications of $\tau$-tilting theory to the representation theory of infinite-dimensional algebras and the study of duality in algebraic geometry. 

Throughout these notes, examples and illustrative diagrams will be used to facilitate understanding, and numerous open problems and research directions will be posed to stimulate progress in the field. These notes are intended to culminate in a suitable resource for newcomers to the subject and a springboard for the continuation of research in $\tau$-tilting theory.

Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric that employs Natural Language Inference to gauge the semantic variety of responses generated by the model. Secondly, it presents a novel data augmentation technique rooted in counterfactual reasoning, which enhances the model's ability to generate distinct and relevant responses. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves substantial improvements in converational diversity and relevance. Moreover, the method exhibits a notable increase in performance when compared to alternative data augmentation techniques. The code and model are available for use at https://github.com/ghrua/ContDA.

The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. By comparing these simulations to observations of the Tolaria protostar, it's possible to estimate the likelihood of finding a similar object with comparable characteristics, including rotational properties, and determine if it could maintain hydrogen burning through gravitational collapse. Additionally, the study examines possible outcomes for objects like the Tolaria protostar, including both hydrogen-burning stars and objects more akin to protoplanets, and provides general guidelines for identifying objects on the mass spectrum that are transitioning between these states. Furthermore, the model is applied to evaluate the feasibility of objects like the Tolaria protostar forming through gravitational collapse, and to assess the potential for detecting similar objects in the Milky Way using upcoming surveys like Euclid and LSST. According to the simulations, objects like the Tolaria protostar can be formed through gravitational collapse, and could be identified in about 10% of stable star-forming regions, with the possibility of discovering up to several dozen candidates in the Milky Way over the course of a decade. However, only a small fraction of these objects are likely to be found as they will be embedded in molecular clouds and therefore hidden from view. Therefore, observations at infrared and millimeter wavelengths would be necessary to uncover these objects and open up the possibility of studying them in greater depth. Consequently, even if no evidence of objects like the Tolaria protostar is found in the near future, it's still possible that further research will uncover similar objects and provide valuable insights into the formation and evolution of low-mass stars. Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. In this study, we explore the relationship between the number of nodes split and the complexity of that scenario, specifically when that number is two, three, or four. When only two nodes need to be split, our algorithm achieves this task in linear time. However, when the number of nodes to be split increases to three or four, the problem becomes exponentially complex. When the number of nodes to be split is five or more, the problem becomes NP-complete. Additionally, a hybrid approach is proposed that first reduces edge crossings through an existing algorithm and then removes any remaining crossings by splitting nodes. This approach demonstrates superior performance in comparison to an alternative method which attempts to remove all edge crossings at once. As a result, this approach can effectively planarize many real-world graphs used for navigation, such as those depicting connections between locations on maps. Furthermore, an open-source implementation of this research is available online for public use. This implementation allows users to upload their own graphs, configure various visualization settings, and download the resulting planar graphs for further analysis. This implementation can be accessed through a web-based interface at this link: https://[user name].entitymap.org/. As an example, a graph representing connections between distinct groups of galaxies, which is available at this link: https://[user name].entitymap.org/#https://arxiv.org/pdf/1702.03532.pdf, may be used to demonstrate the capabilities of this research. This research has far-reaching potential to revolutionize the visualization of bipartite graphs, making it possible to provide clear and easy-to-understand visualizations of complex connections across distinct groups of objects. As a result, this research may have a significant impact on various fields of science, where visualizations of bipartite graphs are commonly used, such as astronomy, social networks, and map visualization.
