Deep neural network approaches have achieved great success in various AI tasks, particularly in image recognition tasks, yet some challenges remain unresolved. The issue of processing continuous visual data streams and dealing with unbalanced datasets in the learning process continues to persist. Past research has tackled these issues independently, despite their concurrent presence in real-world applications. In this work, we address the challenge of learning incrementally from datasets that are not only unbalanced but also grow over time. We examine algorithms that rely on a fixed decision boundary and find that they fail to adapt to new classes due to their inability to adjust the boundary based on the data distribution. We then propose a method that uses an adaptive boundary inspired by the Fisher Linear Discriminant analysis to resolve the issue. In experiments, our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to fixed-boundary algorithms when confronted with growing datasets, albeit slightly outperformed by a method using an infinitely adaptable boundary. Notably, our method excels in datasets with a stable distribution of classes. We further investigate the challenge of handling massive datasets with significant class imbalances and introduce the Super Sample algorithm to overcome it. The algorithm selectively expands minority classes to create more representative samples, thereby reducing the class imbalance. We employ this algorithm to cure the imbalances encountered during the incremental learning process. Our results show substantial improvements compared to fixing the boundary based on current classes, and we achieve the best performance when the algorithm is repeatedly applied across all classes. We test our approach on two growing datasets and one dataset that mimics a real-world scenario with class imbalances and continuous visual data streams. This paper will present our approach to optimizing bipedal robot walking assisted by thrusters, using a nonlinear control technique. By assuming that the thrusters' acceleration can be directly controlled and considering the dynamics of the robot's lower limbs, we leverage nonlinear feedback control to achieve the desired gait. However, implementing this method on actual robots is challenging due to the requirement of precise thruster acceleration measurements and the generation of continuous control signals. The application of thrusters results in thruster and joint accelerations being closely linked, which complicates the implementation of high-gain nonlinear feedback control. To overcome these difficulties, we propose modifying the controller to use state estimates and a slower loop for the thrusters, which allows us to successfully test our approach with an amphibious robot named ZJU-HHRR-1. The robot was capable of transitioning from walking to swimming and back again during our experiments. The results show that feedback control can help reduce the thrusters' acceleration and the robot's joints during the transition phases, which in turn reduces the impact and accelerates the transition. The approach we took and the findings we obtained with the robot underscore the potential of using thrusters to enhance the capabilities of bipedal robots. The proposed method may also be applicable to other multi-domain robots that can transition between different environments. Becker-Denef-Lipschitz first observed in 1979 that over finite fields $k$, the total residue map $\text{res}$ from Laurent series to $k$ is expressible in a specific language, provided $t$ is included as a parameter. This discovery motivated further research into the properties of a specific mathematical theory related to valued fields. In the course of these investigations, the authors proved that this theory does not have a certain desirable feature and demonstrated that, for infinite fields $k$, the associated power series fields cannot be computationally decided. This, in turn, led to an analogous undecidability conclusion for a specific complex-valued field of power series. It was also demonstrated that, when the field $k$ is equipped with a linear form, the total residue map can be computed using a formula that explicitly incorporates the values of the functions at the base field and that this formula is a formula of the associated theory. Building on this result, the authors proved that, for fields $k$ that are equipped with a linear form and have a specific property, the associated power series fields can be computationally decided. It was further demonstrated that this property is equivalent to another property that is closely related to the first one mentioned above. This, in turn, led to an undecidability conclusion for a specific field of Laurent series. The authors also established that, for fields $k$ that are equipped with a linear form, the associated power series fields can be computationally decided if and only if the associated fields of Laurent series are computationally decided. This research was motivated by, and is relevant to, open problems identified by Denef and Lipshitz in 1979. It essentially provides a comprehensive answer to these problems. The studies described in this paper also address related questions concerning the computability of valuation rings, the complexity of polynomial rings with a linear form, and the computational decision properties of fields with a linear form, providing a complete answer to these questions as well. These investigations are, in turn, grounded in an exploration of the properties of a specific mathematical theory related to valued fields, involving the application of a particular approach that draws on tools from model theory, computable mathematics, and algebraic geometry. Our findings reveal that, given the present experimental constraints on the Higgs sector, its contribution to the anomaly could still be significant, assuming the Higgs interacts non-standardly with other particles. Based on unitarity principles, we found that a solution to the anomaly could imply the presence of New Physics at an energy scale of roughly 10-18 TeV, which could potentially be as low as 5 TeV if the Higgs' interaction with the W and Z bosons is in line with Standard Model predictions. The proposed EFT framework can be put to the test through the study of Higgs boson production in association with two muons at existing and future colliders. A localized alteration in knot diagrams is referred to as an unknotting operation. It can be demonstrated that any knot diagram can be converted into a trivial unknot through a sequence of unknotting operations, combined with some variations in the diagram configuration, which are referred to as Reidemeister moves. Unknotting operations hold significant value in the field of knot theory; they serve a purpose in analyzing the intricacy of knots and knot-related properties. Moreover, they also have implications in the fields of biology, chemistry, and physics for studying complexly intertwined structures of molecules, substances, and DNA. The purpose of this paper was to introduce a novel type of unknotting operation, which is called the diagonal move, applicable to classical and welded knots. The study shows that the cross-over change, the delta-move, the sharp-move, the gamma-move, the n-gon move, the pass move, and the 4-move can be achieved by applying a sequence of diagonal moves. The study also delves into defining a distance measure that originates from the diagonal move, as well as examining its characteristics. The concept of the distance measure is found to be extendable to classical and welded knots in the classical and welded knot spaces, while it is not transitive in the welded knot space. The study also explores the relationship between the biaxial move, which is a local alteration, and the 4-move, which is an unknotting operation, revealing that the 4-move can be derived from a sequence of biaxial moves, although the converse is not true. The study further reveals that there are knots that require the biaxial move to convert them into a trivial unknot. The study also introduces the notion of the minimum number of k-type unknotting operations needed to convert a knot into a trivial unknot, which is denoted as the k-unknotting number. The study then determines the 4-unknotting number, which is found to be 3. The study also examines the 2-unknotting number and the 3-unknotting number as well. We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve has a finite set of generators over a specific semifield. This involves identifying a particular finite set that generates the semifield. Furthermore, for finite harmonic mappings between tropical curves, the rational function semifield of the first curve can be expressed as a finite set of elements over the pull-back of the rational function semifield of the second curve. Additionally, we explore two specific semifields: one defined by maximum and addition on the real numbers, demonstrating it is a rational function semifield for certain finite harmonic mappings: it also relates to the Bruhat order. In this context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables several entities to train a robust machine learning model jointly, without exchanging sensitive information about their data. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. Given its versatility, vertical FL is deemed particularly suitable for collaborative training by major enterprises. Two applicable attacks are outlined, one being a customized version of the well-known inverse matrix method, and the other an iterative attack suitable for reduced-dimension scenarios. Our empirical study validates the efficacy of these attacks across various configurations, including various machine learning models and data sets. Neural language models have significantly impacted the field of natural language processing due to their effectiveness, but they can be computationally costly and have limited ability to capture language knowledge. Despite this, the high-quality language models are still required for various applications that rely on them in real-time systems. A group of researchers introduced a method to enhance the performance of neural language models using the statistical $n$-gram models, specifically long short-term memory (LSTM) and transformer models. They discovered that combining the two models resulted in an almost 50% reduction in errors and almost 90% of the performance of the high-demand models, achieving this with only a fraction of the computational cost. This successful approach can be applied to other applications that require significant system resources. Additionally, they found that the performance improvement was attributed to the $n$-gram models accurately identifying the parts of speech and significantly reducing the number of system errors caused by misidentifying word contexts. This technique to enhance neural language models is now available as an open-source tool.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Additionally, our approach overcomes the limitation of cross-pose face modeling by demonstrating the ability to generate accurate 3D faces in novel poses not seen during training. The code and model are available for download at https://github.com/ghoulative/SADRNet.

A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. Furthermore, our research indicates a possible solution - offering price incentives that align with the storage units' risk preferences. By doing so, we could potentially increase the effectiveness of price signals in managing storage units' behavior, leading to a more stable and efficient operation of the grid. Additionally, our results highlight the importance of considering the storage units' risk preferences when designing auction mechanisms, and reveal that a strategy that allocates optimal risk levels can result in significant benefits for both the storage units and the grid, with potential gains exceeding 10% of total revenues. Our work also provides a theoretical framework for evaluating the storage units' risk levels, which could be used to design more effective risk management strategies that take into account the unique characteristics of energy storage systems. Lastly, our study suggests that the value of this approach could be further increased through the integration of weather forecasts, the management of peaking services, and the permissable deviation of storage units from their scheduled dispatch levels. Overall, our work offers a novel framework for modeling the behavior of risk-conscious energy storage systems, and provides a suite of tools that are relevant to various grid management tasks. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as part of this study. When looking at small-sized samples, a well-defined, quantized resistance was observed at low temperatures when these samples were placed in a magnetic field, and the associated Hall voltage showed an exact quantization. This quantization of the Hall voltage is an indication of a perfect, one-to-one correspondence between the charge carriers and the edge states at the sample edges. These edge states form in a specific, helical pattern when there is a magnetic field present. When examining larger samples, a more intricate pattern of resistance quantization was seen at low temperatures. This pattern includes multiple, closely-spaced plateaus in both the longitudinal and Hall resistance. Both theoretical calculations and experimental findings indicate that the number of plateaus in these resistance graphs directly correlates with the number of helical edge states present. Additionally, the spacing between these states directly correlates with the width of the corresponding resistance plateaus. Wireless communication systems can make significant contributions to preventing road accidents through alert message transmission, particularly in high-risk areas like road intersections. Non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) has shown promise for 5G systems, and our proposed adaptive cooperative NOMA (ACN) protocol enhances VC's performance in this area. In a scenario where vehicles on intersecting roads generate interfering signals, we develop a mathematical model for calculating the outage probability of the ACN protocol and provide analytical expressions for the results. By comparing the ACN protocol to existing alternatives, we demonstrate that ACN yields a substantial improvement in outage probability at road intersections. Furthermore, Monte Carlo simulations verify our theoretical findings. The ACN protocol's superiority can provide safer and more reliable communication systems in vehicular networks. Additionally, our work lays the groundwork for exploring other NOMA systems in this context.

In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, turning a critical problem into an NP-hard mixed-integer non-convex challenge. We've developed an efficient and localized solution, separating power allocation and scheduling processes, first assigning power independently to cells, followed by a non-cooperative game determining scheduling modes, with payoffs calculated according to the level of interference and required cell communication. Simulations, set in an outdoor scenario with multiple small cells, reveal our method outperforms static TDD solutions. Despite numerous theories, there has not been a clear understanding of the Hall anomaly observed in type-II superconductors, particularly in their mixed-state Hall resistivity. This study involved an in-depth examination of the magnetotransport measurements conducted on BSCCO thin films, as presented in Zhao et al.'s 2019 paper, to confirm a previously suggested theory proposing that the Hall anomaly arises from vacancies moving within pinned fragments of the vortex lattice. This proposed mechanism is validated by analyzing the vortex states near the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition in the vortex crystal and by comparing the measured activation energies to the calculated creation energy of the vortex-anti-vortex pair and the vacancy energy in the flux-line lattice. No adjustments were required in the calculations, providing a comprehensive theoretical foundation and prerequisites for the vacancy model. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the necessity for considering the vacancy activation energy in the disorder-dependent phase diagram of type-II superconductors. This study provides a clear understanding of the Hall anomaly and sets the stage for exploring vacancy-related phenomena in the vortex state. This understanding can be utilized to improve the transport properties of type-II superconductors by controlling vacancy activation energies at the material level. This knowledge may also be applied to other systems featuring lattice defects and interacting topological defects. This understanding of the Hall anomaly through vacancy activation energy enables the development of more precise theories that describe the interplay between vortex-anti-vortex pairs and vacancies in the flux-line lattice, a crucial aspect of the vortex state near the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition. Researchers suggest employing high-order cumulants and factorial cumulants of conserved charges to gain insight into the dynamics of strongly interacting systems undergoing phase transitions. These conserved charges exhibit fixed point behavior under renormalization group transformations, offering a detailed understanding of how pre- and post-collision factors influence their values. The properties of these cumulants can be investigated using lattice field theory techniques, and studies have already examined the effects of temperature, chemical potential, and spatial volume on the cumulants. However, the dynamics of expanding systems complicates the interpretation of data from heavy-ion collision experiments. The initial conditions and evolution of these systems make it challenging to connect the observed cumulant behavior directly to the properties of the QCD fixed points. Nonetheless, the complexity of the expansion can be accounted for through the introduction of relevant and irreducible cumulants, allowing the connection of observable cumulants to the underlying QCD fixed points. The relationship between the observed cumulants and the corresponding QCD fixed points is explored in a parameter space that encompasses the critical endpoint and the deconfinement transition. The proposed analysis is expected to guide theoretical models in interpreting the results of cumulant measurements and comparing them with first-principle simulations. A characterization of finite-dimensional commuting squares of C*-algebras, resulting in hyperfinite type II_1 subfactors of finite index and depth, is provided, utilizing Morita equivalent unitary fusion categories. We extend the characterization to strongly faithful half-braid natural transformations from the Drinfeld center to the tensor unit, obtaining resources that enable us to characterize strongly integrable boundary conditions for topological quantum field theories of hyperfinite type II_1 index and finite depth. Additionally, this allows us to establish the equivalence to the problem of characterizing strongly integrable boundary conditions for topological quantum field theories, given a type II_1 factor of finite index and depth. We then leverage this framework to solve a variant of the Bost-Connes quantum statistical mechanics algebra's vanishing invariant problem, resulting in the integration of the algebra into the context of topological quantum field theory and the identification of a strongly integrable boundary condition for this algebra. We also prove the solvability of the dynamical system associated with this algebra and the resulting strongly integrable boundary condition. We conclude by establishing the connection to the $\mathbb{Z}$-graded version of the 3-manifolds invariants discussed in the paper by the third author, collecting the results in the context of the universal quantum invariant discussed in the paper by the first author.

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model with only a limited increase in training data. The results show that this approach leads to a significant reduction in errors and delivers a notable improvement in the model's reliability. Moreover, we observed that the model's trustworthiness is maintained even when subjected to a different distribution of instances, indicating that it does not suffer from overfitting. We also applied this system to a real-world dataset consisting of images, where it was able to minimize the difference between predicted probabilities and actual outcomes, thereby enhancing the model's safety. The code for this project is available on an open-source platform noted in the paper.

In x-ray image analysis, identifying prohibited items contributes to maintaining public safety. However, the difficulty lies in detecting low-contrast, color-less objects which can result in unsatisfactory performance. Until now, there have been limited studies in this field due to the absence of high-quality specialized datasets. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel dataset named High-quality X-ray (HiXray), which contains a comprehensive collection of 8 prohibited item categories and comprises 102,928 high-quality images. These images are extracted from real-world airport security inspections and annotated by experienced security personnel. Moreover, to enhance the accuracy of prohibited item detection, we introduce a Lateral Inhibition Module, which emulates the human ability to disregard irrelevant information and focus on distinguishing characteristics. By incorporating a flexible module and leveraging Bidirectional Propagation and Boundary Activation modules, LIM successfully minimizes noise and accentuates identifiable features from multiple directions. Experimental results on HiXray and OPIXray demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing detection approaches. A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Notably, $J_n^T$ yields invariants for virtual and biperiodic links, providing an instance of volume conjecture behavior in a virtual link. Additionally, we outline a relationship between $J_n^T$ and the colored Iowa state sum model, and propose a definition for a link's intrinsic volume, defined as the norm of the link's representation in biperiodic SU(2). Lastly, we demonstrate how $J_n^T$ can be used to investigate the volume conjecture for links in a thickened sphere of arbitrary genus.

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge for enhanced performance.  Additionally, multiple data augmentation techniques have been discovered to be valuable tools in natural language processing tasks.  Building on prior work incorporating BERT and WordNet knowledge, this study explores various data augmentation techniques in context-gloss pairs to enhance the efficacy of WSD.  Experimental results indicate that both sentence and word-level augmentation strategies are effective in addressing WSD, while the incorporation of hypernyms' definitions from a lexical knowledge base can further improve performance.  A comparative analysis of different context-gloss augmentation techniques is conducted, revealing that the application of back translation to definitions produces the most satisfactory outcomes.  The proposed method achieves the best overall outcome in comparison to existing methods, as validated by both manual and machine-based evaluations. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. Additionally, measurements were taken of the ratio of top quark production cross sections in proton-lead and proton-proton collisions, yielding a value of 0.34±0.09 (statistical) ± 0.05 (systematic) times the corresponding result from quantum chromodynamics predictions. These findings contribute to a better understanding of top quark behavior in nuclear environments and provide a basis for exploring top quark interactions with other particles in future studies. These results were initially published as an abstract in the Physical Review Letters journal on April 29, 2019, and have since been expanded into a full research article available under the title "Measurement of the cross section for t t̅ production in proton-lead collisions at 8.16 TeV" in the Physical Review Letters journal on May 29, 2019. That article was subsequently updated on August 28, 2019. The research was based on data collected by the CMS collaboration at the LHC in 2015 and incorporated elements of the Effective Field Theory formalism in its analysis. The research was supported by funding and resources from various institutions and organizations worldwide. The underlying topology of this research has relevance to the search for exclusive diphoton production in proton-proton collisions at 5.02 TeV and 8 TeV, which was the focus of an earlier study conducted by the ATLAS collaboration. That study, published as "Search for exclusive diphoton production in pp collisions at sqrt(s) = 7.62 TeV" in the Physical Review Letters journal on April 29, 2013, yielded a 95% confidence threshold for background-only hypotheses but ultimately did not produce a measurable signal. The ATLAS collaboration has subsequently conducted a review of the methodology employed in that study and has initiated a new analysis of the data using an Effective Field Theory approach

This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for relevance matching. Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering that many existing parsers overlook value filling in synthesized SQL. Experiments on the Spider dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over baseline models in terms of execution and exact set match accuracy when database contents are inaccessible, with further analysis pointing to areas for future improvement. The implemented code can be found at https://github.com/ghrua/zspt2sql. The study is also accompanied by a live demo at https://www.sqlzero.sh/. The paper has been accepted for presentation at EMNLP 2021.

In this research, we propose a method to automatically generate complex road networks for testing the limits of autonomous lane-keeping technology in simulation. By using a set of control points to create a parametric road design, we define a driving task that an equipped vehicle must perform. Modifying the control points significantly impacts the road's overall shape and layout. Our approach leverages optimization techniques to identify a set of control points that creates challenging driving conditions, causing the vehicle to veer off its intended path. We validated our method with three distinct testing scenarios, demonstrating its effectiveness. Furthermore, our results indicate that our approach can discover highly relevant test cases for the vehicle's lane-keeping system in a significantly shorter time compared to human-generated tests. Additionally, we showcase how our method can be applied to target specific components of the vehicle's lane-keeping system. To facilitate replication and advancement of our work, we are making our implementation publicly available. By automating the creation of challenging road scenarios, we can more efficiently and effectively test the limits of autonomous vehicle technologies. Alongside this work, we are also exploring the potential applications of this method to other autonomous system challenges. Our findings suggest that this approach has broad utility in developing and testing autonomous vehicle systems, and we believe it can contribute to the development of more robust and reliable lane-keeping technology. To facilitate user discovery, product recommendations are often accompanied by descriptions. The rise of personalized music playlists through automatic recommendation introduces the challenge of creating descriptive metadata. This paper introduces an innovative approach called music captioning, which leverages audio content analysis and natural language processing to effectively summarize the tracks within each playlist. Although individual song analysis techniques can be applied to caption music playlists, our research demonstrates that a more efficient approach involves concurrent audio processing and subsequent natural language inference to create more coherent and accurate descriptions. We tested this approach using two distinct methods: a sequence-to-sequence model trained on labeled audio data and a more practical solution involving transfer learning with convolutional neural networks processing Mel-frequency spectral features. The results show that music captioning can learn to generate meaningful and relevant descriptions, even without explicit audio feature engineering. Moreover, the paper explores various music captioning applications, illustrating the potential for this technology to enhance the user experience of music recommendation platforms and provide valuable metadata for music databases. Additionally, we investigate the limitations of the approach and suggest directions for future research and improvements. The code and data used in this research are available online for further exploration and improvement of music captioning techniques.

Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Contextual Action Proposal Network, which incorporates contextual information through semi-supervised proposal refinement and context-augmented features, yielding high-quality proposals with strong semantic uniqueness. Our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods by achieving significant accuracy improvements on the ActivityNet dataset. At the time of submission, our code has already been openly shared for further development and improvement.

A recently investigated explanation suggests these structures form when magnetic field eddies caused by edge-localized modes trigger the development of a PTM seed island. However, this study instead seeks to provide an alternate explanation, one which posits that PTM are a manifestation of the edge plasma's inherent turbulence. Edge turbulence gives rise to distinct features known as 'holes' and 'filaments', which maintain parallel currents and overall symmetry. Edge turbulence also exhibits a symmetry-breaking influence of the toroidal mode. Within this framework, the peculiar orientation of the magnetic field in PTM can be accounted for by a turbulence-driven edge current that wraps around the torus. Additionally, the observed long-lived nature of PTM may result from a balance between this current and any plasma motions that seek to disrupt it, with the former slowly being eroded by edge breather modes. This theory is further supported by observations of PTM in different locations across the JET tokamak. This research focuses on resolving collision avoidance for non-holonomic robots moving at constant speeds in a two-dimensional space, leveraging dynamic vortex potential fields and their gradients to create cooperative behavior between the robots. A variable repulsive force field, sensitive to velocity and position of nearby robots, is introduced to prevent the emergence of local minima, and only activates when a robot approaches a potential collision with other mobile robots or stationary objects. It's demonstrated through kinematic analysis that a cooperating robot can evade non-cooperative robots moving at constant speeds or actively attempting to collide, under conditions specified by potential field parameters, and this cooperative approach is verified through experiments using a mobile robot platform. Data from these experiments is used to refine the variables influencing the robots' movement dynamics in real-world scenarios. Additionally, the performance of this cooperative approach is evaluated using a simulation of multiple robots moving at constant speeds. Lastly, the potential for extending this cooperative framework to include robots moving at varying speeds is explored. This non-holonomic robot collision avoidance system could serve as a basis for developing more complex cooperative behaviors, making it suitable for applications requiring multiple mobile robots to work together seamlessly.

Recent advancements in wireless communications research have led to increasing interest in the Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology. Comprised of passive reflective components that can modulate the characteristics of incoming waveforms, such as phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization, an IRS offers a means to actively control the characteristics of wireless channels. Given its promising properties, researchers are looking into the potential of incorporating IRS technology into radar systems to enhance target parameter estimation. This paper provides a theoretical basis for implementing IRS technology in radar systems, with a particular focus on scenarios where the line-of-sight (LOS) link between the radar and target is obstructed. We investigate the potential of utilizing IRS technology to create a virtual non-line-of-sight (NLOS) link, effectively treating the target as if it were in a line-of-sight position. We examine various IRS-enabled communication scenarios, including those involving single and multi-target scenarios, as well as scenarios involving the transmission of raw data and the implementation of the Monte Carlo method to evaluate the effectiveness of this approach. Our results demonstrate that IRS technology has the potential to significantly improve target parameter estimation, even in scenarios where the LOS link is obstructed. Additionally, we investigate different IRS-enabled communication scenarios, including those involving single and multi-target scenarios, as well as scenarios involving the transmission of raw data. Our findings indicate that IRS technology can generate up to 10 dB of additional signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and achieve a 70% reduction in mean absolute error (MAE) for angle estimation. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of various IRS sizes and radar wave characteristics on the performance of target parameter estimation. Our results also demonstrate the applicability of our approach to real-world scenarios, incorporating the characteristics of wireless communications systems. Lastly, our work paves the way for further research into the capabilities of IRS technology in radar systems. Through the evaluation of various IRS designs and their impact on target parameter estimation, we are able to identify key factors that influence performance, including the dimensions of the target, frequency of operation, shape of the target, and characteristics of the radar wave. Consequently, our work presents novel approaches for designing optimized radar waves capable of accurately estimating target parameters, even in scenarios where the line-of-sight link is obstructed. We also present novel metrics for evaluating the performance of target parameter estimation, taking into account the unique characteristics of wireless communications systems. Following the success of pretraining techniques in learning representations, various methods utilizing pre-trained models in continual learning have been developed. Some of these approaches build upon the pre-trained representations by implementing mechanisms for continual learning with minimal or no updates to the backbone models. In this study, we challenge the necessity of complex models by comparing a basic alternative we devised. We propose that a pre-trained feature extractor can achieve high performance in continual learning tasks by simply extracting the extracted features, without the need for additional components. To support this proposal, we developed a straightforward task-to-task adaptation method based on interpolation and achieved notable results. Our results indicate that our method surpasses existing complex methods utilizing pre-trained models and our proposed method proves to be a more efficient and effective approach. Furthermore, our results show that our proposed method delivers high performance and can be applied to various datasets, including MiniImageNet, CUB-200-2011, and tiered-ImageNet. Additionally, we observed that our method's performance is highly versatile and compatible with various data augmentation techniques, including cutmix and FMX, which can be used to enhance the performance even further. Approximately nine years ago, Azrieli and Shmaya introduced a category of $\lambda$-Lipschitz games where each player's payoff function is influenced by a $\lambda$-Lipschitz rate in response to other players' actions. Their work demonstrated that these types of games achieve the level of $\lambda$-approximate equilibria with payoff utilities of at most $2\lambda$ and can be computed via a randomized algorithm operating within a polynomial time frame in relation to the input parameters, albeit with the side effect of increasing the equilibrium precision to a degree of $n$ that is directly proportional to the number of players. In contrast, a diverse range of recent works have established the capacity to find $\epsilon$-approximate equilibria in a diverse range of $\lambda$-Lipschitz games through deterministic algorithms operating within a polynomial time frame in relation to the input parameters, with the degree of $\epsilon$ being directly proportional to the minimum of $\lambda$ and the fraction $\lambda$ divided by the number of players. However, the ability to find a diverse range of $\epsilon$-approximate equilibria with a $\lambda$-Lipschitz feature has remained an unsolved problem for quite some time. In our work, we introduce a diverse range of $\lambda$-Lipschitz games characterized by integer payoffs and establish the capacity to find a diverse range of $\lambda$-approximate equilibria within a polynomial time frame in relation to the input parameters. Furthermore, our work results in an extension of the Myerson-Satterfield theorem to a diverse range of $\lambda$-Lipschitz games characterized by integer payoffs. In our work, the value of $\frac{n\lambda}{\lambda}$ is replaced by a more optimal $\lambda$ that is directly proportional to the logarithm of the number of players. In our analysis, we introduce an diverse range of multi-unit auction mechanisms that are characterized by integer payoffs and provide evidence that these mechanisms give rise to $\lambda$-Lipschitz games. Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Moreover, the time-consuming process of conducting multiple validations for various parameters hinders the use of cross-validation for model optimization. To address this, we present a quick validation method that can be used in place of traditional k-fold CV. By combining the results of multiple rapid validations, we establish a method for parameter tuning. The proposed method is efficient, user-friendly, and applicable to a wide range of machine learning models. Additionally, we explore ways to further enhance performance through enhancement of quick validation methods and data preprocessing. The advantages of this method are demonstrated through its application to common machine learning algorithms, including support vector machines, random forests, and neural networks. Deep Neural Networks with vast parameters have faced challenges in real-time deployment, prompting the utilization of Teacher-Student architectures in knowledge distillation. Initially used to achieve comparable performance with smaller student networks, these architectures have now been applied across various knowledge learning objectives such as knowledge distillation, expansion, adaptation, and multi-task learning. Current research leveraging Teacher-Student architectures has successfully combined multiple teaching directions into a single process and has achieved notable outcomes. This paper delves into the workings and variations of Teacher-Student architectures and explores the possible reasons behind their success and resulting enhanced performance. It also explores novel Teacher-Student architecture frameworks that incorporate several teacher directions, including a proposed general Teacher-Student architecture framework compatible with multiple learning objectives. This framework is then applied in a practical setting to facilitate the knowledge learning of deep neural networks. Experimental outcomes validate the proposed framework's effectiveness, also providing insight into possible reasons behind its performance enhancements. The paper also explores the possible reasons behind the success of Teacher-Student architectures and provides code for the described methods on https://github.com/zhengdw/TSArchs. It also provides the experimental outcomes on https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/_.mw–-QyQ5s.

When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for understanding this transition through a unified perspective that incorporates various theories. They draw from existing models of shear-induced state transitions to identify common principles, incorporating concepts such as stress-sensitive interactions, localized ordering, and grain rearrangement to create a simplified, universal framework. This proposed framework can be applied across a broad spectrum of systems, predicting the existence of a common pathway that governs the transition from stress-induced shear thickening to rigidity. Furthermore, they suggest that viscosity's relationship to the shear rate can be understood as a result of the stress-dependent nature of this transition, and that the formation of shear-induced microstructures can be explained by a combination of ordering and grain rearrangement. Additionally, they recognize that the universality of this transition is reflected in the diversity of systems that exhibit stress-induced shear thickening, and that the transition's onset can be influenced by other factors such as normal stress and shear-induced aggregation. Lastly, they propose that the proposed framework can be validated through the study of the shear-induced state transition's hysteresis behavior.

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. In addition, we found that this exact algorithm can be used to significantly improve the accuracy of results in situations where the null hypothesis is consistently rejected, even when the alternative hypothesis is not supported by additional data. We also introduced two new exact algorithms for calculating paired-permutation test results. One of these exact algorithms is particularly efficient and has the advantage of being much simpler to implement than the other options. In order to make this exact algorithm available to a broader audience, we've included a sample implementation in Python that can be easily adapted for use in various machine learning settings. In our evaluation, we explored the benefits of using this exact algorithm in relation to testing the statistical significance of performance variations in two different NLP systems, one involving neural language models and the other involving text classification. In both cases, we found that using this exact algorithm resulted in significantly more accurate results compared to the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation. As a result of our research, we're providing an efficient exact algorithm that can be used by machine learning researchers to compute paired-permutation test results. A comprehensive dataset of freight rates, shipping quantities, new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrapped ship prices has been assembled from 1966 to 2009 for the six primary shipping routes. Furthermore, instructions on combining and verifying datasets are provided using the knowledge of shipping industry specialists and former top executives. A descriptive analysis of previously unstudied market phenomena known as the "container crisis" is conducted with this data. Structural changes in the data variables are then identified to demonstrate how the dissolution of shipping monopolies affected market behavior. Finally, antitrust policies aimed at breaking up combined shipping companies are evaluated to determine their effect on the industry. These policies, which occurred in 1980 for two specific routes and in 1995 for the others, are treated as natural experiments to analyze how the industry would have behaved without these events. A machine learning approach is applied to an industry transaction history and predicted outcomes are compared with actual ship scrapping decisions. The results indicate that companies would have scrapped more ships in the absence of anticompetitive behavior, highlighting the significant negative impact of monopolies on efficient ship utilization. Graph neural networks have excelled in multiple applications by leveraging relational data. These models combine node features with the graph structure, creating flexible and effective models, but they can be challenging to interpret due to their implicit representation of node interactions and graph connectivity. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called Kedge, which involves explicitly reducing unnecessary graph edges by selectively removing neighboring nodes. By utilizing the Hard Kumaraswamy distribution for edge sparsification, Kedge enables a flexible integration with existing GNN models through gradient-based optimization. Experiments demonstrate that Kedge effectively prunes a substantial proportion of graph edges with minimal accuracy degradation. Notably, Kedge achieved a reduction of over 80% of edges on the PubMed dataset with only a 2% decrease in accuracy, indicating that node features have a more significant impact than graph connectivity. Furthermore, Kedge effectively mitigates the over-smoothing issue prevalent in deep GNNs by maintaining robust task performance even with multiple GNN layers. Source code is available at https://github.com/ghrua/Kedge. Experimental results are hosted at https://kedge-graph.com/.

A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more resilient estimator was proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances the safety by a factor of k (with k being the number of key components) when compared to prior studies on CountSketch sketches. Furthermore, this improved estimator can be used to handle varying input vectors by incorporating a new technique called Dynamic CountSketch. Theoretical guarantees for both the general and dynamic cases are provided, involving specific bounds on the number of necessary queries, error magnitude, and estimated key component sizes. Additionally, this method was applied to improve the current state-of-the-art results for several fundamental problems, such as finding the largest entry of a vector, identifying the top elements of a vector, and estimating the norm of a vector. The proposed approach was also tested on real-world datasets, yielding superior performance when compared to alternative sketching techniques. The implementation of the suggested algorithm, along with the associated source code, can be found on the corresponding GitHub repository. The code also includes the implementation of the Dynamic CountSketch sketches. Effective management of controllable loads relies on the strategic deployment of aggregators that can efficiently convey their flexible capabilities, referred to as aggregate flexibility, to system operators. Current approaches typically involve time-consuming estimates, with minimal focus on real-time coordination between aggregators and operators. This paper proposes a solution to an online optimization problem within a closed-loop system by introducing a real-time feedback mechanism known as maximum entropy feedback (MEF). Analytical properties of MEF are examined, and it is shown that MEF can be approximated through reinforcement learning and utilized as a penalty term in the penalized predictive control (PPC) algorithm, an adaptation of model predictive control (MPC). Key benefits of our approach include (1) reduced communication demands for operators, requiring only MEF information, (2) faster computational processing due to lower variable counts, and (3) lower operational costs, with certain assumptions indicating optimal performance. The proposed PPC is evaluated on an adaptive electric vehicle charging dataset, yielding superior outcomes compared to traditional MPC methods. This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories (EFTs), focusing on beyond-Standard Model Higgs physics. Initially, we consider the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and then compare the predictions with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). Our primary analysis concerns the double Higgs production process in the two EFTs through the dominant subprocess $WW \to HH$. We calculate the cross-section of this subprocess for all polarization channels and relevant effective operators at various energies, and then explore the detectability of the double Higgs boson signal at the aforementioned colliders with the relevant effective operators. We find that while the SMEFT case can be detectable up to $\mathcal{O}(10) \, \textrm{TeV}$ scale, the HEFT case, specifically for the φ4 type, can be detectable only up to $\mathcal{O}(3.5)$ TeV. Nevertheless, if the double Higgs production is mediated by a heavy scalar in the HEFT, the process can be more accessible when studying the decay of the Higgs boson into a pair of photons. Additionally, we examine the benefits of studying the double Higgs production to a pair of bottom quarks at CLIC, given its larger cross-section and lower background compared to the dominant subprocess $WW \to HH$. Lastly, we investigate the potential of the ILC to complement CLIC in discovering the double Higgs production, and determine that the optimal design for the ILC, in the context of this research, is an electron energy of 1 TeV, a luminosity of 100 fb$^{-1}$ at that energy, and a total design energy scale of 1 TeV, which can lead to a precision of 0.49σ in the case of the dominant subprocess $WW \to HH$. Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges due to their large configuration spaces and the difficulties associated with evaluating their performance. Recently, researchers have made progress in this area using probabilistic models in Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO), a technique that rapidly converges to optimal configurations by exploiting expert-provided contextual information about the system's structure. Despite its effectiveness, the SBO approach has limited adoption due to the complexity involved in building probabilistic models. To address this issue, we introduce BoAnon, an SBO framework that enables the discovery of system structures from logs, allowing for the incorporation of expert knowledge. By combining this learned structure with expert-provided performance models and dependency information, BoAnon generates a probabilistic graph model. This model accelerates the optimization process, allowing BoAnon to identify efficient configurations significantly faster than existing methods. Through evaluation of a hardware architecture search problem, BoAnon demonstrates a notable improvement in energy-latency objectives, achieving a 5-7x factor improvement over the default architecture. The innovative approach of BoAnon, based on its contextual structure learning pipeline, now makes SBO applicable to various computer systems, such as databases and stream processors. Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has surged exponentially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, enabling seamless machine readability and interconnectivity.  While such datasets provide numerous opportunities and facilitate numerous applications including those related to semantic search, reasoning, and big data analysis, many of these datasets are of poor quality, containing errors that hinder proper machine reasoning and ultimately, effective use.  In many cases, data quality issues can be addressed through human intervention, but this is not a scalable solution for large datasets and those that continuously evolve dynamically in real-time.  In such scenarios, existing approaches to quality assessment typically rely on machine learning methods that may struggle to keep up with rapid data changes, necessitating a more efficient and effective approach to real-time quality evaluation.  In this paper, we introduce an innovative algorithm called EAGA, capable of monitoring and assessing data quality in real-time, outperforming existing approaches by a significant margin in terms of scalability and efficiency.  Developed using more than 1.3 terabytes of data from 1.7 million subjects and with a focus on entity validation, our algorithm employs a unique combination of SPARQL queries, differential validation, and the identification of interconnected objects to pinpoint objects that validate other objects, ultimately establishing an entity hierarchy.  In this hierarchy, entities are classified as main objects that validate other entities or as secondary objects that are validated by other entities.  Our experiments demonstrate EAGA's superiority over existing approaches, showcasing our algorithm's superior performance, efficiency, and scalability.  In particular, our results highlight EAGA's ability to process large datasets by evaluating the quality of more than 1.7 million subjects in under 50 hours on a single machine.  We also explore various optimization strategies and examine how they impact performance, as well as presenting a real-world application of our algorithm in a dynamic dataset setting.  In this setting, our algorithm detects secondary objects with a high validation rate of over 99% within 10 seconds.  We have made our algorithm available for public use on our GitHub repository along with a comprehensive demonstration of its functionality and performance on various datasets.  We look forward to receiving feedback and contributing to the further improvement of EAGA in the future.  In this paper, we introduce an innovative algorithm called EAGA for real-time quality evaluation of large Linked Data sets, outperforming existing approaches by a significant margin in terms of scalability and efficiency. Additionally, Frisbee identified critical issues in one of its components that had gone undetected following previous testing efforts. The creation of realistic traffic scenarios through automation is the primary focus.
Currently used approaches insert virtual characters into the environment using predefined rules but struggle to capture the intricate nature of actual traffic conditions, ultimately resulting in a gap between artificially generated scenes and real ones. As a consequence, these simulation tools lack the required level of accuracy necessary to train self-driving vehicles. To mitigate this limitation, we propose SceneGen, a traffic scenario model that utilizes neural networks to bypass reliance on predefined rules. SceneGen is particularly adept at inserting a variety of virtual characters into the environment and accurately modeling their sizes, positions, and speeds. Through extensive testing on two large datasets, we demonstrate SceneGen's capacity to accurately mimic the distributions seen in real traffic environments. Furthermore, when combined with sensor simulation, SceneGen is shown to be an effective means of training perception models capable of performing well in real-world scenarios. Ultimately, our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art traffic scenario models and reveals that neural network-based models can generate highly realistic scenes. To facilitate further progress, we make SceneGen available as an open-source tool. When paired with the simulator, it is capable of producing diverse, accurate scenes that can be used to train autonomous vehicle applications. Additionally, SceneGen may also be employed as a standalone Python package to create realistic scenes and is compatible with the OpenStreetMap format. By addressing the limitations of current traffic scenario models and providing SceneGen as a resource, we believe a significant step is taken towards advancing the development of autonomous vehicle technology. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. Furthermore, by combining this new iterative method with an flexible structure, the paper also proposes a more general framework for constructing preservation-based numerical schemes that can be applied to a wide range of time-dependent PDEs. To illustrate this new framework's effectiveness, several classic test cases are considered, including the Burgers' equation, the Korteweg-de Vries equation and the two-dimensional Euler equations, all solved using the proposed iterative method within a flexible generalised Newton framework. As the method allows for different inner iteration types, both the flexible GMRES and a more traditional direct solution are also employed for comparison. The proposed approach's performance is examined in terms of both iteration and asymptotic complexity, and the results show significant improvements over traditional approaches, achieving significant speed-ups while maintaining precision, and highlighting the potential for further improvement by adapting inner iterations to specific problems. The results also highlight the challenge of accurately measuring iteration costs, and the need for the community to adopt a standardised approach to measuring and reporting such costs. Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, is a crucial capability for autonomous vehicles operating at highway speeds. They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar in order to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. Unfortunately, the majority of existing evaluation benchmarks, like nuScenes, don't emphasize this challenge because they only assess performance within a certain range. There are a couple of key reasons for this - firstly, annotating distant objects can be difficult because lidar sensors typically only return a limited number of data points at such great distances, with almost 50% of objects more than 50m away from the sensor containing zero data points. Secondly, the commonly used metrics for evaluating three-dimensional detection tasks apply the same tolerance thresholds to near and far objects, which isn't aligned with either human vision or the disparities seen in stereo images. As a result, the task of far-field three-dimensional detection has not been given the attention it deserves. For instance, it has long been believed that high-resolution RGB sensors are key to detecting distant objects, but a more in-depth analysis shows that lidar-based approaches outperform RGB counterparts on the existing leaderboards. To better assess this challenge, we created a new evaluation protocol and a far-field validation dataset based on the well-annotated scenes from the nuScenes dataset. We also compared a variety of three-dimensional detection methods with this protocol and the results verify the widely-held assumption that high-resolution RGB does enhance detection in the far-field. We've also proposed an innovative approach, a meta-algorithm for detecting objects in the distance, called F3D, which detects three-dimensional objects in the distance by first identifying potential objects and then ranking them by distance before applying a simple classification. When tested against the existing methods, our approach showed a significant improvement of around 11% on the newly-created validation dataset. Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate data during the intraoperative process and subsequent changes to the organ's condition. The limited amount of registration data can lead to inaccurate predictions, especially when confronted with new information. To address this challenge, we've developed an end-to-end learning framework that utilizes two key components. Firstly, it employs a deformable convolutional operation to enable direct processing of the organ's irregular shape. Secondly, the model incorporates temporal information to improve its ability to estimate accurate displacement vectors. The model is trained on simulated data with varying degrees of partial occlusion, different organ shapes, and time-based changes, mimicking the unpredictable nature of the intraoperative environment. The results show that our proposed method yields more accurate outcomes than a baseline model using Laplace matrix filtration. The end-to-end framework also demonstrates a clear advantage over a traditional approach that separates shape estimation and non-rigid registration. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectories can be used to identify areas where object fragments are separating or merging. Precise trajectory estimation enables better separation and merging detection. A common approach to estimating scene flow utilizes point clouds generated by stereo, but these clouds can be incomplete and noisy. Alternative methods use monocular depth estimation for more complete point clouds, but these methods are prone to errors. We propose a new approach that combines a monocular depth estimation model with a semi-supervised training method to achieve more accurate and diverse data. This approach uses a cycle consistency technique to correct depth maps and estimate motion trajectories. A variant of this approach applies a condition to the cycle consistency method that considers the completeness of object fragments, leading to more complete estimates. Both proposed methods surpass current benchmarks and demonstrate the advantage of diverse training data. Evaluations using real-world data show that the proposed methods excel at predicting separation and merging. The code is available at: https://github.com/Trinh-Thanh-Duy/CMSceneflow. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Our research showcases the capabilities of Timeloops by implementing system call learning for individual services and a couple of benchmark applications employing Python Flask, Apache Thrift, and Memcached, among other technologies. Furthermore, we show that Timeloops' performance, despite generating a more limited system call filter, is comparable to that of an unsecured system. In the context of existing methods for verifying system call learning, we also outline various approaches. Finally, we explore the potential for Timeloops to serve as a foundation for other system call learning solutions. Ultimately, our experiments demonstrate the performance benefits of system call learning, resulting in a significant reduction of system calls and related delays. Lastly, we highlight several areas where Timeloops can be applied to a broader spectrum of applications and systems. This leads us to hypothesize that a Timeloops-based system call learning framework can be developed for general use. High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that allow for more accurate matching of observed and simulated data. This study investigates the connection between these two methods, demonstrating that ESI can be viewed as a specific case of WRI with linearized wavefield operators. Furthermore, both WRI and ESI represent subsets of the Generalized Linearized PDE (GLPDE) framework. This framework encompasses all linearized wave equation formulations that can be used for data misfit minimization and facilitates the comparison of these methods with respect to their non-unity Jacobian matrices. Consequently, both WRI and ESI can be viewed as methods that solve the generalized least-squares problem with a focus on efficiency, achieved through approximation of wavefields rather than sources. This study provides a theoretical foundation for comparing these methods and suggests strategies for constructing their respective Jacobian matrices. Finally, numerical experiments are used to evaluate the performance of these methods in challenging scenarios. Leveraging the wavefield-based structure, both WRI and ESI can be implemented with preconditioners that significantly improve their convergence rates, allowing for realistic model updates. As demonstrated, these methods are capable of handling large frequency updates and updating models based on data from multiple frequencies at once. Ultimately, this enables the construction of more accurate prestack time-domain models from data that traditionally pose difficulties for FWI. As a result, both WRI and ESI represent viable alternatives to FWI that can lead to the creation of more accurate and high-resolution subsurface models. Additionally, these methods open up new avenues for the adoption of high-performance computing and the incorporation of additional physics into seismic imaging. Ultimately, this could ultimately facilitate the development of truly multi-waveform inversion approaches that leverage the strengths of these methods. However, further research is needed to fully explore these concepts and make them computationally feasible across all feasible approaches. Nonetheless, as a starting point, both WRI and ESI provide valuable tools for improving seismic imaging beyond the capabilities of FWI. We've developed an all-optical technique for producing optical nonreciprocity on a microchip, achieved through the process of quantum squeezing a specific mode in coupled resonator systems. A key factor in this method involves applying classical coherent light in a one-way fashion to parametrically pump a nonlinear resonator. This selective pumping induces a chiral interaction between photons within the resonators, allowing us to build optical diodes and quasi-circulators. Notably, we've demonstrated the functionality of these nonreciprocal devices even with weak input, using a combination of squeezed-vacuum fields and classical pump light. We observed isolation ratios greater than 40 dB in optical diodes, as well as a high fidelity rate for quasi-circulators. We also found that our quasi-circulators can filter out backflow photons with a purity greater than 90%, achieving a high throughput in the forward direction. We believe this all-optical approach has great potential for creating compact, low-loss, and multi-channel nonreciprocal optical systems. Furthermore, we propose a design for a nonlinear resonator that could significantly reduce photon loss. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of complex nonreciprocal optical integrated circuits, paving the way for new applications in optical communication systems. We also suggest using this technique to build a quantum non-demolition optical memory. We have presented the results from the AstroSat analysis of the high-mass X-ray binary X-ray pulsar IGR J19294+1816 during its Type-I outburst in October 2019. Timing and spectral data from the decline phase of the outburst revealed the spin period to be 12.485 seconds, with significant spectral features. A Quasi Periodic Oscillation was observed at a frequency of 0.032 Hz and an RMS amplitude of 18%. Our joint spectral analysis detected Cyclotron Resonant Scattering and an Iron emission line at 42.7 keV and 6.4 keV respectively, further highlighting the complex nature of this intermediate spin pulsar's behavior during its 2019 outburst. Comparison with historical data shows a significant change in the pulsar's spin period over the past two decades, indicating a possible increase in spin period of 0.036 seconds per year. This study provides valuable insights into the pulsar's behavior and its interaction with its companion star, with possible implications for its future evolution. Lastly, we have observed significant asymmetry in the pulsar's pulse profile, which can be attributed to the effects of aberration and beaming, along with possible evidence of a radio pulse phase lag of approximately 0.16 seconds. The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is being explored to correct spherical aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Researchers have examined the potential for these phase plates to achieve high spatial resolution, both with and without the presence of a crystalline sample, using a TEM with a Cs = 2 mm spherical aberration corrector. Results show that the achievable spatial resolution ranges from approximately 0.1 Angstroms to over 0.07 Angstroms. It was also found that the efficacy of the phase plates is largely insensitive to the presence of a crystalline sample and the temperature of the sample holder. Furthermore, researchers discovered a simple method to determine the optimal pixel size for displaying images and found that it is directly proportional to the square of the achievable spatial resolution. This relationship provides a practical way to estimate the optimal pixel size without the need for complex simulations. Additionally, the extent to which the program electrostatic phase plates can correct spherical aberration was found to be directly proportional to the degree of spherical aberration present. It was also observed that the program electrostatic phase plates can correct spherical aberration even when a crystalline sample is not present, which suggests that the effectiveness of these phase plates is influenced by the electron source rather than the sample. Lastly, researchers discovered that the program electrostatic phase plates can also correct the intensity distribution within a TEM and convert a TEM with a high degree of spherical aberration into one with very low spherical aberration, achieving the same high spatial resolution. This finding has significant implications for the improvement of spatial resolution in TEMs through the use of design modifications. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a set of evaluation tasks to scrutinize the encoder representations used in these models. In experiments, our findings suggest that certain evaluation tasks prove more manageable for certain sophisticated architectures to grasp than others and, interestingly, that RNN-based architectures outperform Transformer models in these evaluation tasks despite underperforming them in standard text generation metrics. This suggests that encoder representations hold a crucial secret to good performance and that raw performance may be a poor indicator of a model's understanding of the underlying structure of dialogue language.
