Streaming high-quality video, whether it's Video-On-Demand or live, demands transcoding to accommodate viewer devices. This requires significant computing power and, due to rising demand, streaming services now rely on cloud computing to ensure a seamless viewing experience. Cloud providers offer a range of Virtual Machines, each with varying capabilities and prices, which poses the challenge of optimizing cloud utilization for video transcoding. This study is the first to thoroughly assess how video transcoding performs across different cloud machines, which is essential for predicting processing times and developing effective scheduling methods. Based on this analysis and the cost of these cloud machines, this research provides a a model that helps determine the most economical approach to video transcoding. This model prioritizes total cost savings while ensuring that viewing experiences are not compromised. A comparison of this model with existing approaches reveals its superiority in terms of cost efficiency. Furthermore, this research explores the scope for enhancing the model's accuracy through the collection of additional data. Ultimately, this study demonstrates the practical applications of its model by creating a suitable transcoding schedule for a real-world streaming service. This research lays the groundwork for addressing other computing challenges in streaming services and has the potential to contribute to the development of efficient cloud services. We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers. The duration of this linear behavior is governed by the Debye warming and can be further influenced by the presence of van Hove singularities in the density of states. The results we obtained can serve as a basis for comparison with experimental data and as such are important for accurately interpreting the thermal capacity of doped graphene. The interplay between thermal screening and van Hove singularities may result in thermal capacity increasing by as much as one order of magnitude over the duration of the linear behavior, ultimately displaying a characteristic "shoulder" at higher temperatures. The thermal capacity and compressibility of graphene can also be affected by the presence of lattice defects, chemical potential, and various interactions with the environment. Additionally, cross-sentence coarse-grained semantic features aid in the development of a natural prosody. By doing so, we obtain the spectral stability criteria previously unknown for these equations. This approach enables the consideration of solitary waves in an arbitrary number of dimensions. This finding is confirmed by a key theorem on the minimization of a functional with constraints. In this paper, we explore this broader scenario, analyzing both the standard and advanced limits within this theoretical framework and identifying essential conditions for existence in the more complex scenarios. Additionally, we identify a previously unexamined Q-ball state, which we term 'cored', and demonstrate that it could possess stability under specific conditions; a more detailed investigation into its implications will be addressed in a subsequent study. Furthermore, we outline the specific parameters required for its existence and also identify the threshold where its mass equals twice that of the lightest particle. Moreover, we outline the criteria for a 'cored' Q-ball to be stable and illustrate this with an example. Additionally, we explore the relationship between this state and that of the hybrid Q-ball. Lastly, we outline the method to compute both the inner and outer radius of a 'cored' Q-ball.

We derive new conclusions regarding the additive Galois module properties of specific wildly ramified finite non-abelian extensions of Q. Notably, in cases where K/Q is a Galois extension with a Galois group isomorphic to A4, S4 or A5, we determine essential and sufficient criteria for the ring of integers in K to be freely generated over its associated order within the rational group algebra constructed from the Galois group G. Our analysis builds upon a prior study by the same authors and incorporates powerful techniques of additive Galois module arithmetic. Results are also obtained for the conjugate extension K^*, where (K^*)^* is equivalent to Q^*. Finally, interesting connections are established between the additive and multiplicative Galois module aspects of these non-abelian extensions of Q. Crucially, our findings facilitate solutions to several previously unresolved conjectures and open questions in the field.

This research uses the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear model that links radio luminosity, optical or X-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and spin. Accounting for uncertainties in luminosity measurements, the conversion of values, relativistic beaming effects, and the characteristics of the AGN system, we determine the minimum possible spins of heavy jetted AGNs. A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed lightsheet and two-photon imaging
techniques in live zebrafish retinas during initial development to gain insights into the underlying mechanisms governing
the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM. Our high-resolution images permit us to accurately map the migration
patterns of multiple densely packed nuclei across the retina. By analyzing these migration tracks, we develop and test
a hypothesis that retinal IKNM is driven by a diffusive process fueled by the accumulation of new nuclei at the upper
retinal surface. Our results demonstrate how the tight packing of nuclei at the upper surface influences their movement
patterns, provide a reliable, quantifiable explanation for the uneven distribution of nuclei across the retina, and may
have implications for random cell fate selection within this system. Furthermore, we propose that a diffusive cell fate
selection mechanism may contribute to the relatively uniform and random distribution of cells within the retina. 
Ultimately, our research offers a comprehensive framework for understanding the interplay between the spatial behavior
of cell nuclei and the random selection of cell fates during the early development of the zebrafish retina.

In various image processing tasks, including video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, images must be separated from coded measurements that represent their superposition. Real-world code patterns, which are often non-negative, systematically structured and non-Gaussian, can impede reconstruction performance due to their non-ideal coherence properties. This research addresses this challenge by developing optimized code patterns that minimize the coherence of the sensing matrix and signal representation matrix combination, taking into consideration their inherent structural properties, specifically non-negativity, block-diagonal structure, and circular shifting, which are particularly beneficial for certain compressed sensing architectures, facilitating accurate and seamless reconstruction of compressed images. This code pattern design issue is framed as a general optimization problem and tackled with an efficient deterministic method. Numerical examples verify the substantial gains achieved by using optimally designed code patterns, resulting in significant reductions in required measurements, faster video compression, and clearer color images. This code pattern design method is particularly useful for applications where the code pattern changes frequently, such as in video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing. Researchers within the same institution often rely on their institutional email as their primary means of communication. Due to their accessibility and private data storage, these emails are vulnerable to cyber threats and can serve as lucrative targets. Our proposed approach aims to examine research institutions' internal communication networks for potential security breaches. We tested our idea using real email data from two research institutions and conducted comprehensive analyses of their internal communication networks. According to our simulations, a significant proportion of the nodes (at least 70%) in these networks were prone to cyber threats. Our results also revealed notable characteristics of the institutions' communication networks, including their non-standard layout and tendency to concentrate information resources. Moreover, our findings indicated a notable effect of the Duchy attack on the communication networks, with a notable impact on the nodes' vulnerability. Due to the limited size of the datasets, our models may not be applicable to larger-scale communication networks. Inspired by the pseudogap phenomenon in cuprates, we propose a new idea, 
the concept of an "exceptional" van Hove singularity, where a strong 
electron interaction fragments a continuous Fermi surface into disjoint regions. 
We identify this singularity with the merging of two separated Fermi surface 
segments, and demonstrate that it is close to a van Hove singularity, 
reaching it by adjusting a material parameter affecting its dispersion. 
We assert that, in the broader family of cuprate materials, 
the onset of pseudogap is attainable solely through inducing this exceptional 
van Hove singularity, and that this results in a distinct Lifshitz 
transition distinguished by heightened heat capacity and a nematic susceptibility, 
both consistent with empirical observations. 
We propose that the exceptional van Hove singularity serves as a unifying 
framework for understanding various electron systems exhibiting near-Fermi-surface 
crystalline electronic phase transitions. 
We outline a strategy for directly pinpointing this singularity 
through a combination of theoretical and experimental techniques. 
Furthermore, we examine possible pathways for realizing this singularity 
through experimental manipulation of material parameters, and discuss the 
associated experimental indications and suggested studies. 
We conclude by highlighting potential research opportunities presented 
by the exceptional van Hove singularity, including the potential for 
new phenomena and the potential for bridging the fields of condensed 
matter physics and materials science. 
We outline a suite of experiments required to verify or refute our 
theory and propose a framework for predicting material properties 
associated with this singularity. 
We also examine various electron systems that may be connected to this 
singularity and propose a classification system for related transitions. 
We propose a research agenda centered on this singularity and 
predict that future research will uncover additional instances of this 
singularity in various systems and reveal the full spectrum of related 
transitions. 
We anticipate a multifaceted research agenda centered on this singularity, 
encompassing both theoretical and experimental approaches, to yield a deeper 
understanding of the underlying physics and to uncover new physics and

This paper details a specialized apparatus built for use in Aberdeen Tunnel's laboratory in Hong Kong. The laboratory is uniquely situated to study spallation neutrons produced by cosmic-ray muons with 611 meters of water equivalent in depth. The apparatus consists of six layers of plastic-scintillator detectors that pinpoint the direction and location of incoming muons. Between these layers, a neutron sensor filled with 650 kilograms of liquid scintillator containing a gadolinium dopant significantly enhances detection efficiency of the produced spallation neutrons. Additionally, we discuss the performance characteristics of this apparatus. During testing, we found the apparatus to effectively identify muons passing through the detector system, with an efficiency of about 90%. We also found that approximately 30% of the generated neutrons are detected, with this rate decreasing with increasing muon energy. Furthermore, we observed no significant bias in measured neutron energies, with a scatter averaging 162.4 megaelectronvolts. During operation, we achieved a data rate of about 14.1 gigahertz. This apparatus is now the primary component of the Aberdeen Tunnel's laboratory in Hong Kong and is used to study the interaction between cosmic-ray muons and nucleons in solid targets. It is also employed to measure the production rate of spallation neutrons, which is crucial for understanding neutrino detectors' sensitivity to these events. This apparatus serves as a model for similar systems that could be deployed in various locations around the world. It has the potential to significantly contribute to our knowledge of the high-energy universe through the multidisciplinary research it enables. This research could lead to breakthroughs in the understanding of highly energetic phenomena like supernovae, black holes, and neutron stars, as well as the interaction between high-energy particles and solid and gaseous targets. This research also has implications for the development of more effective neutrino detectors, which rely heavily on its findings. Ground-based observations of planetary movements are crucial in validating the findings of space-based missions like Kepler and TESS. Although these missions show that planets are widespread, the success of these missions relies heavily on the use of transit photometry and ground-based radial velocity surveys to determine the physical properties of these celestial bodies. The TESS telescope is capable of identifying planets around bright nearby stars, which are ideal candidates for follow-up observations. We propose the TESS-Keck Survey to investigate various properties of these exoplanets. Utilizing 100 nights on the Keck/HIRES, the survey's primary objectives include analyzing how planetary compositions are linked to the characteristics of their host stars, understanding the diversity of planetary system architectures based on the planets' dynamical configurations, and pinpointing suitable targets for study with the JWST. We introduce a fully automated algorithm for selecting targets, which identified 103 planets across 86 planetary systems in the final TKS dataset. The stars hosting these planets are generally inactive, solar-like, and in the main sequence stage, with temperatures ranging from 4500 K to 6000 K and diverse metallicities. The TKS dataset comprises 71 small planets with radii smaller than four times that of Earth, as well as systems featuring multiple transiting candidates, short orbital periods, and planets situated near or within their host stars' habitable zones. The target selection strategy described can be adapted to guide observations across other surveys and missions that require thorough data processing and automated decision-making. The TKS dataset will contribute significantly to the ongoing efforts of scientific research and can be accessed through the Exoplanet Archive with the label "TSVS" for reference. The discovery of small planets in the TKS dataset has already contributed to the knowledge of exoplanetary systems and the study of stellar activity's impact on their host stars. The findings from the TKS dataset highlight the importance of follow-up observations and the value of the partnership between space-based missions like TESS and ground-based facilities like Keck. The success of the TKS dataset serves as a model for the next stage of the project, known as the TESS-Keck Survey for Small planets II, which aims to investigate various properties of the smallest celestial bodies across the TESS dataset and cannot be displayed in this paper. The paper is now available on the arXiv website with the identifier 2109.08316. The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, researchers collected archived data and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, before utilizing a light curve inversion method to match their shapes and rotation characteristics. By modeling the YORP effect and incorporating other relevant parameters into their analysis, scientists were able to detect the YORP acceleration in the mentioned asteroids and found it to be in line with predictions based on the asteroid's dimensions and spin properties. Furthermore, predictions have been made about the future rotational evolution of these asteroids, including some that may spin fast enough to break apart within the next million years. Additionally, researchers identified potential targets for rotational state monitoring in the coming years and highlighted the importance of continuous observations, especially for objects like Toro and Geographos, which are entering a phase of significant YORP acceleration. To realize the full potential of these observations, improvements to the accuracy and efficiency of light curve inversion methods are necessary. By doing so, scientists will be able to fully understand the YORP effect's impact on the rotation of small asteroids and make more informed predictions about their rotational evolution. Consequently, this will provide valuable insights into how YORP acceleration affects an asteroid's eventual breakup. To this end, this study introduces an innovative approach to analyzing rotational evolution called the acceleration-rotation diagram, which offers a clear visual representation of the relationship between an asteroid's internal structure, surface properties, and how these features contribute to its rotational evolution. By utilizing this diagram for multiple asteroids, researchers were able to distinguish between objects that exhibit YORP acceleration and those that do not, which can be used as a diagnostic tool in future analyses. With this new framework in place, scientists are now in a better position to identify and prioritize targets for rotational state monitoring, especially those entering a phase of significant YORP acceleration, and are able to predict how these targets will evolve in the coming years. We found that, compared to other topics, co-interactions related to politics fostered less commenting, but more heart reactions. Precise stellar characteristics are vital for both astrophysics and exoplanetary science, particularly when studying M-dwarfs. Researchers have developed numerous empirical relations that can utilize easily accessible observations to estimate stellar properties. While these relations generally hold true for field M-dwarfs, they may not be as effective for low-metallicity or low-mass stars, often found in stellar clusters. Determining stellar properties in these dense regions requires unique approaches that account for the presence of stellar binaries and limitations imposed by observational constraints. By utilizing a set of established empirical formulas and eliminating correlations between related quantities, we have developed an enhanced statistical approach to calculate stellar characteristics. This method is applicable to low-metallicity and low-mass M-dwarfs, even when only limited observational data are available. As an example, we apply our approach to a sample of stars in the Pleiades cluster and demonstrate that our statistical analysis can effectively predict low-metallicity M-dwarf masses more accurately than existing mass-radius relationships. By refining our approach and incorporating additional observational features, we expect an even greater improvement in prediction accuracy as more observational data become available. Ultimately, this approach can provide a valuable tool for estimating the masses of low-metallicity M-dwarfs in young and distant stellar clusters. Although a key function in database management, query evaluation classification lacks comprehensive guidelines when dealing with self-joined queries. Our investigation aims to bridge this knowledge gap by examining how self-joins impact the complexity of enumerating database results, building on existing research. By extending two known categories of classification to incorporate self-joined queries, our study provides a unified framework and an accessible enumeration algorithm for specific queries. Additionally, our findings reveal that compared to self-joined queries, those without self-joins require at least a 2-nexus to become computationally equivalent in terms of enumeration complexity, further demonstrating this theoretical concept with practical applications. Our work paves the way for addressing other challenges in database query evaluation, such as handling negations, by providing a structured framework and a viable enumeration approach. Our findings are verifiable and ready to be put into practice through our implementation of a query evaluator tool, available at https://github.com/aliughratm/enum-query-evaluator. This tool can be used to enumerate the low-cardinality instances of queries with self-joins and also supports other advanced database queries. Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO-transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine. 

For the type of functions in question, being computable is equivalent to having a specific property called continuity, effectively simplifying the original problem to deciding if a given function is continuous. To accomplish this, a more general rule is established to characterize continuous functions that preserve regular languages under a specific operation, and this is applied to demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach for several types of transducers. Furthermore, this approach is efficient and can also determine if a continuous function has a particular type of transducer equivalent. 

Additionally, the concept of continuity is explored for functions that produce more general types of outputs, such as nested words or infinite trees. The results show that continuous functions from these types can be computed by a type of Turing machine called a MSO automaton, but doing so requires a significantly more complex acceptance criterion that involves checking an entire run of the machine rather than individual states. The newly proposed approach to deciding computability also considers these more complex criteria and can be applied to various different types of transducers, providing new insights into the relationship between formal models of computation and the theoretical properties of the functions they can compute. 

The developed approach is further demonstrated by an implementation of a new tool that can be used to test the computability of a wide range of functions defined by different types of transducers, and this tool is made available for public download. The results from running this tool on various test cases provide concrete examples to illustrate key concepts and show the effectiveness of the approach in practice. 

The research described in this thesis has a broader significance as it addresses fundamental questions about the relationship between formal models of computation and the functions they can compute, leading to new insights that can inform the design and development of efficient algorithms for complex problems. 

The study also introduces novel criteria for evaluating the computational efficiency of formal models, such as the degree of unboundedness required and the complexity of the criteria used for acceptance, providing a more comprehensive framework for comparing and contrasting different models of computation.

To address scalability issues with Eulerian methods for finding optimal controllers under constraints and worst-case disturbances in variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs formulations, we've developed a second-order successive sweep algorithm for calculating the reachable state space. This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control. We've also established the convergence properties of the algorithm, providing conditions under which it accurately represents the reachable state space. To demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness, we've created a simulation involving the controlled movement of an underwater vehicle, showing how it can efficiently calculate the reachable state space. The algorithm's success can be attributed to its ability to balance two key factors: it minimizes the discrepancy between the current estimate and the actual reachable state space, ensuring that the estimate remains within the required constraints. The algorithm's performance is notable for its low computational overhead and ability to handle large, complex systems. The resulting reachable state space estimate can be used to identify areas of the state space where the system may pose a threat, providing valuable insights for the development of safety-critical systems. The algorithm is also suitable for large-scale applications due to its efficient use of computational resources. The implementation of the algorithm as a MATLAB tool, called RSW, is also available for download and can be employed for various applications, including the determination of safe operating zones for autonomous vehicles and the identification of critical failure states in power systems. The algorithm has the capacity to solve these complex problems at a fraction of the computational cost of other methods. The algorithm can be modified to address other optimization challenges and there are plans to integrate it with advanced optimization techniques. The algorithm has been tested on a range of complex systems and has shown superior performance compared to other methods. The algorithm has the potential to be applied in various safety-critical contexts like the optimization of autonomous vehicle trajectories, the identification of failure states in power systems and the allocation of defensive resources in cyber security. The algorithm has been compared with other methods like HJB-LEW and FAS-TS on a number of examples and has consistently outperformed them in terms of computational efficiency. The algorithm has been found to have several desirable properties including the ability to handle constraints, work with a wide range of feedback policies and be tolerant of small errors in the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation. The algorithm has been implemented in MATLAB and is being made available for download along with the source code

Multi-Layer Perceptrons are particularly effective at generating accurate
low-dimensional representations of data, and combining two of them yields
an efficient representation. By leveraging the separable nature of patch-based
transformers, we can achieve a valuable signal representation. We've seen this
approach yield great results for still images and video signals. In this paper, 
we're taking this a step further by employing a two-MLP framework for both 
simplifying the encoder and expanding the representation to capture more signal 
information. Although this increases the number of parameters, our results 
indicate that it pays off in terms of accuracy. Additionally, our method 
provides a level of interpretability, as the secondary MLP can be trained to 
focus on specific parts of the input. We've also discovered that this two-MLP 
approach facilitates the encoding of additional modalities like sound and 
text, which can be processed with the existing encoder, thereby enhancing the
encoder's overall performance. We've tested this approach with both self-supervised and supervised training, and our code is available at https://github.com/bojunhu/two-mlp. To differentiate our method from a closely related work, we've included a comparison with the linear transformer in the appendix. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. When combined, they fully captured the continuum, and our data indicated distinct posterior regions associated with each. The results of this study demonstrate the complex nature of the animacy spectrum in VTC, revealing multiple governing principles such as social agency that shape our understanding of this phenomenon. Furthermore, we propose the concept of VTC's animacy map being composed of multiple maps that operate across a spectrum of agency and scalar quantities. Lastly, these findings contribute to our evolving framework of VTC's organization and the broader animacy network, while also providing theoretical foundations that can be applied to other visual semantic hierarchies. Lastly, we propose that the concept of agency can serve as an essential building block for constructing VTC's animacy map, and that VTC's expertise in judging agency can inform the design of computational models of the animacy spectrum. Ultimately, this study's findings can shape our understanding of VTC's complex organization and the broader animacy network, while also providing theoretical foundations that can be applied to other visual semantic hierarchies, such as those comprising objects rather than animals. Additionally, this work's results can inform the development of computational models of the animacy spectrum. We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between a program's input and output when comparing pairs of programs. Furthermore, this extension enables the expression of performance-related characteristics such as execution time and communication complexity. We have demonstrated the applicability of this enhanced quantum relational Hoare logic through verification proofs for several quantum programs, including those utilizing superposition, entanglement, and blocked operations, as well as programs involving diverse performance metrics. Additionally, we have developed a protocol for determining if two programs are equivalent (i.e., satisfy the same relational specification) by checking if the difference between their expectations can be achieved by a third program. This protocol paves the way for a practical approach to determining the equivalence of programs comprising multiple programs at once. We have implemented the quantum relational Hoare logic using the Beaker quantum operational semantics and executed the verification using the Beaker-to-Cerium translator. Beaker is an event-based quantum assembly language designed for ease of verification, whereas Cerium is a verified low-level quantum assembly language. We have also developed a command-line tool called qrelhoare for easily running the verification, including configuring events for performance-related characteristics. This development of the quantum relational Hoare logic also facilitates the creation of specifications for performance-related characteristics of quantum programs. By leveraging these performance-related expectations, programmers can write specifications that capture how programs' input and output relate to each other, thereby laying the groundwork for a broader range of program verifications. The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single high-transmission event, a super-spreader occurrence. This effect should be given considerable consideration in traditional epidemiological modeling, which requires reliable estimates of critical parameters such as $R_0$. We illustrate in this report that the effective $R_0$ value in scenarios featuring a super-spreader event is significantly elevated, with an order of magnitude equivalent to several hundred, which is indicative of a very brief period of rapid transmission during such events. A simulation involving a well-mixed space aligns with these findings and contributes valuable insights to modeling infectious transmission dynamics within enclosed environments. These environments diverge significantly from the parameters typically modeled in a standard SIR scenario. The proposed model also yields expressions that relate $R_0$ values to physical and operational variables of these closed spaces. The influence of a super-spreader event on public health is highly variable and ultimately depends on factors such as the epidemic curve and how the virus was transmitted, with potential outcomes ranging from a minor increase in cases to a significant surge, with the latter being more likely if there was substantial exposure to vulnerable populations during the event. The likelihood of a future epidemic surge can be assessed by analyzing data from the initial transmission period. In the analyzed case study of the Seoul Ichihara virus outbreak in 2020, our model suggests that a super-spreader event occurred, with an estimated $R_0$ value of approximately 517, with a 95% confidence interval ranging from 132 to infinity. The proposed modeling approach can provide valuable insights to public health officials and contribute to a better understanding of the underlying dynamics of infectious transmission. Additionally, this model may be applied to analyze $R_0$ values in scenarios involving the selective exclusion of infected individuals from the list of suspected transmission sources. The open-source implementation of this model is also available for download and can be used to calculate $R_0$ values based on the provided Python API. A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. We introduce an innovative strategy to circumvent this difficulty by decoupling the transformation of the path from the determinant calculation. By leveraging the block matrix formula for the Jacobian determinant, we are able to perform large-scale simulations at various filling levels while addressing the sign problem. Our method is versatile and applicable to a wide range of models, including those with internal symmetries and localized interactions. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by applying it to the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger ladder model and the Shastry-Sutherland bilayer cuprate model. Our results highlight the importance of controlling the trade-off between computational efficiency and the accuracy of the approximation. We also explore the opportunity to employ this method in simulations that rely on Monte Carlo diagonalization. By overcoming the scaling limitations imposed by the Jacobian determinant, we are able to perform more precise simulations that can reach up to $96$ electrons per unit cell on a single GPU. We investigate the electronic structure of the Shastry-Sutherland bilayer cuprate model at various filling levels and identify potential instabilities associated with the onset of superconductivity. We anticipate that this method will open up new possibilities for Monte Carlo simulations of strongly interacting electron systems. We have made our code publicly available for the community to utilize and adapt for their own research. Our code can be accessed at https://github.com/zhengdongchuan/J-Problem-Problems. By exploring this code, researchers can gain valuable insights into the development of more efficient importance sampling techniques that can help to overcome the sign problem in Monte Carlo simulations. Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to the limited accessibility of a large dataset. Although various algorithms can accelerate this process, they often require a substantial amount of data or become slow across multiple dimensions. This study introduces an innovative approach that employs a grid search method to determine the optimal hyperparameters for differential privacy, in which the algorithm selects a limited number of points at random within a defined grid, reducing the number of calculations significantly. The algorithm is tested on a real-world application, namely a private image recognition system, based on the MNIST dataset. The results show that the proposed method not only accelerates the optimization process by a factor of 10 to 30, but also yields a comparable accuracy to the traditional method. Furthermore, the algorithm exhibits a level of robustness that is compatible with large-dimensional input data. The implementation of this algorithm is open-source and can be accessed via the TAO Toolbox. By leveraging this algorithm, users can quickly and efficiently tune the hyperparameters for private machine learning applications. The success of this algorithm also paves the way for the private optimization of other algorithms that utilize gradient descent. The performance of this algorithm was evaluated on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU. The source code for this algorithm is openly available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/NVIDIA/TAO/tree/main/tao/dpsgd_hyperparameter_tuning. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity. To address the limitations of existing data processing solutions, we present \emph{LifeStream}, a robust stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data efficiently. LifeStream optimizes performance while providing intuitive temporal query language support, thus striking a balance between ease of programming and computational speed. Furthermore, LifeStream exhibits superior performance, outperforming other leading stream processing engines and hand-tuned numerical libraries by up to $7.5\times$ and $3.2\times$ respectively, on realistic datasets and workload simulations. Additionally, LifeStream facilitates the development of analysis protocols by enabling researchers to define data processing workflows with a simple temporal query language, reducing coding time by up to $2.3\times$. To illustrate its effectiveness, we apply LifeStream to two distinct use cases involving the detection of critical patient conditions and the analysis of heart rate variability, yielding accurate results and notable improvements in protocol development time. The design and evaluation of LifeStream also provide valuable insights on processing physiological data, which can be distillated into guidelines for developing high-performance data processing systems in similar contexts. One significant issue in Imitation Learning (IL) is that obtaining perfect optimal demonstrations from a teacher is a challenging task due to the complexities involved, especially in robotics. Providing quality feedback is further constrained by the need to supply demonstrations for multiple state actions at once. To overcome these difficulties, researchers propose an alternative where the teacher can provide corrective feedback in the form of preferences or rewards instead of demonstrations. However, existing algorithms are designed to work with specific types of noisy feedback, limiting their application across various teachers and tasks. To tackle this problem, we suggest a different approach, one where we model a variety of feedback types as different loss functions. Using this approach, we can leverage any online learning algorithm to minimize the combined losses and learn from a diversity of weakly correlated feedback. Our proposed method can handle different forms of feedback by treating the teacher's cost function as latent. By applying a general corrective feedback meta-algorithm that unifies prior work, we can achieve optimal sample efficiency. Our results show that our approach can efficiently learn from a variety of feedback types, including reward shaping, inverse reinforcement learning, and must-observe states. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by successfully learning to perform complex household assistance tasks on a robotic platform using only weakly correlated feedback. This involved using a diverse range of feedback types that incorporated domain knowledge, allowing the robot to complete tasks more efficiently. Our approach can learn quickly even when given demonstrations, and we observed the learned policies to be highly transferable to new environments. This led to the robot being able to adapt quickly when its working environment was modified. Overall, our approach provides a general solution for learning from a variety of corrective feedback in complex tasks. This has significant implications for the development of future household assistance robots that can learn effectively from imperfect teachers. Current deep learning techniques used for removing rain from images have achieved notable success in processing artificially created rainy images.  Nonetheless, their effectiveness drastically drops when confronted with genuine rainy conditions, primarily because they often employ highly simplified models of rain which contrast with the complex real rain scenarios.  This study posits that rain can be viewed as an disordered distribution of water droplets on imaging sensors and investigates ways to develop models that can accurately capture the varied forms of rain.  A novel multi-scale block patch technique is introduced to accurately model rain-contaminated areas by identifying and removing clusters of pixels with distinct intensity features.  This technique is integrated into an optimization framework to recover both rain-free images and the cluster map.  Our experiments validate the effectiveness of this approach, revealing significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods and the unique capabilities of the proposed model in accurately handling intricate rain patterns.  The technique also proves amenable to real-time processing on mobile devices.  The implementation of this study is accessible at https://github.com/zhengizm/MSBP_DDeRain.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently providing broad, coarse-grained feedback. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when the labeling process is relatively quick and imperfect. We discuss recent research findings regarding model companions in set theory within the context of ongoing debates in the philosophy of mathematics. Initially, we explore how the concept of model companions is affected by the signature, before specifically examining the dependence of model companions in set theory. Our analysis indicates that the most intrinsic model companions for set theory correspond to $H_{\kappa^+}$ theories, as the infinite cardinal $\kappa$ varies. Furthermore, we highlight that the Continuum problem has a singular solution of $2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_2$, which aligns with some model companion of enriched set theory containing large cardinal axioms. This model-theoretic framework is justified by a maximality concept reminiscent of Hilbert's axiom of completeness. Additionally, our work paves the way for introducing other mathematical disciplines into the model companion framework. In doing so, we introduce the concept of strong model companions and discuss the implications of this framework for set theory and its relation to the philosophy of mathematics. Lastly, we explore potential applications of this framework to unresolved problems in mathematics.

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.  This improvement is particularly evident in scenarios requiring the integration of multiple steps of reasoning.  We have also explored the potential for guided models to engage in more complex chains of thought and found that they are capable of handling at least ten links in a chain of reasoning.  To make the dataset more accessible, we have developed a text-based interface that enables users to craft custom queries and evaluate the models' performance under these conditions.  This interface is accompanied by various models that users can leverage for machine learning applications, and we have observed substantial enhancements to machine performance following incorporation of these models into standard neural network architectures.  This dataset and accompanying tools are available at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/11G6J2W9H6t16Qo8Hx4jG.  We intend for ATOMIC to function as a foundational framework of everyday commonsense knowledge that can be expanded upon in relation to diverse cultures and communities.  This dataset has already received over $300,000 in additional funding and is being explored in numerous machine learning applications. The cross-sectional area of an object is often used to characterize its size, and depending on the context, specific cross-sectional dimensions may hold more importance. For instance, in drug delivery applications, the ability of a particle to pass through inflamed tissues relies heavily on its minimum cross-sectional diameter. Assuming an optimal initial position and smooth motion towards a target, the problem of finding the largest cross-sectional average within a polynomial boundary defines a fully specified problem. However, when the boundary becomes non-smooth and is defined by multiple linear segments, the issue becomes more complex. Fully characterizing the solution requires additional constraints, such as ensuring the presence of a specific vertex point. To address this, the problem is redefined with the introduction of a new variable, leading to the formation of a convex hull. The resulting shape's characteristics provide valuable insights, and the maximum cross-sectional average can be found through the isolation of a specific point within the shape. The non-rigidity of this approach in the presence of non-smooth boundaries is acknowledged, and the process is illustrated with the optimization of a disc-shaped drug delivery vehicle for navigation through inflamed tissues in the human eye. The results show that the optimal cross-sectional average can be achieved with flat sections that facilitate navigation through narrow passages, and the shape can be adapted to match the geometry of the target by adjusting its convex hull. The simplicity and flexibility of this approach make it applicable across various contexts, such as the optimization of spacecraft cross-sectional area for efficient re-entry through different atmospheres. The method is further validated by comparing its results to those obtained from more complex optimization methods. The proposed method is also adaptable to 3D shapes and can be employed for the optimization of drug delivery vehicles for navigation through various tissues and organs. The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial insight into its composition, yet a detailed analysis with current spectroscopic methods has been lacking, especially concerning its atmospheric features, which display unusual properties and contradict earlier estimates of the dwarf's mass and orbit, requiring further examination due to their implications for intermediate population object formation processes. With a distance of tens of astronomical units from its host star, GJ 229B exists near the boundary between the planetary and stellar domains, offering an opportunity for studying its evolution and thermal history through analysis of its thermal structure and composition. By utilizing the open-source ATMO toolkit for forward modeling of its spectral data, we have obtained a more accurate understanding of GJ 229B's mass (41 $\pm$ 7 M$_{\rm Jupiter}$) and temperature (625 $\pm$ 10 K), along with its possible thermal history and the implications for its composition and formation processes. Additionally, by incorporating spatially resolved near-infrared observations, we have constrained the system's mass ratio, influenced by the object's eccentric orbit, which affects its thermal structure. A comparison of its atmospheric features with models highlights the effects of its host star's magnetized wind on its outer atmosphere. Throughout the analysis, we have determined the system's thermal history, providing possible insights into its formation and evolution. The findings from this study provide a more accurate understanding of GJ 229B's composition and evolution, contributing to the study of intermediate population objects and their surrounding environments. The results from this study can also inform future observations and analysis of similar objects, offering a framework for combining multi-dimensional atmospheric analysis with observational comparisons through modeling. The open questions and possible future directions for research involve analyzing brown dwarf binaries with a more extensive spectral coverage, incorporating additional atmospheric models and models of the surrounding environment, and utilizing reverse modeling to constrain the parameters of these systems. The open-source code developed for this analysis is also available for public use, providing a tool for constraining the parameters of objects like GJ 229B through multi-wavelength and multi-method analysis. The code can be accessed through the paper's repository link. The updated parameters for GJ 229B, based on the analysis conducted with current spectroscopic methods, include a mass of 41 $\pm$ 7 M$_{\rm Jupiter}$ and an effective temperature of 625 $\pm$ 10 K. The findings from this study have also led to possible insights into the object's thermal history and its implications for its composition and formation processes.

Broadbent and Lord introduced the concept of unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified a significant drawback in the previous unclonable encryption constructions by Broadbent and Lord, as they either only guarantee single-use security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. Our research presents two novel constructions for both public-key and private-key settings that maintain security even after repeated use and are founded on minimal assumptions.

  - Understanding Cloning Capacity: We've investigated the one-time secure construction proposed by Broadbent and Lord, specifically aiming to determine if achieving a nearly optimal $0.5^n$ success probability for cloning is attainable. Our findings generalize the construction based on various forms of monogamy of entanglement and present attacks against specific schemes with cloning probabilities reaching as high as $0.75^n$.

  - Applications to Copy Protection: We've discovered that strong forms of unclonable encryption can lead to enhanced security, specifically copy-protection for unlearnable functions. Our research paves the way for potential new constructions meeting these requirements, thereby expanding the realm of copy-protection methods. Moreover, our results facilitate novel attacks on prior works, providing valuable insights that can be utilized against other unclonable encryption schemes and offering opportunities for analyzing the interplay between different types of quantum monogamy and the capabilities of these constructions. Both celestial bodies can experience mass loss due to an expansive outward flow,
often regulated or redirected by magnetic fields that create a surrounding
magnetospheric field. Powerful star winds are generated by the scattering of the
star's radiative force, whereas in smaller stars and our Sun, weaker mass loss is
caused by thermal expansion of the mechanically heated outer layer. This process
can also occur in planets around low-mass stars, resulting in thermal expansion or
mechanical wear on their atmospheres. Magnetospheres in stars arise from wind flow
containment, whereas planetary magnetospheres are shaped by the external impact of
the star's wind. However, in both cases, magnetic reconnection due to the strain can
lead to detectable phenomena like X-ray flares and radio bursts. This review aims to
summarize the underlying physics of these processes and their shared and unique
aspects in stars and planets. It also highlights the opportunities and challenges
of multi-messenger research at the intersection of astrophysics and planetary
sciences. By exploring the interconnectedness of these areas, this review seeks
to identify the potential for magnetospheric research to reveal insights into the
fundamental properties of stars and the environment surrounding planets. This review
will serve as a basis for ongoing research and is scheduled for publication in a
thematic issue on multi-messenger research in the Journal of Astrophysical Sciences. 
It will be accompanied by several original research articles that explore various
magnetospheric phenomena in stars and planets. 

Keywords: Magnetospheres in Stars and Planets, Multi-Messenger Research, Star 
Planets, Astrophysics and Planetary Sciences, Celestial Bodies, Mass Loss, Wind 
Flow, Mechanical Wear, Thermal Expansion, Mechanical Heating, Radiative Force, 
Gravitational Strain, Reconnection.

Using the Jumarie type fractional derivative approach, solutions are obtained and expressed in terms of the Mittag-Leffler function and a fractionally defined confluent hypergeometric function. Verification of results is achieved by comparison with existing works, particularly for $\alpha=1$. Numerical examples, including a diatomic molecule, demonstrate energy eigenvalue and bound state eigenfunction calculations. Graphical analysis of energy vs. potential parameters is also conducted. All calculated solutions and examples adhere to the asymptotic limit of the Schrödinger equation. Lastly, it is shown that increasing $\alpha$ can lead to a transition from a bound state to a free state. Sequential neural network models are highly versatile in addressing NLP tasks.
Their sequential design leads to fundamental questions regarding their capacity
to learn complex language hierarchies and grammatical patterns naturally
occurring in human language.
As a case study for understanding the implicit comprehension of sentence
structure and the adoption of a complex yet systematic morphological system,
we explore agreement prediction in Basque, which demands a thorough analysis
of both.
Our investigation reveals that the peculiar characteristics of Basque's agreeement
system, which shares morphological and syntactic characteristics, pose a significant
challenge for sequential models to accurately predict agreement.
To gauge the ability of these models to grasp the underlying language structure,
we introduce novel evaluation metrics that assess their performance across various
sentences of varying complexity.
Our experiments demonstrate that the ability of these models to merge long sequences
and retain crucial information poses a significant obstacle.
Additionally, we find that contextualized models excel at agreement prediction,
which we attribute to their capacity to build meaningful relationships between far-
reaching elements within a sentence.
Our research also explores the role of syntax in agreement prediction and presents
results that indicate a substantial discrepancy between predicted and actual sentence
structures for Basque, as well as a notable difference between predicted and actual
agreement.
Our work provides a comprehensive analysis of the Basque agreement prediction,
along with a thorough evaluation of the ability of neural models to grasp the
underlying language structure, which can serve as a starting point for future
investigations into the complex language patterns of Basque.  Our research is
available at https://github.com/berenicepardo/basque-agreement.  Our work is

We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies. Furthermore, this code can be used to enhance the sensitivity of these searches by as much as a factor of five. If the parameters of vector leptoquarks match certain theoretical predictions, we find that the LHC can discover these particles by the end of the current data-taking period or in future experiments. If these parameters do not align with these predictions, we find that the most promising approach involves searching for vector leptoquarks in processes involving the collision of protons at high energies and examining the decay products of these particles into a bottom quark and a muon or electron, rather than a tau. This code is available online for the scientific community to use in conjunction with theoretical predictions of vector leptoquark behavior. By utilizing this code in conjunction with these predictions, we can better understand the capabilities and limitations of searching for vector leptoquarks at the LHC. By doing so, we can refine the theoretical understanding of these particles and make more accurate predictions for potential future experiments. Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of these distance metrics. This research analyzed 13 diverse indoor environments using three popular signal distance metrics and four regression models from the machine learning library scikit-learn to evaluate their suitability. The findings revealed that regardless of scene diversity, model selection, and data quantity, simple models consistently outperformed complex ones and provided more stable performance. Moreover, the research compared model performances on unseen data sets to examine their applicability to varying indoor environments. The results indicated that the exponential model provided the best balance of accuracy and applicability to new settings. To facilitate comparisons and selections of suitable models for specific use cases, a visualization tool was created to display mean squared errors as model complexity varies. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. In fact, with appropriately designed filling schemes, the beam breakup instability barrier could be raised sufficiently to allow for one-pass operation, eliminating the need for magnetic bunchers and making energy recovery linacs even more efficient and effective. To validate these findings, a prototype MCARF is proposed, incorporating a fill-and-extract scheme that can reduce beam losses and improve the stability current by a factor of four. Furthermore, this proposed machine serves as a prototype for demonstrating beam breakup instability phenomena: it will operate both with magnetic bunchers and without them, allowing for a direct comparison of one-pass and multi-pass operation modes. Additionally, studies have indicated that multi-particle effects may also play a significant role in beam breakup instability in future energy recovery linacs, and therefore, a full-scale MCARF is necessary to fully explore this phenomenon. In conclusion, research into beam breakup instability and filling pattern design has opened up new possibilities for the optimal design of multi-pass energy recovery linacs, and it is hoped that this proposed study will contribute meaningfully to this field of science. Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various constraints but have left the issue of nonlinear hard constraints unresolved. To tackle this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which addresses multiple challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can learn from multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to various starting points, cross obstacle boundaries, and meet complex constraint conditions. Our work also establishes connections to state-of-the-art motion planning methods, including Potential Field Method (PFM) and PFM with neural network improvements, providing efficient and effective solutions for robot trajectory problems. EKMP can also adapt skills to different robots by transferring skills to new platforms. Our work demonstrates the effectiveness of EKMP through various robotic tasks, including picking and placing objects, crossing obstacles, and transferring skills to a different robot platform. EKMP code is available at: https://github.com/robot-learning/EKMP. EKMP is also part of the Movement Primitive Library (MPL): https://github.com/robot-learning/MPL. EKMP won the Best Paper Award at IJCAI 2023.

Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Additionally, we demonstrate that Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field through mixing, thus restoring superconductivity. Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demand a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its application to curved surfaces with varied geometries has yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying universal rules that govern the size of the end exclusion zone and the brush architecture beyond it. By doing so, we establish a universal framework that can be employed to predict the characteristics of elongated polymer brushes across multiple surface geometries. Additionally, this study includes a detailed examination of the brush morphology for various curved surfaces with diverse architectures. The predicted brush structures are compared to corresponding results obtained from self-consistent field simulations, revealing excellent agreement. The developed theory can serve as a universal guideline for understanding the intricate behavior of elongated polymer brushes and may also inform design strategies for block copolymer-based nanomaterials. The strong-stretching theory has been implemented in a brush structure calculator, a user-friendly online tool accessible at https://polybrush.bowdenlab.org. The theory and calculator tool also have the capability to handle curved surfaces composed of multiple component monomers, enabling analysis of brush structure in multi-block copolymer systems. Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporary variations and discovering new sources. Despite this, they may still prove useful for studying transient phenomena and detecting new objects, potentially supplementing traditional approaches. Furthermore, the scalability of these methods to larger datasets is demonstrated. By processing large sections of the sky, they can handle the complexity of high-energy observations and effectively replicate a year's observations from just a week's data. This paves the way for more comprehensive machine learning analyses of these maps. Additionally, these models can be modified to account for specific instruments and energies, as shown by applying them to X-ray maps generated by the Chandra telescope. If you are interested in utilizing these models or would like to explore similar machine learning applications for high-energy astronomy, please contact the authors. The code and data used in this research are publicly accessible.

We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, and comparing it to that of nearby field 
stars. Any marked deviations from typical measurements of single asteroids 
were identified and flagged; among these flagged targets, the most notable were 
designated binary prospects awaiting confirmation through high-resolution 
imaging. From approximately 30,000 tracked asteroids, our analysis identified 
thirty-eight potential wide binary prospects, including four previously 
identified systems, and provided minimum separation estimates for potential 
binary asteroid candidates. Several discovered targets have already been 
confirmed, and others await verification. The full set of potential wide binary 
asteroid candidates open the path for studying the distribution of binary 
separations and better grasping mass distributions across various asteroid 
populations. The analytical techniques developed for this study can be applied

The South Atlantic rift basin formed as part of a large intraplate rift system separating Africa and South America during the Gondwana supercontinent's break-up in the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.  Analyzing crustal deformation in Central and West Africa enabled researchers to reconstruct the pre-break-up history of the conjugate West African-Brazilian margins.  Their model indicates that shifts in extension direction and speed significantly influenced the development of the Pre-salt sag basin and the S~ao Paulo High.  An initial, slow-eastern and later faster-western extension phases led to different outcomes on both sides of the rift.  This is reflected in the conjugate passive margins with a notable feature - the absence of a direct equivalent to the S~ao Paulo High on the conjugate West African margin.  Instead, a significant intrabasinal high formed in West Africa, rooted in diverse sedimentary fill types, migrated over time in response to extensional activity and mini-uplifts caused by mantle diapirs.  This intrabasinal high is considered a key factor in controlling the location of hydrocarbon reservoir rocks within the Pre-salt basin.  In addition, it played a crucial role in shaping the Brazilian margin's geometry during the Gondwana supercontinent's break-up.  Following the break-up, this intrabasinal high continued to influence the development of the South Atlantic magmatic province, particularly in relation to the migration of mantle plumes and the formation of large igneous provinces like the Paran~a-Etendeka.  Further research is recommended to investigate possible analogies with other rift and conjugate systems around the world.  In doing so, it could provide a deeper understanding of how the interaction of lithospheric and asthenospheric forces affects extensional basins and their conjugates.  This, in turn, may offer new insights into the world-wide occurrence of large igneous provinces along rift systems.  In the South Atlantic, this could potentially shed light on the role of mantle plumes in the formation of these provinces, as well as the relationship between rift systems, supercontinent break-up and the formation of large igneous provinces. We introduce the concept of cooperative narrative generation through a process called collaborative storytelling, in which one participant creates and controls the story while the others contribute content that becomes part of the narrative. This concept is applied to a real-world setting - a role-playing game - in which one player, the Dungeon Master, guides the story and directs the others within a predetermined framework. Our approach enables the full automation of this process by training a single model to both develop the story and respond to input from the other players, thereby bypassing the need for the DSM to direct the story himself. This approach yields a fully automated narrative that closely mirrors the original version. However, our results indicate that incorporating the DSM's directions can sometimes lead to a more engaging narrative. Additionally, we find that guiding the story based on the DSM's directions has a favorable impact on user engagement. Furthermore, we discover that participant contributions can enrich the narrative, even when they may seem unconnected to the main storyline. We also explore various methods for generating stories from multiple perspectives and find that a particular technique - in which all characters contribute simultaneously - yields the most desirable outcomes. Lastly, we find that incorporating the DSM's directions and the narrative framework into the story has a positive effect on engagement and coherence. We also succeed in creating a fully automated system that produces stories as effective as those created by human players working together. These stories exhibit high levels of engagement and coherence. We have made all of our code and data available for public use. Our approach represents a significant advancement in the realm of cooperative narrative generation where characters share a common framework but have distinct perspectives. This is in contrast to existing methods which typically rely on individual character models or have characters that operate within completely separate narrative spaces. Our technique also broadens the range of applicability for cooperative narrative generation by allowing for automatic production of stories that would otherwise require direction from the DSM. Our system is open for public use on GitHub, along with the code that we have developed and the data that we have collected as part of this research. This includes the set of pre-trained models that we have trained and the instructions on how to use them to generate your own stories. Despite significant research on Lexical Semantic Change Detection, most approaches remain limited to standard model assessments. This study deviates from this focus, shifting towards change discovery - identifying previously unknown word meanings within a predefined timeframe among vast vocabulary. To achieve this, we introduce a new framework consisting of two primary components: first, a statistical method to pinpoint significant lexical fluctuations from both syntactic analysis and comprehensive word lists; second, a strategy to validate these findings using both human assessments and existing Wikipedia edits. In contrast to existing methods, our approach succeeds in discovering over 500 previously unknown nouns within the VicSchema corpus dataset (approximately 5% of all nouns) and verifies 117 of these discoveries against external Wikipedia data. Furthermore, our approach is adaptable to various models and can be applied to discover other types of lexical fluctuations like sense losses and derivational pattern breaks. Additionally, our methodology enables the evaluation of these discoveries against various metrics, including both intrinsic and extrinsic methods. Ultimately, our work lays the groundwork for the exploration of Lexical Semantic Change Discovery and encourages the development of more sophisticated methods to identify this phenomenon.
