The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations. By examining the time-dependent folding processes, we reveal that proteins with shallow knots undergo a rapid conversion from the double-loop structure to their final, knotted form. In contrast, proteins with deep knots undergo a prolonged transition, first reversing their inner loop before finally achieving their knotted state. Our research employs a knotted protein database that consists of non-redundant protein structures with trefoil knots, obtained from the Protein Data Bank. The analysis is extended to other protein types by comparing the folding processes of proteins with shallow and deep knots, as well as proteins with knotted and unknotted structures. The methodology used in this research is versatile and can be applied to the study of other complex molecular structures. The statistical approach used in this research highlights the unique folding processes of proteins with trefoil knots by comparing their structures and analyzing their temporal folding pathways. The findings of this research provide valuable insights into the mysterious relationship between protein knots and their folding processes. The results of this research can be accessed through an interactive visualization tool that enables the exploration of the knotted protein structures and their folding processes. The code used for this research is an extension of the 3DNA software package and is publicly available by integrating the knotted protein database and the molecular dynamics simulations. The research is also accompanied by a comprehensive tutorial that explains the code and the statistical approach used in the analysis. The research is also discussed in the context of the ongoing debate regarding the intrinsic versus extrinsic nature of protein knots. The research is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations and compares the predicted folding processes with existing experimental data. The research is a crucial step towards understanding the mysterious relationship between protein knots and their folding processes

Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby generating versatile and practical models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new types of data. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a language model to generate phrasal alterations that maintain a word's part-of-speech, while a classifier module assesses the semantic changes. Human assessments of generated text show that the counterfactuals created by this framework are not only highly diverse but also often indistinguishable from human-generated text. When incorporated into a learning algorithm, this counterfactual data enhances the accuracy of a classifier on new data by at least 5% and as much as 10%. Moreover, we observe that employing counterfactuals with distinct degrees of semantic change enables the creation of models with varying levels of generalization. Human and objective evaluations of these models reveal they can indeed capture the causal framework of a task and excel at generalizing to new types of data. Counterfactual data generated by the DISCO framework is open to the public for use. The code can be found at https://github.com/google-research-datastudio/disco.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures allows for more precise alignment with the underlying graphene lattice. This finding provides the first experimental evidence for remote epitaxy and suggests that this process can be controlled with temperature to produce desired superstructures. Moreover, a theoretical model was developed to provide in-depth analysis of this case study. The results indicate that the rotation trend can be understood through a simple surface energy vs. anisotropic lattice mismatch model. This relationship could potentially be applied to predict suitable systems for remote epitaxy, giving guidance on how to experimentally verify this process for various materials and combinations. The potential for rotating domains to contribute to unique transport properties in remote epitaxy is also discussed. The results of this research could open up a new pathway for the synthesis of mismatched materials with desired electronic properties. By leveraging these methods, our approach can efficiently handle large portfolios and accurately compute moments of the probability function within seconds. We primarily focus on the long-only strategy and develop an adaptable method for this type of investment. By representing the stock market as a geometric space, our cumulative distribution function enables a score for each portfolio based on the percentage of its returns exceeding a certain threshold. We derived closed-form equations for the first four moments and an innovative algorithm for computing all other moments, demonstrating a direct connection between the cross-sectional returns and the moments of the distribution. All of our methods are highly versatile, covering scenarios including when asset returns are equal. We used our score-based approach to design new performance metrics and found the portfolios it produced less concentrated and less prone to high risks than those from the mean-variance model. We found our score-based approach to be effective in reducing risk even when there are anomalies in the data. Additionally, we found that our score-based approach outperforms the mean-variance approach when there are anomalies in the data. We validated our methods with real-world data, including the S\&P 500 index, and found them to be highly effective. We made our code publicly available for other researchers to use and further develop our methods.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to provide personalized results for individual users. In this study, we explore the potential of wearable data and its surrounding environment to enhance machine learning performance through multi-modal fusion techniques. By combining data from the wearers themselves and their physical surroundings, we achieve better overall performance compared to traditional single-modal approaches. As an example application, we demonstrate a personalized sports coach that uses a combination of data from wearers and their surroundings to provide advice on training routines, sleep schedules, and diet. This approach results in improved performance in multiple sports, including running, swimming, and cycling, with a notable increase in efficiency - our models achieve similar performance with 50% less data. This progress comes despite the fact that wearable data often has limited labeling, which poses another significant challenge in this domain. To address this issue, we introduce a technique called multi-modal fusion with latent variables that effectively exploits correlations between different data types, leading to significant improvements over single-modal approaches. This technique proves particularly effective in tackling the challenge of limited labeling. As a complementary effort, we explore an alternative approach using a less complex model that can be trained in an efficient, online fashion. This approach proves effective in certain scenarios, but its performance is less consistent compared to our primary solution. Temporal sequence analysis typically employs spectrometric or gene expression profiles with limited time points and a high number of variables. Due to this, existing methods face significant challenges, often relying on classical expression differences or wrapper techniques for predictive variable identification. A key issue lies in the small sample size common in such studies. In contrast, our proposed supervised learning approach, Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time, successfully tackles these challenges by creating a low-dimensional grid mapping for temporal sequences. A hidden Markov model and relevance learning help the algorithm handle limited data samples and pinpoint important time points. Through a case study involving breast cancer cell gene expression profiles, we demonstrate the effectiveness of STTM in predicting the survival probabilities of new patients. Our results indicate that models trained on just four time points can effectively capture the temporal sequence data, proving that a small number of time points can be sufficient for analyzing temporal sequences. Furthermore, our study highlights the advantage of using relevance learning to identify key time points that are specific to each patient and provide valuable additional information. Ultimately, our algorithm offers a versatile solution for analyzing temporal sequences in various applications. The implementation of STTM is available online as an R package.

We tackle current, striking discrepancies in flavor anomalies observed within the $K$ and $B$ meson systems, specifically addressing CP-violating Kaon decay and lepton-flavor universality violation in $B$ meson decays, with the introduction of heavy flavorful vector boson masses around the TeV scale. These new particles interact with standard model gauge fields and interfere with processes involving gluons, generating constraints from matrix unity preservation. Our framework also suggests the presence of heavy scalar and tensor particles, although their masses and properties become derived factors of the vector boson masses, offering possibilities for their direct or indirect detection. With the interplay of flavour and collider constraints, our model maintains the freedom to explain both flavour and collider anomalies with parameter settings that keep it within the reach of ongoing and forthcoming experiments. Our prediction can be tested at the Large Hadron Collider through direct production of these new particles or through searches for resonances in diboson processes. Furthermore, our framework offers multiple avenues for verification in forthcoming $B$-factory and $B$-meson dedicated facilities, as well as in deep underground direct detection experiments, potentially uncovering all components of this model through multiple facets. The proposed vector boson masses in the range of 2-7 TeV will define the landscape of this model until direct production at a future 100 TeV collider either confirms or refutes it. Our work highlights the significance of thoroughly exploring flavour-anomaly explanations in extensions of the standard model that aim to address its most pressing problems. Levenshtein initially introduced the sequence reconstruction problem in 2001.
It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and yields distinct outputs at a decoder.
These outputs represent the probabilities of different sequences being transmitted.
The objective is to determine the fewest number of transmissions needed to accurately
reconstruct the original sequence.
It has been proven that this number equals the maximum number of distinct outputs
obtained during a single transmission, though this maximum can be challenging to
achieve programmatically even for basic transmission models like erasure, symmetric
discrete memoryless, and binary symmetric channels.
In this research, we explore the sequence reconstruction problem when the set consists
of permutations of integers that satisfy a certain linear equation and demonstrate its
connection to another well-known problem, the shortest path problem, by presenting a
more efficient algorithm to solve it. Additionally, we analyze the sequence reconstruction
problem for certain transmission models and provide recommendations on optimal strategies. 
Our results include proving that the sequence can be reconstructed from a single transmission
for a specific model, determining the minimum number of transmissions required for another
model to be $\lceil \log_2 k \rceil$ where $k$ represents the size of the set, and providing a more
efficient algorithm to solve it than the initial proposal by Levenshtein. 
Our research also explores new transmission models such as the insertion-deletion channel
and a multi-letter transmission model in which each letter of the sequence is observed as
a vector by the decoder, and we discuss the implications of these models on the sequence
reconstruction problem. 
Our work is a part of a larger project aimed at preparing a book about the sequence
reconstruction problem and its applications, including protein structure prediction from
genomic data, phylogenetic analysis, molecular dynamics, and protein function prediction
from sequence data. 
These applications involve other computational problems such as the traveling salesman problem,
protein folding problem, alignment of sequences, molecular alignment, and prediction of
protein secondary structures, and we provide a survey of the sequence reconstruction problem
in these contexts, presenting new algorithms and evaluating existing ones for these problems. 
Our research is focused primarily on protein structures and mutations of proteins but it
also explores other types of molecular structures such as DNA, RNA, carbohydrates and
lipids, and it discusses various computational tools and databases related to these
structures and mutations available at http://www.ksu.edu.tr/~yildiz/.

Research on using deep learning to identify musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand the scope of identification in a few-shot learning scenario. We enhance prototypical networks with a hierarchical loss function that takes into account the relational data, resulting in a framework that learns both instrument features and their place in the hierarchical structure. When tested on a recently created dataset consisting of 100 classes, our approach showed significant improvement over baseline methods and even generalizes effectively to unfamiliar classes when given just a handful of examples. Compared to a non-hierarchical approach, our method achieves a 27% increase in average accuracy across 27 novel classes and reduces the gap between open and closed-world few-shot learning by half. Moreover, our technique proves effective at generating pseudo labels for unsupervised cases, resulting in a 11% boost in open-world closed-set accuracy. The code is available at https://github.com/sonicsonic89/Musical-Instrument-FSL.

This conclusive finding addresses two unresolved conjectures from "The TASEP speed process" and enables us to develop the ASEP speed process. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts are being made by both humans and machines to provide the etymology of the used abbreviations, although their accuracy varies greatly. Presently, there is no universally accepted measure to assess the correctness of such provided definitions. This paper proposes a novel metric, centered on the concept of set similarity, to evaluate the efficacy of these proposed definitions when compared to the actual meanings. This proposed metric can be applied across multiple domains and also offers a straightforward method for identifying definitions considered distantly similar. To illustrate this metric's applicability, it is put to use in analyzing three distinct domains - movie titles, software names, and textual communications. Furthermore, this paper addresses a secondary challenge, which involves distinguishing the proposed definitions from other nearby words whose meanings might be related but are not definitions at all. To tackle this, a straightforward ranking mechanism based on the cosine similarity of word embeddings is introduced. This proposed metric and method for defining nearby words are then incorporated into a machine learning model, which in turn enhances the model's performance in predicting the meanings of abbreviations in unknown texts. Experimental outcomes across various domains demonstrate substantial gains in this ability. Additionally, this model is capable of distinguishing definitions from related words with higher accuracy. Consequently, this paves the way for effectively handling definitions of unknown abbreviations in machine learning models. In these cases, stable atom-molecule pair formation can occur due to collisions that transfer one unit of spin. However, in systems where light-based association distinguishes between different magnetic states, stable atom-molecule pair formation can occur due to collisions that transfer two units of spin, resulting in an effective three-body recombination equivalent to collisions that transfer one unit of spin. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. In this work, we demonstrate the ability to replicate the $\mathcal{ T}$-wall, a hallmark of topological materials, in quantum gas systems subject to an harmonic potential and light-matter interaction, and show that this model can be used to monitor the topological effects and associated edge states in quantum systems exposed to dissipation. Furthermore, we illustrate the capability to observe the $\mathcal{ T}$-wall in quantum gas systems consisting of two coupled circular disks, a setup amenable to experimental observation. The findings of this work have the potential to contribute to a deeper comprehension of topological effects in quantum systems and provide a framework for designing artificial systems that can replicate the behavior of topological materials. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations to quickly determine visible regions and integrate illumination maps. This approach allows for real-time shadow rendering and visible region rendering, making it suitable for real-time applications and efficiently integrating with deep models. To evaluate our approach, we investigate its applicability to three inverse problems: scene layout estimation, texture identification, and whole-scene reconstruction. Our results demonstrate that our approach can generate realistic synthetic images, outperforming other approximation methods, and surprisingly, can be used to interpret real-world images, revealing shadow-based clues that can inform other image processing techniques. Additionally, our approach facilitates the efficient training of a deep renderer model on data without ground truth annotations. Source code is available at https://github.com/daostin/differentiable-renderer. Our project webpage is at https://instintin.github.io/differentiable-renderer/. Our video results can be viewed at https://youtu.be/8Q6fO5u8QdA. Our approach has release permission for commercial use.

A popular technique, widely used for enhancing video playback on television and recording, is interlacing. This technique doubles the perceived frame rate without boosting the bandwidth, yet generates undesirable effects like visual distortion and flicker during playback. Present methods fail to balance real-time processing with satisfactory quality. They either prioritize real-time processing over visual clarity or improve quality at the expense of processing speed. This research proposes a groundbreaking approach utilizing deep convolutional neural networks, capable of delivering both high-quality results and real-time performance. Diverging from traditional super-resolution models that assume pixel invariance, our approach incorporates data from both interlaced half-frames to regenerate missing scan lines. This innovative system runs on a single GPU, achieving real-time processing speeds through the use of a shared architecture. Comparative tests confirm that this method surpasses all existing techniques in both accuracy and processing speed. In particular, our approach demonstrates a notable 2x improvement in PSNR over the current top-performing model, while also outperforming all competitors in real-time processing. This groundbreaking approach proposes a new direction for the development of high-performance systems capable of processing video. This could pave the way for the widespread adoption of advanced techniques like deep learning across consumer electronics. Moreover, our research is open to feedback and open for anyone to build upon. The code and model have been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/kuangck/ISR. The standard scaled Wigner matrix and its corresponding semi-circular distribution, particularly its 2kth moment which relates to non-crossing pair-partitions of the set {1, 2,... 2k}, has been extensively studied. Building upon existing knowledge, this paper contributes a broader extension that also reveals novel insights. Given an $n \times n$ symmetric matrix with independently distributed entries under certain assumptions, our study confirms that a limiting spectral distribution indeed exists with probability or certainty. However, the existing results for standardized Wigner matrices or their equivalents are surpassed, requiring instead the consideration of non-crossing partitions of a larger set. Moreover, the proposed method introduces a key improvement, significantly simplifying the required assumptions on the matrix entries. The underlying idea involves applying a diagonalizing unitary matrix that minimizes the operator norm of a modified Wigner matrix, achieved through the Stieltjes transformation and the determination of a specific spectral distribution that concentration inequalities can ensure with high probability. The outcome directly leads to the proof of spectral distribution limits, while the introduced technique also facilitates the proof of a central limit theorem for linear spectral statistics. The central concept of this paper is also the basis for extending similar results to non-hermitian eigenvectors, confirming the convergence of empirical eigenvector ensembles to specific limits, and establishing the validity of a CLT for non-hermitian matrix variables. The derived conditions are shown to be tighter than existing bounds, thereby further improving the applicability to various important situations. The resulting tools are then utilized to solve two distinct problems. Firstly, under moderate scaling with an exponentially decaying scalar product structure, or under a specific condition involving a deterministic variance profile, we establish the convergence of empirical eigenvectors to their corresponding limits with probability or certainty. The validation of a CLT for linear spectral statistics in these cases follows naturally. Secondly, the previously unknown spectral distribution limits for standardized non-hermitian matrices with independently distributed entries, specifically confirmed for the case of a complex general Wigner matrix, contribute significantly to solving an open problem posed by Bourgade. The determined spectral distribution limits provide a crucial stepping stone for validating a CLT for linear spectral statistics in these non-hermitian matrix scenarios. The derived spectral distribution limits can also be applied to model and analyze various critical phenomena in random matrix theory. The used techniques, centered on the concentration inequality for the modified Wigner matrix and its operator norm, introduce a novel approach that can be useful for solving other related problems. Recent studies have uncovered the prevalence of gradient masking in purportedly robust adversarial defenses. Consequently, defense strategies based on this concept are considered ineffective and can be readily bypassed. Notably, research into quantifying the occurrence and extent of gradient masking across different networks remains limited. This study addresses this gap by exploring the mensurability of gradient masking as a multi-dimensional rather than a binary phenomenon. In addition, we introduce novel metrics designed to evaluate the presence of gradient masking in diverse neural networks. These proposed metrics not only offer computational advantages but also facilitate comparative assessments between models without necessitating elaborate tailor-made attacks. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the efficacy of these metrics in gauging the prevalence of gradient masking across different network configurations. The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes an innovative energy-based objective function to optimize model performance. Furthermore, theoretical justification is provided and experimental results validate the benefits of this formulation in both supervised and semi-supervised settings. Our findings reveal that optimizing this new function yields significant improvements in prediction accuracy and calibration. Additionally, uncertainty-based models exhibit improved performance when compared to their confident-only counterparts. Our results also demonstrate that models utilizing this formulation achieve superior performance in compared to standard softmax, with minimal additional computational requirements. Our code is available at https://github.com/kuangqi/kesm. Our work provides a critical step towards developing machine learning models that accurately quantify their own uncertainty.

In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and the mechanisms that lead to regime shifts is highly beneficial. This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators, competing for a common prey, engage in explicit interference. The model is reworked to display a singular perturbation with rapid prey movement and slower predator movement, allowing for a regime close to the singular Hopf bifurcation to be analyzed. Near this point, the model exhibits chaotic, mixed-mode oscillations, consisting of long-lasting, concatenated periods of small and large amplitude movements. These eventually transition into the model's steady-state equilibrium. To determine the initiating factors behind a large amplitude oscillation in the mixed-mode orbit, the model is reduced to a suitable normal form, located at the singular Hopf point. The resulting normal form reveals a separating surface that distinguishes two forms of oscillations, and the occurrence of a large amplitude oscillation depends on whether the trajectory crosses this boundary. Conditions derived from the normal form can predict whether the model will enter a regime of steady-state equilibrium before returning to the singular Hopf point. These conditions include the rate of movement within the parameter that causes the singular Hopf bifurcation, as well as the magnitude of this parameter. The theory developed is applied to provide early warning indicators for the extinction of the two predator species in the two-level ecosystem. The model's mechanisms for the emergence of chaotic, mixed-mode oscillations are also clarified, and the implications for the discovery of similar phenomena in other models of population dynamics are explored. The methods used to analyze the model can be applied to any system that exhibits a singular Hopf bifurcation, and thus has broader applications to the study of population dynamics and regime shifts in ecological systems. Recently, cache coherence protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade have gained more recognition due to their minimalistic design, potential for increased performance, and reduced energy consumption. However, these protocols introduce memory instruction reordering, leading to additional complexity in program behavior analysis. In this research, we introduce a protocol that combines the advantages of SIP-3D and COHI protocols, considering only local conflicts and maintaining spatial coherence, thereby achieving significant performance gains with limited increases in memory access latency. Our analysis reveals that this hybrid protocol yields a 2-fold improvement in program speed with a mere 10% increase in memory access latency, ultimately leading to a 20% decrease in overall energy consumption. Furthermore, we show that this protocol permits program slowdowns due to conflict memory accesses to be minimized. Additionally, we present a design of cache coherence protocol based on reordering memory instructions that demonstrates its practical applicability. This design can be utilized across various processor architectures and provides a flexible framework for optimizing different components of the system. Our study also introduces novel program models that facilitate the analysis of program behavior in the presence of cache coherence issues. These models are capable of analyzing both finite and infinite programs, offering a novel approach to understanding how programs interact with cache coherence protocols. Our research provides a comprehensive framework for exploring cache coherence protocols and is applicable to various processor architectures, making it an invaluable tool for conducting further studies in this domain. Our work is coupled with an open-source implementation that is available for public use and can be employed for conducting additional research, as well as for conducting simulations and creating new protocols. This implementation is compatible with FinSim, a Verilog-based finite-state machine simulator that can be used for studying the behavioral interactions of programs and cache coherence protocols at a finite-state machine level. FinSim is also an open-source project and is available for public use along with our cache coherence protocol research. This combined set of research and implementation is intended to stimulate community engagement and invite further contributions in this domain. Our study is also designed to be modular, allowing it to be extended across various processor architectures and capable of accommodating novel protocols. Additionally, our research is accompanied by a set of previously unresolved finite program instances that have been specifically created to evaluate and benchmark various cache coherence protocols. These program instances are unique and distinct from other program models that are available in the public domain. Our research is focused on exploring cache coherence protocols for asynchronous systems and is intended to be a starting point for community engagement. X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this could potentially aid healthcare providers in directing limited resources towards high-risk patients.  Unfortunately, the relationship between these X-ray features and clinical outcomes in COVID-19 patients remains poorly understood.  A major obstacle in exploring this connection is the lack of a suitable imaging analysis framework capable of processing high-volume medical data.  To address this challenge, we developed a specialized pipeline utilizing attention-based convolutional neural networks to analyze X-ray images and extract semantic features.  This approach was successfully applied to three different types of medical images: COVID-19 chest X-rays, X-rays of patients with pulmonary embolism, and X-rays of patients with pleural effusion.  The results showed that our method can identify distinct patterns in each type of image, even when presented with limited and low-quality data.  Furthermore, we found that the extracted semantic features correlate with clinical assessments, specifically in the case of COVID-19 patients with severe symptoms.  Additionally, our model was able to distinguish between normal and abnormal lung images with high accuracy.  The code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghulammustafa/Attention-Patch-Net. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the model learns tenuous associations between objects and relationships. Our solution involves introducing an auxiliary task to distinguish real from fabricated object-relation pairs. By incorporating this additional task, we observed a significant decrease in the model's false positives. Our proposed method, dubbed Anti-Confusing Baseline (ACB), serves as a starting point for further improvement. ACB's effectiveness is demonstrated through various experiments, including reducing the models' false positives by a factor of over 3 times on the VCAD dataset and achieving a notable improvement (by 5.3%) on the MS-Coco dataset when compared to the current state-of-the-art method, considering only baseline models. Current cutting-edge neural code models excel at generating individual code segments but often struggle with complex tasks, like entire function code production. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that leverages static code analysis for weak supervision. Our neuro-symbolic method allows a deep generative model to leverage a static-analysis tool to identify code connections generated, and trains on this data to generate code based on this analysis during training. When tested on the task of creating full Java functions within existing classes, our results reveal our approach outperforms state-of-the-art transformer models and a method that tries to learn program meanings. Our neuro-symbolic approach also succeeds in producing code that static analysis considers safe, whereas the other methods often fail in this regard. Our code and model are available at https://github.com/gh0lst/CodeGenerationNSM.

Real-time anomaly detection in continuous data streams presents difficulties for conventional and advanced methods due to shifting concepts and ongoing learning requirements. Existing approaches, such as using hash functions or nearest neighbors with fixed memory, can struggle to accommodate frequent fluctuations, remove smooth outliers, and adapt to deep neural network architectures. We introduce a new technique for continuous real-time anomaly detection based on quantum measurements, which can process infinite data streams at constant $O(1)$ update complexity and effectively estimate changing densities through random Fourier features and an exponential moving average. This approach was thoroughly evaluated by comparing it to 12 prominent algorithms for real-time anomaly detection on 12 diverse data streams. The results show our quantum-inspired method consistently excels in terms of precision, outperforming top-performing algorithms by an average of 5% and sometimes achieving a 20% increase in precision. Furthermore, our approach demonstrates robustness in handling infinite data streams and adapts quickly to changing environments, achieving a 20% improvement in average relative change and a 10% improvement in average relative standard deviation. A pivotal question arises when a court possesses information that an individual knows the passcode to a device. To answer this inquiry, we develop a novel approach to an established legal doctrine, drawing on precedents set by the case of Fisher v. US. Our overarching objective is to create a framework that clarifies whether any action taken has already provided implicit evidence accessible to the authorities. Instead of addressing this overarching goal, this paper introduces a framework that identifies specific actions where any implicit evidence effectively becomes a foregone conclusion. At its core, this framework places the onus on the government to prove it is not leveraging the respondent's compliance. Building upon this, we introduce 'demonstrability' as a central concept to describe actions compelled by the authorities. Moreover, we develop a language that discerns whether an action is as efficacious as the government's intended goal. Subsequently, we apply our framework to evaluate the compelled actability of several cryptographic tools, such as decryption, multifactor authentication, and hash functions, and arrive at a novel conclusion about compelled decryption. Notably, we observe that compelled decryption does not equate to compelled access. Lastly, we explore the interconnections between our proposed framework and other theoretical concepts, such as computationally induced equivalence and statistically induced equivalence. This framework is relevant to the ongoing debate over compelled decryption in the context of encrypted devices and may contribute to the legal and technological discourse surrounding encryption policy. Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary non-negative functions.

This research is extended to CSPs with constraints that have multiple possible values. The only restriction for such constraints is that they contain an element that is at least as acceptable as all other elements.

A new PTAS is presented for general-valued CSPs with constraints that have distinct values, such as 0 and 1, but with specific limitations. The technique was previously applicable to classes where Baker's approach worked, except possibly fractionally-treewidth-fragile classes. The property is essential for a new intractable class, called the Diagonalised Claw, where all constraints are fractional winnows, i.e., they only restrict at least one element and allow all other elements. This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we verified the reliability of the stellar seismic parameters through multiple analyses. Additionally, we ruled out any potential errors due to instrumental or analytical limitations. Furthermore, by eliminating alternative explanations such as stellar composition affecting its rotation or signs of spin-down through mergers, we confirmed that our explanation holds. To place KIC 9267654 in a broader context, we compared its internal rotation to other stars and identified the smallest discrepancy so far between core and surface rotation rates. With an estimated mass of 1.5 solar masses, KIC 9267654 is now among the most significant discoveries of internal stellar rotation variations. Its unusual internal rotation pattern suggests the possibility of the star having experienced a merger with a smaller companion, which contributed to its enhanced mass while affecting its internal rotation dynamics. This finding opens up theoretical and observational avenues for further exploration and could provide insight into the merger process and its effects on the host star's evolution. Moreover, detecting similar cases will help establish a typology for merger-induced stellar evolution and possibly identify merger remnants that contain a substantial share of the merged object's mass. By incorporating KIC 9267654 in a broader study of hybrid stars with both main sequence and giant characteristics, we highlight the significance of investigating the possible merger history for each individual star. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and the harm it causes. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, their limitations become apparent during unexpected events. These events often result in sudden shifts in language use, making it difficult for existing systems to adapt. Furthermore, the small amount of data available for training models in these situations further complicates the issue. 

To address this problem, our novel approach, called Generalizable Fake News Detection, is proposed. This method involves first identifying the language use that is characteristic of truth-telling on social media platforms. It does this by analyzing verified and true posts and identifying the key features that set them apart. 

Next, it employs a different technique called adversarial training to enhance the model's performance. This model is then tested on data related to an unexpected event and a long-term trend, with the results showing its capability to adapt quickly to new situations. Compared to traditional methods, our method demonstrates a notable capability for generalization, with results indicating a significant reduction in fake news being mistaken for true news. 

The model's ability to distinguish itself from low-quality models is also evident, with our method outperforming baseline models that suffer from performance degradation. The generalization of our approach is verified across various platforms and after a comprehensive analysis of various generalization techniques, it is concluded that the proposed method yields the best outcome. $$

This is in contrast to a previous study which found that a specific non-local equation with $f(u)$ term and without the fractional dissipation term can have a smooth solution over an infinite period of time, given certain conditions. This paper investigates the age of information (AoI) in a discrete-time status updating system that employs the Ber/G/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that utilizing a two-dimensional state vector which simultaneously monitors AoI and packet age enables derivation of the stationary AoI distribution via analysis of a constituted stochastic process. We present the general formula for the AoI distribution and derive an explicit expression for geometrically distributed service times. A comparison between discrete and continuous AoI is provided, including mean values for the M/M/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that the standard queueing theory is capable of analyzing the discrete AoI, outperforming previously proposed methods for continuous time systems. Finally, we examine the M/M/1/1 system with varying arrival rates to showcase the impact on discrete AoI distributions. This study offers novel insights into the AoI and provides a framework for analyzing this performance metric in complex queueing scenarios. This research is an extension of a previously presented study at the 2021 IEEE Conference on Decision and Control, now featuring additional results.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad. Further, a method is described to construct GCM pairs and quadruples using Reed-Muller codes. This is followed by discussion on the applications of multi-dimensional GCM and potential research directions. Few examples and GCM pairs in higher-dimensional spaces are provided as an appendix. 

Keywords: Golay complementary arrays, multi-dimensional spaces, omnidirectional precoding, ring theory, construction methods.

We introduce an infinite family of recursive formulas for calculating the counts of binary integer partitions that fulfill specific divisibility criteria, giving an early formulation for a long-standing conjecture related to the sums of squareful numbers. Additionally, we derive an explicit formula for calculating the nth term of a particular sequence that meets a particular divisibility condition, providing a novel proof for a sequence of numbers previously shown to be equivalent to a specific family of powers of two over a particular set of numbers. Our approach utilizes a novel multiset-generated sequence framework, offering a unique perspective on the interconnection between recursive formulas, Toeplitz determinants, and Chinese Remainder Theorem applications. Strong nonlocality, a phenomenon where systems demonstrate nonlocality without entanglement, can be seen in multipartite states with certain properties. Unextendible product bases (UPBs) have shown nonlocality without entanglement in previous research, and their strong quantum nonlocality is therefore a topic of interest. However, many UPBs of minimal size cannot demonstrate this strong quantum nonlocality. In this research, a series of UPBs of various larger sizes for systems of three and four parties were constructed in dimensions of $d_A, d_B, d_C, d_D \geq 3$. It was also shown that these UPBs have strong quantum nonlocality, answering open questions from Halder and others, and providing a connection between this phenomenon and UPBs. To locally distinguish one such UPB in $3 \otimes 3 \otimes 4$, an entanglement-assisted protocol was proposed, using less entanglement than previously known protocols. To locally distinguish one such UPB in $3 \otimes 3 \otimes 5$ or $3 \otimes 4 \otimes 4$, another protocol was proposed. It used less entanglement than previously known protocols, but in the case of $3 \otimes 4 \otimes 4$, the number of qubits needed was optimal. Furthermore, this research investigated the relationship between strong quantum nonlocality and the convex roof dimension (CRD). It was found that in systems of two parties, CRD is equivalent to strong quantum nonlocality. However, this is not the case for systems of more than two parties, as demonstrated by one such UPB in $3 \otimes 3 \otimes 4$, where CRD is two and strong quantum nonlocality is present. This answers an open question from Halder and others. This research therefore provides various connections between UPBs, strong quantum nonlocality, entanglement-assisted local distinguishability, and CRD. It also raises questions about whether certain UPBs of minimal size can demonstrate strong quantum nonlocality and whether there are systems in dimension $d \otimes d \otimes d$ with strong quantum nonlocality. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with the goal of extracting unique codes representing each data point's identity. These codes are then used to derive the data points' position and category, ultimately achieving the goal of feature extraction. Our results demonstrate that our framework surpasses current methods in both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. Additionally, our framework's flexibility allows it to be applied to a variety of real-world image datasets, yielding impressive performance. We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while exhibiting quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within a class of twisted wreath structures. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs. This new family includes the likes of $T_{\frac{3}{2}}(3,4)$ and $T_{\frac{3}{2}}(3,5)$, as well as all $T_{\frac{3}{2}}(p^f, q^f)$ structures for prime numbers $p$ and $q$ where $p \neq q$. Moreover, a particular type of these graphs, specifically those featuring a prime vertex stabilizer, contribute to answering a question posed by Li and Praeger. Our results are derived from a method of constructing twisted wreath structures and the application of a recent theorem by Giudici, Li, and Praeger.

Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance is evaluated under high-dimensional conditions and compared with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model size. Notably, when applied to categorical data from the Life Insurance Industry, our method reveals the importance of age in risk modeling. Additionally, a user-friendly R function incorporating the two-step algorithm is made available as part of the rz package. A research extension is also explored where the Group Lasso is utilized as part of a larger generalization. A related manuscript has been published in Journal of Statistical Theory and Practice but the extension researched here is novel. 

Keywords: Clustered models, Group Lasso, model selection, sparsity, z-score.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique on a vast knowledge base like Wikidata outperform conventional T5 models in various evaluation benchmarks. Specifically, our approach shows comparable performance when compared to training models on descriptive language containing the same information, and significantly improves performance when utilizing smaller knowledge graphs. One key advantage of this method is the absence of a requirement to synchronize knowledge graphs with text data, making it highly suitable for large-scale knowledge graphs. We also observe that models pre-trained with this approach effectively leverage the learned structured knowledge to enhance their general language abilities. We believe our approach to be a significant step towards enhancing the ability of LLMs to manage structured knowledge and facilitate the effective use of vast knowledge graphs. We have made our implementation and experiments available at https://github.com/ghrua/StructAware-LLMs.

When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, are fitted with sensors that can accurately track the direction of gravity. Based on this assumption, the axis of cameras in such configurations can be assumed to be aligned or adjusted accordingly, thus reducing the necessary alignment parameters to one dimension. Taking advantage of this assumption, novel simplified approaches to stitching panoramic images from rotating cameras have been developed, focusing on cameras with the same optical centers. Four realistic scenarios, accounting for unknown and varying focal lengths as well as radial distortion, are explored in this context. Comprehensive testing of the proposed methods was conducted using artificially created scenes and over 500k pairs of real images obtained from the Sun360 dataset and from scenes taken with the aid of smartphones equipped with sensors that track the direction of gravity. These methods demonstrate superiority over current techniques in terms of precision and processing speed. Furthermore, practical applications of these methods in generating 360-degree images and videos from multiple views are also highlighted. Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results when approximating the anti-aliased effect through multiple triangles. In an attempt to rectify this issue, this study introduces a straightforward yet high-performance algorithm utilizing two triangles to replicate fan-shaped line joins via alpha operation. Our findings indicate that this technique yields a genuine anti-aliasing effect while reducing memory consumption, raising frame rates, and preventing overlap rendering. Furthermore, our solution also offers a straightforward approach for rendering curved lines and eliminates the necessity for precise vector data, thereby making it suitable for various map applications. Our method is then employed in the development of a real-time Navi-system and demonstrates its effectiveness in real-world scenarios. Additionally, our technique is compared to alternative anti-aliasing methods, including the utilization of pixel shaders, multi-triangles, and the Sutherland-Hodgman algorithm, and showcases its advantages in terms of memory consumption, computational demands, and visual outcome. In conclusion, our proposed algorithm serves as a straightforward and high-performance solution for inducing the anti-aliasing effect in line joins on vector maps, and is readily applicable across various map applications. Lastly, our technique is made available for public use via the SourceForge website.

In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the work of Franke and Nielson, we establish the convergence rate of this new interpolation formula, demonstrating a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}(h^4)$ when compared to the multivariate multiquadric. It has been observed that employing this new interpolation function leads to an increased rate of convergence compared to the multiquadric, especially under conditions of high smoothness. It has also been found that the optimal method of determining weights minimizes the error in a manner consistent with the minimum norm property of the multivariate multiquadric. We further investigate the relationship between this new interpolation function and the widely used piecewise linear interpolation method, demonstrating that it converges at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(h^2)$ when compared to the linear method under smoothness conditions of order 2. It is also shown that, like the linear method, it exhibits a first-order Knopnitz inequality. To verify the effectiveness of this new interpolation function, we apply it to a common problem in statistics - the estimation of a density function based on empirical data. We compare our results to those obtained using the multivariate multiquadric and empirical evidence suggests a preference for the new function. Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A recent advance in artificial intelligence has enabled the creation of a dataset containing images describing various weather scenarios.
However, this dataset is currently the only comprehensive resource for weather image data.
The developers of this dataset recognized the importance of capturing diverse conditions found on German roads, thus creating the RFS dataset.
It contains  15000 images categorized into five main categories: rain, snow, night driving, fog, and sheltered roads.

To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. Notably, with only 0.8 million parameters, the DPCRN model achieved an overall mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.57 in the wideband scenario of the Interspeech 2021 DNS challenge. Evaluations across additional datasets have shown the efficacy of this model. Additionally, comparisons with other models revealed the DPCRN's superiority in low-complexity configurations, verifying its efficiency in speech separation tasks. The model's code is available online at https://github.com/HuangHaoChen/DPCRN.

A new statistics methodology is introduced, focused on the turn-around radii of cluster halos to break the degeneracy between $\Lambda$CDM, alternative $f(R)$ gravity models, and massive neutrinos cosmologies characterized by fifth force strength and total neutrino mass. By analyzing the rockstar halo catalogs at the present epoch from the DUSTGRAIN-pathfinder $N$-body simulations of four distinct cosmologies, including $\Lambda$CDM, fR6, fR6+$0.06$eV, and fR5+$0.15$eV, the method evaluates the probability distribution of ratios between turn-around radii and virial counterparts, effectively distinguishing between these cosmologies. It is found that fR6 and fR5+$0.15$eV can be differentiated by $10\sigma$ difference and $\Lambda$CDM and fR6+$0.06$eV can be differentiated by $3.2\sigma$ difference. Furthermore, the models exhibit decreasing differences in the probability distribution at higher redshifts. The method provides a new approach to analyzing the fundamental properties of cluster halos and offers a promising technique for distinguishing between various cosmological models through sub-$\sigma$ level precision achieved in the turn-around to virial radius ratios. This could potentially be applied to future precise halo radius measurements from cosmological surveys like Euclid and LSST. By utilizing cluster halos at $z=0.5$, the method can boost the sensitivity difference up to $5.2\sigma$. However, in order to achieve reliable results at these higher redshifts, more accurate initial conditions are required. The turn-around to virial radius ratios show less model dependence at higher redshifts, which makes them more suitable for distinguishing between cosmological models at these stages. In this research, we establish a precise inequality relating anisotropic mean curvature and capacity in the L^p norm, applicable to any bounded area in R^n with smooth borders.
As a result, we derive inequalities including an anisotropic Willmore inequality, a sharp anisotropic Minkowski inequality, and a sharp volumetric anisotropic Minkowski inequality. Our proof involves a novel approach in nonlinear potential theory recently described in the reference provided. A key proof tool involves a mysterious mapping that originates from a mystery-based approach. The mystery behind this approach is then clarified, and the associated mystery map is now understood to be a specific case of a more comprehensive mapping that follows from a more general approach in nonlinear potential theory. Consequently, both the willmore-type inequality and the minkowski-type inequality can be formulated in a more general framework of complete, embedded, and minimal surfaces in a given anisotropic Riemannian space. Moreover, this general framework also yields a novel, sharp anisotropic Minkowski-type inequality for certain specific geometries that were previously unknown. The novel results presented in this research can be found in the references provided. The purpose of this research is the presentation of one novel result. The novel result presented in this research has a corresponding counterpart in the context of generalised Willmore-type inequalities. However, this counterpart has not been formally established. The reason for this is because the associated potential-type energy functional is not weakly stable. The associated mystery-based approach, therefore, cannot provide the required inequality. The associated potential-type energy functional includes the anisotropic Minkowski inequality, the anisotropic Minkowski inequality with volume constraints, and the anisotropic Minkowski inequality with surface area constraints. We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the particles varies according to the activity gradient and is influenced by a nonequilibrium phase transition. The resulting equilibrium states can be classified into two categories: one with asymmetry that increases over time and another where the particles display a tendency to move in opposite directions, also exhibiting a nonequilibrium phase transition. This phenomenon occurs in which the asymmetry of the structure is lost and it behaves like two separate particles that could be equated to a swimmer that switches direction. The coexistence of these two states occurs near a nonequilibrium critical point and we explore the possibility of observing this behavior with colloidal dimers. Additionally, we examine the influence of hydrodynamic interactions by comparing our findings with existing studies. Our most compelling discovery is that the nonequilibrium phase transition is possible even when the particles are in a state of thermal equilibrium as long as they exhibit an asymmetry in their movement. This finding opens up the possibility of studying the nonequilibrium phase transition further with colloidal dimers composed of different materials that have varying levels of asymmetry. The minimum strong shortest path cover with k-hops in a graph G is the smallest number of sets needed among all k-hops strong shortest path covers, where we also examine 2-hops covers for certain graphs and show the general k-hops cover problem is NP-complete. Specifically, we investigate the NP-hardness of computing exact values for some graphs and provide approximate algorithms for general graphs. Additionally, we analyze the performance of a 2-hops cover approach on various graphs, including some with known minimum strong shortest path cover values. Our results reveal interesting patterns of behavior for different graph types and highlight potential applications of this approach in efficient computation. Our methods also inspire a new approach to finding minimum strong shortest path covers, which can be used for other cover problems by restricting or modifying the underlying graph. As the number of frogs per site grows, the frog model's behavior shifts from transient to recurrent on a d-ary rooted tree. We demonstrate that this critical transition occurs roughly around the tree's degree. Additionally, we provide an accurate estimate for the critical value of the frog model, showing it lies between (d-1)/2 and d/2, and this interval becomes increasingly narrow as the tree's degree increases infinitely. Our findings are achieved through a new proof that the biased random walk's recurrence or transience directly influences the frog model's behavior, and we calculate the critical value using the walk's transience threshold and the tree's degree. We derive this threshold value using a diagram, and it offers an intuitive explanation for the frog model's transition. Our approach is an all-inclusive method, applicable to any rooted d-ary tree regardless of its connectivity. Moreover, it broadens the possibility of exploring more general k-frog models by considering a continuum of frog densities. Lastly, we propose a new research question related to the k-frog model on a cubic tree.

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a sampling-based method is employed to increase efficiency. Experimental results show that this approach yields a 1.5 times performance improvement compared to traditional distillation techniques. Furthermore, the proposed method achieves comparable performance to transfer learning when access to the original data is allowed. Additionally, the study demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach on a real-world computer vision application. A strong geodetic subset of a graph~$G$ comprises a selection of vertices~$S$, which allows for the coverage of the remaining vertices in~$G$, achieved by emitting geodetics between pairs of vertices in~$S$. The Strong Geodetic problem (SG) involves determining if a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$ have a subset of vertices~$S$, with $|S| \leq k$, which is strong geodetic. This problem has been proven to be NP-hard for all graphs. This study introduces the concept of strong geodetic graphs and examines the relationship between this new property and other existing graph properties, including metric, geodetic, and irreducible properties. Additionally, this study establishes upper and lower limits for the strong geodetic number in various types of graphs, including metric, geodetic, and chordal graphs. The ultimate goal of imitation learning is to develop efficient policies using nearly optimal expert examples. Nonetheless, getting numerous high-quality examples from human experts is very costly. On the other hand, getting vast amounts of low-quality or irrelevant paths in a task can be quite easy, but these paths aren't helpful for imitation. Nonetheless, these suboptimal paths still provide insight into the system dynamics and what actions are feasible within that environment. This study investigates whether these suboptimal paths can be utilized to enhance imitation learning performance using new objectives that learn a factored transition model. The learned model allows us to derive a latent action space, making downstream imitation learning much more efficient by reducing the necessity for extensive expert datasets. This is achieved by leveraging additional non-expert data. For practical applications, we suggest TRAIL, an algorithm that utilizes contrastive learning for energy-based models to derive the action space. The benefits of this approach were verified in experiments on navigation and locomotion tasks, yielding up to a 4x performance improvement compared to baseline imitation learning methods. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also prove and validate the Pareto distribution of PAC code computation complexity. Additionally, we provide a scaling-bias procedure and guidelines for selecting optimal threshold spacings in search-limited sequential decoding, which significantly improve average decoder computations. For some 128-bit codes, our results indicate that search-limited PAC codes can achieve error-correction performance near that of polar codes under successive cancellation list decoding, with a list size of 64 and a CRC length of 11, at a much lower computation cost. Furthermore, our technique is applicable to any PAC code generated by various design methods, such as successive cancellation list decoding and Kronecker factoring. To facilitate code design, we introduce the concept of design margin, defined as the gap between the code's error-correction performance and the polarized cutoff rate, providing a criterion for evaluating code excellence. We also identify distinct code regimes based on their design margin and computational complexity, which we seek to minimize. To this end, we investigate simple yet effective design codes, such as rate-1/2 PAC codes generated by all-zero sequences or random sequences, demonstrating excellent computational performance. However, such codes exhibit poor design margin and high error-correction error rates. Consequently, such codes should not be used for actual data transmission but can be employed as design codes. As alternatives to search-limited PAC codes, we examine conventional convolutional codes and certain low-rate PAC codes, which exhibit good computational performance but inferior error-correction performance. As design codes, these codes outperform our proposed PAC codes, which outperform them for actual data transmission. Still, our results indicate that PAC codes, despite their superior error-correction performance for low-rate codes, require large depth decoding computations. To mitigate this limitation, we suggest employing PAC codes with shallow depth computations followed by conventional error-correction techniques, such as list decoding or sequential decoding, for correct path detection. This hybrid approach combines the benefits of both codes, yielding superior error-correction performance at a lower computation

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in a single image frame. A mathematical transformation and a key point matching algorithm allow us to accurately estimate end-effector pose based on rotation and key point data. Enhanced system robustness is achieved through multiple predictions and a statistical analysis of model output. Experimental results show our system's ability to calibrate the end-effector with high precision (<5 mm, <25 degrees) when confronted with low-quality, real-world data rather than simulated data. Notably, our approach surpasses traditional approaches that utilize fiducial markers by eliminating the need for pre-deployment calibration, reducing overall system deployment time from several hours to just a few minutes. Additionally, our method can be employed for calibrating end-effectors with varied shapes, including those lacking critical points. Lastly, our system's ability to accurately estimate end-effector pose from a single image enables autonomous recalibration. 

This research is a critical component in the development of autonomous and collaborative robots that can safely work alongside people in complex, dynamically changing environments. Our system's ability to easily integrate with popular end-effector systems and easily deployable nature make it a practical solution for industrial and healthcare applications. 

Our approach involves two primary components: a pose estimation model that identifies the end-effector's position and rotation in relation to specific objects, and a key point detection model that pinpoints critical points on the end-effector in a single image. By combining these models with real-world depth camera data and mathematical transformations, we can accurately estimate the end-effector's pose even when the system is initially deployed. 

Our system's robustness is ensured through the use of multiple model predictions and a statistical analysis of the results. We validated our approach through a series of experiments using a variety of objects and end-effectors, achieving an average error of less than 5 mm and 25 degrees. Our system can be found at https://github.com/kaist-robotics/end-effector-calibration.

We further prove this word problem to be equivalent to the complement of a combined cyclic variant of several context-free languages, and for some of its generators, the combined cyclic variant of four deterministic context-free languages is sufficient. This relationship reveals that the time complexity of solving V's word problem deterministically is no more than quadratically scaling with input size. This result may be of interest to researchers in the field of combinatorial group theory and the development of combinatorial proofs for this word problem's undecidability. Additionally, this relationship leads to a proof that the complement of a cyclic variant of 4-letter context-free languages is Turing complete. This concept expands our understanding of how context-free languages can be used to represent computationally complex tasks. It also highlights the potential applications of this representation in the context of combinatorial group theory. Additionally, we explore the properties of a generalized version of this language when evaluated in different rational bases.
