In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. Current Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) applications often excel at extracting texture information but tend to produce vague boundary definitions. Expert medical analysts, for instance, primarily utilize organ edges when performing manual segmentations. Influenced by these observations, this study proposes Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), an easily integrable module that complements standard encoder-decoder networks, capable of prioritizing edge and texture information extraction. By incorporating the proposed EG-CNN module into common network architectures, significant improvements in edge detection accuracy were achieved, along with minimal declines in texture representation performance. Notably, EG-CNNs demonstrate particular advantage in complex medical imaging scenarios. Moreover, an accompanying easy-to-use open-source code is provided to facilitate the incorporation of EG-CNN modules into various CNN architectures. By doing so, the project offers a versatile solution that can be readily adapted for diverse edge-guided tasks. Experimental validation, encompassing both public datasets and real-world medical imaging cases, confirms the proposed approach's effectiveness. As a result, the open-source code is now available on GitHub at https://github.com/zwang84/Edge-Gated-CNN.

The success of medical image analysis using machine learning largely relies on high-quality datasets.  However, when these datasets contain biases, the models can learn them, compromising their ability to generalize and produce reliable results.  While research exists on developing machine learning models with fewer parameters that can handle low-resolution images, its application to image analysis tasks is limited.  This study argues that models should be designed to produce quantifiable uncertainties to balance analysis accuracy on low-resolution images and prevent the learning of biased data.  To achieve this, we developed a simple, efficient model called the dual-axis UNet, which can operate on 16-bit images (accurate to within a pixel) and handle the uncertainty quantification.  To prevent model bias, we utilized rate-distortion optimization to limit its capacity, packaging the model into 137 million parameters.  When tested on the Common HIPOCAMM dataset containing mammography images, the dual-axis UNet outperformed existing methods that use more parameters.  Moreover, we observed that model bias was significantly reduced when deploying the dual-axis UNet on the large and noisy dermoscope dataset.  The model and associated code are available at https://github.com/ghassen89/dual-axis-UNet.  All dataset used in this study can be found at https://data.tiddc.org/ and https://github.com/HIPOCAMM-Dataset.  The associated pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/ghassen89/dual-axis-UNet/tree/main/models. We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO), a four-layer Aurivillius compound, under the influence of high hydrostatic pressure.  Our X-ray diffraction data does not exhibit a phase transition under pressure but lattice changes suggest a series of structural adaptations as the pressure increases.  Initially, BFTO displays a quasi-tetragonal symmetry but transforms into an orthorhombic structure beyond 8 GPa.  Our Raman spectroscopy analysis reveals local structure alterations at 5.5 GPa, contradicting crystallographic changes, and our Nuclear forward scattering measurements disclose the onset of magnetic order in BFTO above 5K under high pressure conditions, with enhanced magnetic order with increasing pressure.  Conversely, NFS at 6.4GPa and varying temperatures indicates magnetic loss at higher temperatures (20K), with the structural changes potentially influencing this magnetic phenomenon.  Additionally, our results demonstrate the capability of structural and magnetic changes detection via combined in-situ XRD, Raman and NFS measurements at extreme conditions.  We also propose BFTO as a reference material for future magnetic and structural studies at high pressure conditions.  Furthermore, our study highlights the complex interplay between structure, composition and pressure on the magnetic properties of BFTO, a phenomenon that warrants further exploration.  Through the combined application of in-situ experiments, our research highlights the intricate relationships between material structure, magnetic order and other factors at high pressure conditions, with vast, yet to be understood, phenomena waiting to be uncovered. Hybrid methods tackling continuous shortest path problems start by local optimization
of discrete shortest paths in spatial networks. The convergence to optimal solutions
depends on the discretization error caused by restricting the global search to a network,
with specific implications on the choice of network density. A notable application
is flight planning, which involves determining optimal routes considering factors such
as flight time, fuel consumption, and weather conditions. Advanced algorithms for
discrete shortest paths can be used to compute starting points for locally convergent
methods in optimal control. We establish a priori and localized bounds for the
error in estimated flight times compared to optimal continuous trajectories, taking
into account network density and wind field. These bounds facilitate designing
networks with optimal connectivity, and the derived bounds are illustrated through
benchmarks, which show significant improvements in localization but still offer scope
for refinement through additional estimators. The resulting method is used to optimize
the placement of weather stations, which can be further optimized by marginal gain. 
The method is made available on an interactive web visualization at https://flight-redux.web.app/. 
The method is also available as an open-source repository at https://github.com/ral-levi/flight-levei.

Through phase space reconstruction, our findings reveal the deterministic chaotic nature of these dynamics by confirming the existence of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent at specific traction velocities. The outcomes are supported by a theoretical model highlighting the deterministic source of acoustic emissions, and their connection to stick-slip behavior is clarified. Our approach also yields the distinction between two distinct force regimes, and it is demonstrated how the deterministic chaotic nature of one of these regimes gives way to intermittent behavior in the other. Additionally, the relationship between our findings and the deterministic nature of related phenomena such as stick-slip and supercooling are briefly discussed. Furthermore, the applicability of our approach is shown through the identification of unstable periodic orbits within the phase space. The methods employed in this research can also be applied to a broad range of natural phenomena characterized by chaotic dynamics and marked by sharp transitions, exhibiting features of intermittent behavior. Lastly, the potential of using acoustic emissions as a controllable and adjustable tool for exploring the internal dynamics of complex systems is explored. This could provide insight into the physical mechanisms governing these systems by manipulating and measuring the effects of variations in external influences on the emergence of chaotic behavior. This could offer a new approach for investigating the mechanisms underlying acoustic emission phenomena observed in other natural phenomena, such as supercooling and spinodal decomposition. The temperature has a significant impact on these devices, causing a crossover from macroscopic quantum tunneling to phase diffusion. The threshold temperature for this crossover varies greatly, influenced by the device design and material properties. The threshold is highest in plain JJs, followed by SQUIDs and the lowest in SIS junctions. The temperature at which the crossover occurs also has a notable effect on the hysteresis loop and switching current in these devices. The threshold temperature also affects the current-phase relationship, modifying the shape of the potential barrier in its ground state. The shape of the barrier is significantly altered at high temperatures, allowing for the possibility of optimizing device performance by manipulating this shape. The threshold temperature can be manipulated through the design of the device, including the length of the junction and the loop area in SQUIDs. The design of these devices, including the thickness of the insulator and the presence of magnetic material in SQUIDs, also has an impact on the crossover and subsequently the device's switching current. The devices exhibit optimal performance when the crossover temperature matches the operating temperature, whether that is room temperature or cryogenic temperatures. The devices also demonstrate optimal performance when the shape of the barrier is optimal, allowing for minimal energy to switch the phase. The devices also need to be designed to minimize phase diffusion, with a optimal design allowing for a higher switching current. By applying variational techniques, we develop a limiting model for a set of functionals subject to linear differential constraints. This framework models the energy of a heterogeneous material with a high-contrast composite structure at a microscopic scale, comprising a periodically perforated matrix filled with a dissimilar substance. Our key finding involves analyzing the $\Gamma$-convergence as the material periodicity diminishes, demonstrating that the limit functional comprises two components: the stored energy within the matrix, and the stored energy within the fillings. To overcome the coercivity issue inherent in the material structure, we employ two-scale convergence methods, while novel results are established for addressing the linear differential constraints via existence proofs for potentials and constraint-preserving extension operators. Ultimately, this leads to a suitable definition of the limit functional and its associated minimizers. This research has implications for the study of damage and phase-transitions within high-contrast materials. Leveraging these methods, we also obtain a priori bounds for sequences of minimizers of the approximate functionals. Lastly, this is accompanied by a discussion on adapting these techniques to accommodate additional spatial homogenization. This work is an extension of a previous study involving homogenization of a rate-independent phase-transition limit for a Stefan problem with nonhomogeneous diffusion. It introduces high-contrast inclusions to model damaged or melted regions within the material, exhibiting distinct stored energy profiles. This research lays the groundwork for exploring more complex material structures involving interacting sinks and sources. It also paves the way for investigating other phase-transitions and damage models. Notably, this work provides a model for studying the evolution of sharp interfaces. It also highlights the challenges posed by non-coercive material structures and offers strategies for addressing them. Given its focus on variational methods and material science, this study is of interest to researchers in both fields. It is also relevant to applied mathematics researchers working in nonlinear analysis, partial differential equations, and computational physics and mechanics. It is anticipated that this work will motivate further research into the homogenization of nonlinear material models, particularly in relation to the development of efficient numerical methods for solving related partial differential equations. It is also believed that this study will contribute to a deeper understanding of the effects of material structure on the evolution of interfaces and the development of non-coercive energy models. This achievement builds upon prior work of the second author concerning the maximum of several functions within the same space, now expanded to account for all maximum values. Specifically, our result demonstrates that for any set of functions $f_1, \ldots, f_m$ within the space $L_p$ on the Cartesian product $[0,1]^{n(m-1)}$, there exists a continuous, non-increasing function $T: [0, m^{\frac{2p}{p^2}}] \to [0, m^{\frac{2p}{p^2}}]$ such that for $p \geq 2$, $T$ can be expressed as a $d$-variate function with $d = (p-1)m^{\frac{2p}{p^2}}$, and for all $x, y \in [0,1]^{n(m-1)}$, $\left|\frac{T(\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}x_i^p)}{\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}x_i^p}\right| \leq \frac{T(\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}y_i^p)}{\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}y_i^p} \leq m^{\frac{2p}{p^2}}$. In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics data collection, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, yielding precise insights into long-range beam-beam effects, as predicted by the improved TRAIN code. The results from these scans significantly contributed to the understanding of beam dynamics and the development of more accurate particle tracking models, ultimately informing the design of future colliders like CLIC and SPPC. The success of the emittance scans served as a crucial basis for introducing "Scans at Minimum Betatron Radius," which provide even more detailed information about the beam's innermost regions and are now an integral part of the standard beam diagnosis procedure at the LHC. The results presented in this paper offer a comprehensive review of the emittance scans, highlighting their key features, achievements, and future applications. The paper also explores the implications of these studies for the development of future colliders and discusses the importance of combining experimental measurements with sophisticated simulation tools in the quest to fully comprehend the complexities of the LHC beam scenario. The paper will be of particular interest to those attending the 24th International Conference on Frontier Problems in Particle Physics (ICPP24), as it provides a timely and relevant review of the subject matter being presented in the session. The paper is currently available on the CERN Document Server under the identifier arXiv: 1905.13413. The authors have also presented an updated version of the results in the paper, which is now accepted for publication in the European Physical Journal C, Volume 82, Issue 9. This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve agents behaving maliciously, which leads to a misdirection away from optimal solutions through the spread of false information and significant communication costs. To address this issue, we develop a distributed optimization algorithm based on gradient updates, where trustworthy agents share quantized data with each other. Theoretical proof of solution convergence near the optimal solution is provided, along with the effects of communication constraints and malicious behavior on solution accuracy. This is further illustrated through numerical experiments presented in the study.

The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for current and future cosmic microwave background experiments. This framework incorporates the characteristics of modern instruments and can produce simulated data at a pace comparable to that of actual data acquisition. Additionally, it incorporates features that make it easy to incorporate into large-scale analyses and pipelines. By providing this capability, researchers can thoroughly assess and mitigate the effects of their instruments' systematic flaws on real cosmic microwave background data. This code can also be used to create realistic simulations for papers and education. As the most sophisticated of its kind, this framework has the potential to greatly enhance the credibility of such simulations in the scientific community. In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). We also establish the convergence rate of DR-DSGD, demonstrating that it achieves a comparable rate to that of the standard DSGD under equal data distributions, and we further develop a robust decentralized Newton method for improved performance. Our results also provide a new variant of DR-DSGD with reduced communication overhead, leading to potential applications in large-scale data analysis. Through numerical experiments, we verify the efficacy and efficiency of our proposed methods. Notably, our evaluation of a real-world image recognition scenario reveals that DR-DSGD can reduce communication costs by a factor of around 1000 while maintaining comparable accuracy. Moreover, our results indicate that DR-Newton, the decentralized Newton method, can achieve up to 50% higher accuracy compared to existing methods under limited communication. Our work opens up avenues for the study of other robust decentralized optimization algorithms and fosters the development of theory for distributionally robust machine learning. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Furthermore, our study reveals the limited diversity of users within the Forsage network at various levels of the hierarchy. By combining transaction data with promotional content analysis, our study demonstrates the capability to effectively study modern, complex pyramid schemes built into blockchain smart contracts. Our research also warns about the risks posed by Forsage and other similar schemes to users and about the necessity of strictly regulating the use of blockchain technology in the development of such schemes. Lastly, our study highlights the necessity of enhancing user financial literacy to prevent such schemes from succeeding in the future. Due to the unique characteristics of blockchain-based pyramid schemes, their study will continually require the integration of blockchain transaction data with social media analysis. This integrated approach will provide valuable insights into the intricate workings of these schemes and facilitate their detection and prevention. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.4 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed possible alpha-element variations and temperature across the cluster and found no notable differences, indicating they have similar basic characteristics. We compared our findings using the Hubble Space Telescope for three of the closest clusters (VVV-CL124, VVV-CL160 and VVV-CL188) by calculating their central temperatures as 10360 degrees, 10358 degrees and 10357 degrees respectively, and combining them with previous research, indicating a possible trend of decreasing temperature as birth date increases. We also discovered possible variations in the rate of death of low mass stars across the cluster and suggested it could be linked to variations in heavy elements. We suggested forming near the galaxy's center and moving towards its outer parts as possible characteristics for these cluster candidates based on their heavy element variation and movement patterns. We proposed forming the galaxy's bulge over a duration of 10 billion years and suggested future research should analyze possible variations in the galaxy's bulge's stellar movement and heavy element composition. We compared our research using the VVV survey with the ESO's VST survey and proposed future research should analyze possible variations in heavy element composition across the galaxy's cluster and its possible links with heavy element variation across the galaxy.

We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to each other, with a focus on identifying which approach yields more accurate results. We demonstrate that the dipole-based model exhibits reduced size-disorder effects when compared to its velocity-based counterpart. The disparity in behavior is attributed to the varying inclusion of nearest-neighbor and on-site terms within the two models. The results suggest that a finite system may display characteristics analogous to those of a continuous system when the velocity-based model is employed. The findings of this research provide a greater understanding of the simulated phenomena and will aid in making informed choices regarding the selection of a suitable model for specific light-matter interactions. The results also highlight the potential for extracting tight-binding model parameters from experimental data collected using dipole-based models. A theoretical analysis of retinal chromophore photoisomerization in rhodopsin utilized a model incorporating thermal baths and dual states. It was observed that quantum yields in a steady-state condition (occurring 10 ps after the reaction begins and onwards) differ notably from their short-lived counterparts, indicating an imperfect correlation between transient and sustained behaviors. Furthermore, the steady-state quantum yield was shown to be exquisitely sensitive to minor adjustments in system parameters, as opposed to the relative insensitivity of transient dynamics. Analysis of this sensitivity in relation to nonadiabatic perturbation theory revealed a significant role of diabatic terms, whose impact is tempered during short-lived phases but emerges prominently in longer durations. Conversely, the initial reaction phase remains heavily influenced by adiabatic principles. Consequently, this study highlights the importance of considering both short- and long-term dynamics when assessing the functional integrity of biological molecules susceptible to light-induced damage. Additionally, it suggests that retinal chromophore photoisomerization may serve as a valuable model for exploring the intricate connections between transient and steady-state processes governed by nonadiabatic dynamics.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.

cycle-aware time-encoding framework for time characteristics that is universally
applicable and provides a more comprehensive time representation. Our unified
framework focuses on processing time-sensitive data within temporal knowledge graph
embeddings. Experimental results show that our proposed solutions equal or outperform

Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. The ability of the model to produce compact sentence representations also opens up possibilities for text generation tasks that require low computational memory. The code for the SparseGAN model is available online at https://github.com/hjdw/SparseGAN. The paper has been accepted for presentation at the 28th Conference on Computational Linguistics.

This scenario posits that spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs at the highest energy level, causing a cascade of symmetry violations at lower energy levels resulting from subtle mixings between them. A simple model has been devised to illustrate this idea using scalar portals, where the significant difference in energy scales, such as the Planck and electroweak scales, arises from the multiplication of several small factors related to the mixing coefficients. The formation of dark matter fields is also examined in this framework, where it is possible for these fields to emerge from matter fields located on one or more intermediate energy levels between the highest and lowest. The produced particles would then be connected to the highest energy level through nonlinear interactions, making them challenging to detect directly. The presence of these fields can be inferred by analyzing the effects of their linear interactions with the fundamental fields on particle collision data. The simplest model including dark matter contains three scalar fields and has been analyzed in terms of spontaneous symmetry breaking, where the vacuum structure relies on the interplay between two intermediate scales. The minimal setup also allows for the investigation of dark matter properties such as its stability, coupling to the weak force, and potential association with dark energy, fueling further theoretical developments fueled by ongoing and future experiments in the field. The proposed concept also raises fundamental questions about the nature of the highest energy level and whether it could be equivalent to the multiverse, prompting a deeper examination of cosmological implications and the potential for the emergence of deformed effective theories during the symmetry-breaking process. Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once.  This method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  Notably, our study reveals that capture-recapture models alone can infer parameters for resource selection functions, enabling the exclusive use of capture data to investigate space usage, albeit with lower precision.  Nonetheless, using telemetry data yields superior precision.  Our method allows researchers to investigate the relative precision of different modeling approaches, which can inform future studies and enhance the value of existing and future research.  As a case study, we applied our method to river otter data collected in a coastal river ecosystem and discovered that otters exhibit localized occupancy patterns, likely influenced by habitat features such as river bends and adjacent wetlands.  Our findings highlight the potential of combined capture-recapture and resource selection analyses to advance our understanding of animal spatial ecology and inform management and conservation decisions.  We also provide a suite of R functions tailored to analyze space-use data collected along linear features and incorporate relevant ecological insights.  These functions can be utilized independently of our proposed method.  Our code is available through an interactive RStudio companion piece that includes customized visualization tools and allows users to explore and exploit otter occupancy models.  As a result, our study offers novel statistical approaches, cutting-edge research case studies, and customizable tools that can inform management decisions and encourage the use of integrated capture-recapture and resource selection analyses in wildlife research.  We also provide a companion piece to this article as an interactive RStudio document, which includes customized visualization tools and allows users to explore and exploit otter occupancy models. Evaluating defensive strategies in team sports can be complicated due to the limited availability of data from individual game events. Previous researchers developed methods for assessing football teams' defensive prowess by predicting the likelihood of gaining possession of the ball and being attacked, based on the location of all players involved. These earlier approaches, however, underestimated the importance of such events, assumed a perfect understanding of every player's position, and failed to account for diversity factors, such as player nationality and sex. To overcome these limitations, we present a revised approach to valuing defensive teams, by scaling the predicted probabilities of game events according to their scoring impact. By utilizing the publicly available player location data from broadcast videos of men's Euro 2020 and women's Euro 2022 football matches, we explored the effect of varying player numbers on prediction accuracy and validated our approach through an analysis of game data. The results showed that to accurately predict instances of being attacked, scoring, and conceding, it was sufficient to focus on all players involved, but ball gain predictions were most accurate with information on three to four key offensive and defensive players. Furthermore, our approach enabled us to provide insights into the superior defensive performances of finalist teams in the 2020 European Football Championship, and to investigate the impact of diversity factors on game dynamics. By providing a flexible method for valuing defensive teams, our approach can be applied to a broader range of situations and diverse datasets. Additionally, we highlighted the potential for this approach to be used in the prediction of game events, based on player location data, combined with other valuing methods. Our approach and associated data and code are available online for further research. Ultimately, our approach paves the way for a deeper understanding of game dynamics and player contributions, and could ultimately contribute to strategic team coaching and training. Highly flexible recurrent state-space models can capture complex patterns in time series data, but typically assume a static and unchanging dynamic, a rare occurrence in real-world situations. To overcome this limitation, many systems demonstrate patterns that are similar yet distinct, a phenomenon that state-space models struggle to capture on their own. To address this, we introduce the hidden multi-dimensional state-space model (HMSM), a model that can efficiently handle multiple overlapping dynamics. By combining HMSM with well-established inference techniques and efficient optimization methods, we've developed a practical way to use this model for real-world applications. Through the use of well-known time series datasets, we demonstrate that HMSM outperforms alternative models, including the widely used recurrent state-space model. Additionally, we show that HMSM can be employed for forecasting, a critical application where existing models like RSSM fall short. To facilitate future research, we've made our code and data available for download.

Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already known to result from this property. We've established an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant random matrices. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the derivation of asymptotic conditional freeness. Specifically, we demonstrate the empirical spectral distribution of randomly rotated matrices converges towards a conditionally free convolution. We've also identified new relationships between infinitesimal freeness, type $B$ freeness, conditional freeness, cyclic monotonicity, and monotone independence. Moreover, we show that the BBP phase transition in an additive rank-one perturbation of a GUE matrix is a consequence of asymptotic conditional freeness. This line of reasoning applies as well to an analysis of outlier eigenvalues in various unitarily invariant ensembles. Lastly, we discuss the implications of our discoveries to freeness and ease of calculation in large but finite unitarily invariant matrices. 

This work builds upon the work of Benayouen, Capelle, and Shye which initiated the exploration of asymptotic conditional freeness in unitarily invariant matrices. Our study delves deeper by providing a precise analysis of the rates of convergence, a detailed examination of the outliers in the GSE, and a broader examination of the effects of monoticity in unitarily invariant matrices. Our study also introduces new relationships between freeness, conditional freeness, cyclic monotonicity, and additive constraints, and showcases the practical utility of these concepts in the context of matrix-valued functions. 

In the process of achieving these outcomes, we establish the speed of convergence in the asymptotic conditional freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant matrices. Our methodology for assessing the rate of convergence involves employing the total variation distance and the Wasserstein distance. Our study indicates that the rate of convergence is on the order of $N^{-2}$, which is analogous to the rate of convergence in the asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for iid matrices. However, it's essential to note that the method used to establish this rate of convergence in the context of unitarily invariant matrices is distinct from the method used in the context of iid matrices. Our study also examines the rate of convergence in the specific case of GSE with an additive rank-one perturbation, which is characterized by an outlier at a specific location.

We construct a genus-3 curve X, such that its Jacobian is connected to a product of the Jacobian of D and X's Jacobian, the Jacobian of C being an isogeny. If the base field is algebraically closed and X's Jacobian has complex multiplication, we prove the existence of a degree-2 cover, with the cover's ramification locus being the geodesic connecting two Weierstrass points on C, for any given pair of C and D. If the base field is a finite field with p^g(C) elements, we demonstrate the existence of a degree-2 cover D, with the cover's ramification locus being any desired set of p^g(D) Weierstrass points on C. If the base field is a finite field with p elements, we show the number of degree-2 covers of a non-hyperelliptic genus-2 curve C to be (p+1)*p*(p^2-1).

Determining the extent of polarization within social systems is vital to studying its effects on political structures. While numerous methods are employed to analyze polarization in social networks through structural evaluation, our analysis revealed that eight commonly used methods yield elevated polarization scores even in artificially constructed networks that closely mirror real-world networks in density and distribution. Furthermore, some of these methods proved sensitive to specific characteristics of polarized groups, such as degree distribution and size. We proposed introducing a standard normalization to mitigate these issues, alongside a comprehensive set of criteria for effective measurement of structural polarization. By normalizing the scores, the classification performance increased by up to 220%, and notably, the choice of measurement method became significantly less crucial, with most methods surpassing the previous best performance following normalization. Our research lays the groundwork for a thorough evaluation and comparison of different structural polarization measurement methods. Additionally, we introduced the NSP dataset, a diverse set of artificial social networks suitable for testing such methods. The dataset is readily available for use by other researchers. The results of our analysis have been incorporated into the Polarize R package to facilitate replication and further exploration of the findings. The package, including the NSP dataset and a comprehensive documentation, can be accessed through an R repository. The research underlying this paper has been published in the journal Scientific Reports Volume 13, 2023, DOI: 10.1038/s41598-023-30645-5. The corresponding author of the study is J. Pablo Parra. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators within multilayer networks by applying a joint matrix representation. This technique provides a compact representation of the multilayer system that maintains equivalent dynamics. As a result, we can determine solutions for the reduced system and then extend them to the multilayer network. Furthermore, we can investigate the stability of these solutions by analyzing the reduced system and obtaining insights into the multilayer system's Jacobian. Our method is adaptable to different interlayer node connections. Ultimately, our research enables the exploration of multilayer networks through simplified representations, facilitating a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics underlying these systems. As such, it can be readily applied to other stochastic network systems. By doing so, we gain a more precise understanding of how multilayer structures influence system behavior. By utilizing the parametric representation of the boundary via a mapping, we develop an operator that converts the boundary conditions into initial conditions for a modified equation set. This operator, which we term the'reformatting stress operator,' has a notable property where it can be expressed as a composition of two identifiable differential operators. With the'reformatting stress operator,' we create an new set of modified equations whose solutions are closely tied to the original Navier-Stokes equations. Ultimately, our analysis yields conditions for the solvability of the Navier-Stokes equations based on the format of the boundary. Our method also introduces the concept of'stress conjugate' boundaries that have a significant implication where the original and modified equations have the same set of solutions. This leads to a deeper understanding of the role of the Cauchy stress operator in the context of differential operators. Our study expands the current knowledge by providing a meaningful application of the operator in the Navier-Stokes equations. It also reveals the crucial function of the boundary where it plays a key part in the classification of the global smooth solution of the Navier-Stokes equations. It further indicates that the non-compact boundary with which the stress conjugate plays a key part, may lead to an infinite dimensional unstable manifold, which has an orthogonal space with a finite dimensional stable manifold. This finding is novel and provides a theoretical explanation for the recent numerical simulation result conducted by Layton and Rakich. In this setup, hyper-prompts can be optimized end-to-end by a HyperNetwork. By employing hyper-prompts as global task memories, HyperPrompt enables networks to learn task-specific features while facilitating flexible information sharing among multiple tasks. Notably, HyperPrompt offers a balance of high performance and efficient use of resources - it achieves exceptional performance with significantly fewer additional task-conditioning parameters compared to other methods, amounting to $0.14\%$ of the parameters required, ultimately showcasing great computational efficiency. Through thorough experimentation on diverse models and benchmarks, such as the GLUE and SuperGLUE tasks for Natural Language Understanding, HyperPrompt has consistently outperformed prominent multi-task learning approaches like Prompt-Tuning, HyperFormer++ and T5. The code is openly accessible at https://github.com/ghrua/HyperPrompt.

integrated with existing traffic signal control systems.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces accurate solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. Our results show that this method can produce highly accurate metric configurations, with constraints satisfied to a level of $10^{-5}$ or better, across a wide range of spin parameters and cloud sizes. Additionally, this method proves to be at least as efficient as other conformal rescaling methods, with some cases showing a significant improvement. With this approach, the time spent solving constraints is essentially negligible compared to the overall computation time. As such, it represents a reliable and efficient alternative for generating initial data in scenarios involving fundamental fields. Our code is also freely available for public use. Our study further highlights the ability of this method to handle black hole initial data, producing compact objects with correct physical properties and accurately satisfying the constraints. The metric components around the event horizon are shown to be in close alignment with the generalized Israel formalism. The scalar field within the ergosphere is found to be directly linked to the spin parameter of the black hole. As such, this method provides a suitable approach for producing accurate initial data in scenarios involving fundamental fields, making it an ideal tool for studying processes involving the interaction between black holes and scalar fields. Our approach also paves the way for investigating more complex scenarios, such as binary systems involving black holes and scalar fields. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. Our results demonstrate that the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity share a common material-based intrinsic mechanism, exhibiting a linear correlation and displaying the same symmetry properties. Moreover, our results also illustrate the theoretical model of the anomalous Hall effect can be applied to a limited extent to the anomalous Nernst effect. Notably, our study highlights the significance of considering thermal gradient-induced spin polarization and the electronic disorder at the material interface when analyzing the anomalous Nernst effect. Lastly, our research highlights the potential applications of antiferromagnetic antiperovskite materials in thermal spin Hall effect-based devices and offers a framework for further interdisciplinary research. Our study's results provide valuable insights for the development of more accurate theoretical models of the anomalous Nernst effect and can serve as a benchmark for comparing with first-principles calculations and other models. Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently handle these issues. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Furthermore, our method has been successfully integrated into a real-world commercial search platform. Source code is available at: https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/PTE/tree/PILE.

This work revisits linear gyrokinetic theory for geodesic acoustic modes and develops a general dispersion relation applicable to various ion distribution functions. A specific bi-Maxwellian ion distribution is analyzed to determine the impact of temperature anisotropy on mode frequency and growth rate, which shows significant increases due to anisotropy, heavily influenced by the electron-to-ion temperature ratio. Additionally, the effects of mode location near rational surfaces on low-mode-frequency states are investigated, revealing how GAM-like modes can transition to toroidal GAMs once the mode frequency breaks the innermost ELM threshold. Further investigation into the interplay between GAMs and geodesic modes suggests that torque imbalances could cause mode instabilities at mode frequencies slightly higher than rational surface resonances. The proposed model is verified by comparing its linear results to existing linear gyrokinetic simulations. The findings also suggest that the proposed model may be used to explain observed phenomena such as low-mode-frequency states and the relationship between GAMs and geodesic modes through torque imbalances. The model predicts that modes with frequencies between rational surface resonances and the innermost ELM threshold may be influenced by geodesic acoustic modes, while modes with frequencies above the innermost ELM threshold are likely unaffected. The proposed model can be applied to various tokamak devices, such as JET, JT-60, and ASDEX, and its implications for nonlinear mode saturation and edge pedestal stability are also discussed. A promising technique known as quantum annealing has been proposed for efficiently solving combinatorial optimization problems embedded in the Ising Hamiltonian's ground state. This approach involves two types of Hamiltonian dynamics: classical and quantum, which are intertwined to achieve the desired solution. Including unwanted quantum interactions can hinder the process by introducing a non-trivial global minimum and making the solution more difficult to find. Surprisingly, including anti-ferromagnetic interactions within the Hamiltonian results in an easier solution finding process. This phenomenon results from quantum annealing's increased sensitivity to the phase transition between the ground states' minimum and global minimum. Additionally, we demonstrate that incorporating decoherence has an unexpected effect - it can enhance the probability of finding the ground state for certain Hamiltonian parameters. This unexpected behavior stems from the interplay between annealing's dual Hamiltonians. Finally, we find that quantum annealing can be safely used even in the presence of strong decoherence, as it will eventually reach the ground state, as demonstrated through exact numerical simulations and the application of Kac-Wieland's criterion for quantum Metastable States.

This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the lab's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's efforts were impeded by World War I and the Dutch Academy's decision to discontinue the plan in 1919. Despite these setbacks, the lab managed to complete the project in 1925. The success of the project allowed the lab to proceed with planned surveys, including the PM Survey, which aimed to measure the proper motions of stars within a specific latitude of the galactic plane. Although the PM Survey made substantial progress, the findings were ultimately hindered by the Great Depression and the onset of World War II, which caused the loss of key data. The lab then shifted its focus to the construction of the Zwicky galaxy atlas, a comprehensive atlas of nearby galaxies, which was initiated by Fritz Zwicky using the Palomar Observatory. The lab completed the atlas by observing 267 galaxies but was unable to finish the project due to the war. The Zwicky galaxy atlas demonstrated the potential of the Zwicky method, which involved studying individual globular clusters within galaxies, which could provide insights into the masses of these galaxies. The lab decided to apply this method to the Andromeda galaxy (M31) by selecting specific areas within the galaxy and estimating the mass of its globular clusters. The study revealed a significant correlation between the mass of these clusters and their luminosity, which could be used to estimate the total mass of M31. The findings suggested that the mass of M31 was approximately 1000 times greater than the mass of the Milky Way, which was a startling discovery at the time. The lab's research on M31 was, however, ultimately disrupted by the war. The essay also highlights the difficulties the lab faced during van Rhijn's tenure, including the loss of key staff and the challenges of conducting astronomical research during times of conflict. The legacy of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory during this period was marked by significant achievements, which laid the groundwork for future research in the field of extragalactic astronomy. The essay also explores the contributions of the lab's directors, Pieter Johannes van Rhijn and Peter van Rhijn's nephew, Hendrik Christoffel van Rhijn, as well as the influential role of the Dutch Academy

In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high correlation with functional connectivity maps derived from independent component analysis. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal model can identify specific time points and individual variations. Furthermore, our model's dynamic nature allows it to capture various time scales, and the inclusion of a minimal model reveals the essential structure underlying connectomes. With its flexibility and high-performance classification capabilities, DECENNT represents a valuable tool for analyzing complex, directed, and dynamic graph structures. Our code is available at https://github.comius/DECENNT.

Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the evolutionary histories of various species, enabling them to incorporate reticulate evolutionary mechanisms such as lateral gene transfer and gene recombination. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more comprehensive view of the evolutionary process. To facilitate accurate phylogeny reconstruction, various stochastic processes have been developed to generate random phylogenetic trees or networks, which can be used to validate results or inform Bayesian analysis. Notwithstanding the creation of numerous network generation tools, a shortage of discourse and comparison among these tools persists. To address this disparity, we undertake a comparative analysis of a range of phylogenetic network generators by evaluating and assessing the topological characteristics of the generated networks as a function of the number of reticulations present. The variability observed in the topological features of these networks is captured through the enactment of several popular phylogenetic retrieval tasks. Moreover, the efficacy of these comparisons is assessed via synthetic networks as well as real-life datasets derived from various organisms, including bacteria, archaea, eukaryotes, and viruses. The results garnered from this comparison are subsequently made publicly accessible on an interactive visualization platform designed for user exploration. The platform is readily available online at our designated URL. The methodology employed for this comparison is also based on our proposed framework for evaluating the accuracy of phylogenetic networks, which involves multiple criteria including tree-like minimization, rootenced identification, and the detection of monophyly and polyphyly. The findings from this comparison will hopefully direct the development of network generators towards creating more precise models of phylogenetic networks. Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for each scenario, is introduced to support and evaluate the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach effectively detects biolocomotion across various scenarios, outperforming the alternative approach. Furthermore, biolocomotion detection is demonstrated to improve overall object detection accuracy by focusing on the unique characteristics of biological movement, leading to potential applications in the study of biological systems in real-world settings. The developed method and associated dataset are made available to facilitate future research in biolocomotion and its connection to object detection and the analysis of mechanical systems. The advent of intense and highly brilliant x-ray pulses generated by fourth-generation synchrotron light sources and x-ray free electron lasers requires the development of accurate and fast iterative matrix inversion methods for data analysis. These methods can provide precise results and efficiently handle data at a fraction of the cost of classic direct inversion methods. However, they can be challenging to implement on existing computing infrastructure due to their complex computational nature and limited parallelization potential. We introduce GELDA, an open-source, general-purpose GUI-based code that enables users to easily create and customize model-based projection matrices and associated residual calculation functions. It can also be used to develop model-based iterative reconstruction algorithms and leverage the benefits of iterative methods. We include an example application of GELDA in the form of the x-ray free electron laser data analysis code, PENELOPE, to demonstrate its capabilities and showcase the code's flexibility and efficiency. This code can be modified to accommodate various data types and analysis requirements and has been successfully deployed on multiple datasets. Like PENELOPE, it is open to feedback and collaboration to further develop the code and explore its potential uses. We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary and continuous disorders on topological phases in the context of several models, including the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, the Bernevig-Hughes-Kane model, and the Dirac fermion model. Our analysis employs both numerical simulations and analytical approaches to characterize the topological Anderson insulating phase and the localization phase. The precise disorder classes that influence these phases are determined, and the associated topological phase diagrams are constructed to provide guidelines for future experimental and theoretical investigations. Moreover, we analyze the distinct transport properties of these systems and investigate the relationship between their topological features and conductance. Notably, we find that the topological Anderson insulating phase can be induced in otherwise topologically nontrivial systems by introducing specific types of binary disorders. This finding is particularly relevant to the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, where the topological Anderson insulating phase can arise through the creation of zero-energy flat bands. This scenario has implications for the design of topological phases in experiments involving magnetic and non-magnetic impurities. Additionally, we investigate the effect of correlated disorders on topological phases in two-dimensional systems described by the Bernevig-Hughes-Kane model and the Bernevig-Lee model, and we include a discussion on the topological phase transition mediated by correlated disorders in these systems. This study provides a comprehensive overview of the topological and localization phenomena that arise in correlated disorder systems and offers insights that can be applied to a broader range of scenarios. This research is particularly relevant to the design of topological phases in experiments involving magnetic and non-magnetic impurities and can be extended to systems described by the BCS model and the surface state of topological insulators. Recent breakthroughs in declarative networks and related work have demonstrated the capability of differentiating the solution mappings of continuous parametrized optimization problems. This has the potential to embed mathematical optimization problems within trainable end-to-end models. By providing an alternative expression for computing derivatives, this differentiability enables the reduction of model updates to non-expansive functions, resulting in faster and more stable training. However, formulating certain problems, such as sparse constraints, as differentiable optimization problems has presented a challenge. This challenge is addressed by developing sparse and multi-task declarative networks that can efficiently learn from data. The proposed approaches leverage variational inequalities and complementarity functions to accurately model sparse phenomena. Comprehensive experiments validate the enhanced representation learning capabilities and practical applications of these models. Furthermore, substantial improvements in modeling sparse data are achieved, outperforming competing methods by at least 5% in accuracy according to mean average precision metrics. Additionally, notable gains in multi-task learning are observed, achieving a notable increase of 11% in mean average precision when switching from single-task to multi-task training. A cell's behavior during spreading and movement is influenced by various interrelated events that are activated by external stimuli at different scales. Due to the cell's living nature and complex response mechanisms, it is not sufficient to apply traditional material mechanics principles to it. Rather, cells comprise constituents with repeatable reactions such as contractility in single fibers and actin networks but also exhibit non-deterministic reorganization upon external stimuli. With consideration of this complexity, our goal is to develop a multi-faceted framework for modeling cellular spreading and locomotion, taking into account the movement of proteins across lipid membranes. Our proposed approach successively considers protein movements at the membrane surface, depending on their location within filamentous structures or larger networks. By establishing appropriate governing equations at each level, we then create a hierarchical model that connects them. Our model exhibits all necessary characteristics, including spontaneous contractility in stand-alone fibers, contractility with membrane-bound protein movement, and contractility with internal cytosolic protein movement. Our model also displays the capability to adapt to changing external conditions, as seen in cytosolic protein recrossing. With this framework, we explore various scaling limits that allow for the determination of the outer spread of the cell and its spread dynamics. Our results can provide a foundation for further investigation into the interplay between mechanical and biological aspects during cellular spreading and locomotion. With slight modifications, our proposed approach can also be applied to the study of other living cells that consist of similar cellular components. Our results also highlight the significance of considering cross-membrane protein movement in the modeling of cellular spreading. By doing so, our study can contribute to a deeper comprehension of the mechanical properties of cells that cannot be achieved via sole mechanistic analysis. Our research is particularly relevant to the exploration of cells under dynamic conditions, particularly where cells display complex responses during spreading and movement, as seen in cancer cell invasion, cell migration in narrow channels, and cells under time-varying external loads. The unique combination of decentralization, redundancy, and pseudo-anonymity in public blockchain platforms has made them appealing for cryptocurrency adoption. However, these same features have enabled cybercriminals to exploit vulnerabilities in blockchain technology and deceive users through social engineering to execute malicious plans. Existing methods for identifying malicious actors typically rely on transaction history from specific wallet addresses, but often neglect the underlying money trails. In contrast, we propose an innovative approach centered on money trail analysis, incorporating new features to detect suspicious activities within cryptocurrency blockchains. Specifically, we investigate the cyclic behavior present in temporal transaction graphs within a blockchain, focusing on uncovering hidden patterns. By applying our methods to the Ethereum blockchain, we reveal distinct cyclic patterns indicative of malicious activities such as gambling, phishing, and money laundering, as well as identify two specific temporal cyclic transfers. Notably, our approach is versatile and adaptable to other cryptocurrency blockchains with suitable modifications tailored to the characteristics of the underlying cryptocurrency. By leveraging our features and the structural attributes of temporal transaction graphs, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in identifying malicious actors through an experimental evaluation on the Ethereum blockchain. Especially in scenarios where context dimensions are substantial. This paper addresses a decentralized, memoryless contextual linear bandit learning problem. In this problem, agents that observe the context and make decisions are physically isolated from the learner. This learner executes the learning process but remains unaware of the context. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. This indicated the feedback controller's effectiveness in managing the robot's movement over a range of ground conditions. Ultimately, the robot reached a height of approximately 30% of its overall height. This study demonstrated the capability of a one-legged robot to use feedback control to navigate terrain with granular material, and the potential to apply this approach to more complex multi-legged robots. This work also highlighted the value of the DEM in simulating ground reaction forces and identifying the limitations of the RFT model. To take the take the robot's movement to the next level, the model must be refined to capture the robot's acceleration effects on ground deformation. This work laid the groundwork for the development of more advanced controllers and a more comprehensive model of ground reaction forces that can be used in locomotion research. This study's findings have the potential to contribute to the development of more efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground, and could ultimately enable multi-legged robots to navigate diverse terrain with ease. This distinction highlights the respective utility of these approaches in solving optimization problems and observing temporal quantum phenomena. Nonetheless, both methods can be employed in the creation and study of quantum phases, offering a common framework for investigation. This review paper focuses on the concurrent emergence of quantum phases and functional materials properties in both annealing and quenching processes. Furthermore, the existence of work-stealing algorithms enables seamless simulation of both annealing and quenching processes on quantum annealers, thus allowing for direct comparison and matching of theoretical and experimental results. The findings from such experiments and simulations can be further integrated with the design of novel quantum materials, enabling the development of tailored materials where the structure of the material dictates the quenching process. extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
anti-ferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
ground state becomes itinerant. With strong screening, the $s$-band's shift is
prevented and the ground state becomes itinerant again. 
However, when we include weak screening from the $s$-band to the $d$-band,
a more complex ground state state is produced in which strong correlations
cause a band-shift, but now the more freely moving $s$-electrons move into
a less freely moving $d$-band, and this state displays a mix of itinerant
and localized characteristics. 
This one-band model's behavior is used as a basis for a discussion of the
limits to its applicability. 
For a more realistic representation, the model should be a true one-band
Hubbard model, and this occurs when the screening factor falls within very
narrow limits which are unlikely to be met.

electronic properties are dominated by a particular orbital type.

$d$ and $s$ orbital in infinite layered nickelates.

anti-ferromagnetic ground state as the two-band model.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread disruption, with numerous countries enforcing strict lockdowns and millions of lives affected. In an effort to cope with the emotional impact, people are increasingly expressing their sentiments on social networks, utilizing microblogging platforms as a means of seeking comfort. Twitter has emerged as a prime platform for exchanging ideas, with users posting diverse sentiments aimed at promoting awareness about staying home and maintaining social distancing. However, there is a growing concern regarding the dissemination of fake news that aims to frighten people, emphasizing the need to differentiate between positive, negative, and neutral thoughts to effectively disseminate beneficial opinions to a wider audience. Consequently, identifying and interpreting the context of large datasets on Twitter has become a significant challenge. In this paper, a comprehensive analysis of Twitter data using various machine learning algorithms was conducted to evaluate sentiment, and subsequent context learning of the dataset based on sentiment was explored. Our research utilized J48, Random Forest, and Multinomial Naive Bayes classifiers to compare the accuracy of sentiment identification, followed by context learning of the dataset based on sentiment using decision trees, random forest, and naive bayes classifiers. Ultimately, our research demonstrated the efficacy of combining sentiment and context for improved classification effectiveness. This innovative approach can be applied to analyze and understand various contexts in big data datasets. Additionally, it may also find application in areas like improving customer service, promoting healthy eating habits, and preventing the spread of false news. Our dataset is available online for further research purposes. In the future, incorporating neural network models, incorporating additional context using salient sentence detection, and conducting additional context learning using deep learning methods could be explored. However, determining the maximum-weight Tai mapping between two unordered trees is a well-known NP-complete problem. We now introduce a contrasting concept - anti Tai mapping - as a binary relationship between two trees. An anti Tai mapping, defined as the subset $M$ of $V_1\times V_2$, excludes any node pairs $(x,y)$ and $(x',y')$ that would conflict with each other's ancestral hierarchy, given that $x<x'$ indicates $x$ is an ancestor of $x'$. Calculating the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping plays a significant role in solving the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem through integer programming by applying the cutting plane method. We provide an efficient algorithm for computing a maximum-weight anti Tai mapping when one tree is a path. Additionally, we show that by applying a restricted version of anti Tai mapping, where nodes sharing the same path as their ancestors must not correspond, we can obtain a polynomially computable lower bound for the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping between any two trees. We also present an efficient algorithm for solving this restricted version directly on unordered trees within $O(|V_1|^2|V_2|^2)$ time. We believe our research on anti Tai mapping will contribute to solving other NP-complete problems, such as determining maximum-weight Tai mapping, by applying the cutting plane method. We also propose using restricted versions of anti Tai mapping as a lower bound to accelerate the convergence of these algorithms. We support our theoretical research with concrete experiments using randomly generated trees and assess the computational performance of the cutting plane method with our proposed anti Tai mapping lower bound. We observed a significant improvement, achieving an order of magnitude increase in efficiency compared to the baseline. We further explore the applicability of our anti Tai mapping research to rooted colored trees and present an efficient algorithm for computing a maximum-weight anti Tai mapping in this context within $O(|V_1||V_2|^2)$ time. This research addresses the challenge of protecting machine learning (ML) model outputs from an untrusted client and a semi-reliable server. Inside the optical disk of M101, the HI velocity field appears ordered, whereas there is a significant disturbance in the outer disk. These HI clouds have estimated masses of 1.3$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$, 2.4$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$, and 2.0$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$ respectively. In contrast to the relatively slow star formation rates in satellite galaxies like M101, its large HI reservoir suggests potential for bursts of star formation induced by interactions with the Great Andes Cloud and other nearby galaxies. This is further supported by features such as HI clouds and tails observed in M101. These features imply recent and ongoing interactions between M101 and its neighbors.
