The challenge of representing a positive entity as a sum of squared components dates back centuries to notable mathematicians Bachet and Lagrange. Though successful methods exist for certain types of structures (such as integers or polynomial equations with rational coefficients), the task remains an open question for numerous other fundamental structures and fields. In this study, we introduce a direct procedure for dividing any element of a global domain (either a number domain or a global function domain) into the sum of the minimal-length squared components. This technique works seamlessly for domains with a maximal order and can be easily adapted for use in algorithms. As an example of its usefulness, we show how it can be applied to give a direct answer to the question of expressing a totally positive integer as the sum of squared integers. This question has been studied by famous mathematicians such as Fermat, Bachet, and Lagrange. We also demonstrate the advantages of this method over existing approaches for certain domains and show its connection to a previously known but unpublished result by N. Schwartz. In this context, we also correct the related proof by Schwartz. As an additional contribution, we present an alternative approach for dividing any element of a global domain into the sum of squared components, although this alternative approach is more complicated and only works under stricter domain conditions. This complication suggests that our direct procedure may be of broader interest. A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting when working with highly confident labelled data. The method has several advantages over alternative techniques such as adversarial and generative models, primarily due to its minimal computational requirements. Evaluations using publicly available MRI datasets - specifically ACDC and MMWHS - demonstrate that this proposed technique outperforms existing semi-supervised models, with source code available on GitHub.

Specifically, the jet FEX (jFEX) system aims to enhance jet identification and calculate global variables within an extremely tight latency constraint of under 400 nanoseconds. Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$, a function $\eta(\theta)$ and an unknown distribution $G$ as the mixing distribution. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. By applying the GMLE approach, we derive an estimator $\hat{h}_n(\eta)$ to estimate $\eta_G$ by maximizing the likelihood function $L_n(\eta)$ which is defined as the product of $f(y_i|\theta_i)$ raised to the power of $h(\theta_i)$. It is proven that under certain regularity conditions, the GMLE estimator $\hat{h}_n(\eta)$ is consistent and converges to the same distribution as the empirical distribution of i.i.d. samples of size $n$, where each sample is associated with a parameter $\eta$ and is independent of other samples. Moreover, we establish the asymptotic normality of the GMLE estimator $\hat{h}_n(\eta)$ by applying the conventional delta method. By setting $\eta(\theta) = \theta$, the proposed GMLE estimator provides an alternative to the non-parametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE). It is noteworthy that the proposed GMLE estimator outperforms the NPMLE estimator in various settings as evidenced by lower MSE values. Moreover, the GMLE estimator enjoys better theoretical properties such as stronger consistency and asymptotic normality. Finally, the proposed method is applied to a mixture model involving concentrating parameters and shows that the GMLE estimator can distinguish between the concentrations of these parameters. The associated R software is provided for users to employ the GMLE estimator and the related NPMLE estimator directly. The performance of these estimators is evaluated through simulated and real data sets. The R package can be found at the URL https://github.com/chenwen0702/GMLE". Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. We have publicly released PyKT and the associated research results at https://pykt.org/. We invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of deep learning knowledge tracing.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals. Experimental results confirm the modified algorithm's effectiveness, revealing better convergence rates compared to the original FedBuff, especially when systems experience delays. The benefits of the algorithm become particularly apparent as the number of active clients increases. The evaluation also highlights how the algorithm adapts to varying dataset distributions and integrates secure aggregation protocols. The feasibility of the algorithm is further demonstrated through an experiment involving a real-world smart meter data set. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER). When combining both methods, we achieved a substantial 36% decrease in WER compared to a straight transfer from English. We also found that our technique worked across various Czech dialects. Additionally, our technique allowed us to accomplish Czech ASR with only 1% of the Czech data, substituting it with a mix of dialects, and surprisingly, it even enabled us to succeed with no Czech data at all, realizing a 13% decrease in WER. We've investigated how this extra dimension affects the rate of Hawking radiation in black holes and found that their perception of it causes the radiation to slow down. We discuss how this affects the possibility that dark matter consists of primordial black holes and estimate a suitable mass range of 10^14 to 10^21 grams, which expands on the existing four-dimensional theory's scope by three orders of magnitude in the lower mass range. Furthermore, primordial black holes with a mass of approximately 10^12 grams may be responsible for the Galactic 511 keV gamma-ray line, assuming they make up a very small fraction of total dark matter. We also examine how an additional dimension affects the black hole's density distribution and, for the first time, its cross-section in five-dimensional Einstein gravity. We've developed a non-perturbative model to describe the evolution of primordial black holes and found that their density distribution is nearly indistinguishable from its general-relativistic counterpart unless the gravitational precession causes a significant slowing of Hawking radiation. We're exploring the implications of this theory for other types of black holes and black holes in other extra-dimensional spaces. The behavior of black holes in this scenario raises interesting questions about the validity of the Dyson et al. argument regarding black hole firewalls. Lastly, we're investigating how this theory relates to the Swampland program's predictions for the presence of an additional dimension and the associated gravitational precession. The latter could provide a solution to the dark matter problem if primordial black holes make up a significant fraction of dark matter. The implications of this theory also suggest that it may be possible to directly detect the effects of an additional dimension on the behavior of black holes. Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to underwater navigation.  Our approach also has a model-based variant known as SPGP-TD, and with minimal modifications, this variant is obtainable.  Our findings are backed by extensive simulations and actual underwater robot learning experiments.  This work lays the groundwork for exploring other marine tasks and extending SPGP-SARSA to real-world human evaluations.  We have openly shared our code, data, and methods to facilitate replication and to contribute to the development of SPGP-SARSA in various aquatic environments. This project is led by the EU's Horizon 2020 program and involves top research centers and companies in the field. This paper explores the concept of sorting networks consisting of comparators with more than two input values. We focus on the interplay between three parameters: the comparator arity (k), the number of inputs (n), and the depth (d). Our model has a unique characteristic where d is limited to 2 ceiling(log2(k)), which allows us to discover interesting relationships between k, n, and d. In particular, we found lower bounds on the comparator arity required for constant-depth sorting networks, with specific values for powers of 2 (e.g., a of at least 5 for n = 16, 6 for n = 32, and 7 for n = 64). We also found that the upper limit for k in the context of sorting networks is sqrt(n), which is currently achieved by a sorting network with a comparator arity of 4. Additionally, we investigated the relationship between k and n for constant-depth sorting networks and found that k should scale linearly with log2(n) in order to minimize depth requirements. Based on these findings, we propose open questions regarding the fundamental limitations and flexibility of sorting networks with multi-input comparators. Moreover, we outline potential applications and related concepts that could further explore the capabilities and limitations of our model. These masked scans were then utilized as more balanced data for our primary infection-aware classification network. To rectify data imbalance, we incorporated the Contrastive Mixup technique, which rearranged low-density samples with similar characteristics to enhance generalizability across different grades. Through the contrastive process, the network was able to extract valuable information from the infected region masks, ultimately leading to better grading performance. Notably, our approach demonstrated superior results, outperforming the current state-of-the-art methods by achieving a higher score than the competition's provided baseline on the test dataset. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains. The results show that the model excels at adapting to new languages with just 2000 sentences, surpassing the baseline multi-task transfer approach that requires access to additional data. Moreover, the model exhibits a notable ability to generalize to non-European languages. The code and data are available at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMIC4GEC. The paper has been accepted by the Findings of the 28th Conference on Computational Linguistics (2020).

Rounding is an essential concept used extensively in research, yet its implications on discrete random variables have not been extensively explored. To understand changes in rare events such as suicides, officials may release rounded statistics of deaths, which can distort the actual findings if rates are already low. In this research, we focus on estimating negative binomial distribution parameters when the underlying data is rounded, acknowledging that over-dispersion is inherent in several epidemiological studies. Initially, we analyze how rounding affects the maximum likelihood estimator and derive an alternative method for calculating the standard error. Notably, our findings demonstrate that while rounding significantly impacts the estimation of rare events, a certain level of over-dispersion is masked. Building upon these results, we investigate the effects of rounding on Poisson distribution parameters, comparing our methods to existing work. Through a simulation of real-world scenarios, including the previous example of suicide prevalence, we assess the performance of our estimators. Interestingly, our research reveals that while rounding distorts the estimation of rare occurrences, it actually reveals themselves more clearly. To facilitate practical application, we develop a publicly accessible R package capable of handling data with rounding errors and integrating results with well-established epidemiological tools. By employing our methods, researchers can gain a more accurate understanding of rare events and their underlying causes. The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we examine whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the allocations generated are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, this latter fairness condition holds in a weakened form. Additionally, we established a lower bound showing that, for allocation rules with any number of agents, there are situations in which all pure Nash equilibria induce EF1 allocations, as well as a lower bound indicating that no mechanism will always result in pure Nash equilibria that are fair allocations up to any good. Our investigation provides a broader understanding of the interplay between fairness and self-interested behavior in the allocation of goods. It also highlights various research opportunities for identifying mechanisms that produce fair allocations in various economic settings. In our analysis, we drew upon the concept of valuation functions additive in their components, often referred to as the Leontief form, for our examination of envy-free allocation among self-interested agents. It is our hope that our investigation will contribute to the development of novel mechanisms for achieving fair allocation in diverse economic contexts. In our research, we diverge from the standard practice in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) of employing a direct one-to-one correlation ('mapping') between source and target domains. Instead, we utilize stochastic translations to account for the inherent ambiguities in domain transformations. This strategy enables us to achieve better results by generating a range of possible outputs and selecting the most likely one, thus utilizing both cross-domain and co-training techniques to produce more accurate results. Through the generation of diverse outputs and the application of likelihood screening, we are able to reduce data imperfections and achieve greater precision. Our novel approach, which we refer to as stochastic adaptation, is capable of producing adaptable models that are efficient in terms of computational requirements. Our experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms current UDA practices and achieves comparable performance to the current state-of-the-art methods while utilizing significantly less computational resources. Our code is available for review at https://github.com/chen3086/stochastic-ada. Our primary contribution with this research is the introduction of a stochastic strategy for UDA, which we believe will serve as a starting point for the exploration of further innovative techniques.

This study explores how uncertainty about chance influencing job success and earnings impacts redistribution policies in a diverse group of people. We gather responses from a group of participants, who consider various scenarios in which good luck can affect worker outcomes. The results show that participants generally want to reduce the gap in earnings, but are less motivated to do so and react differently to circumstances where luck has an impact on job success rather than overall income. These findings have implications for research aiming to model people's opinions on income inequality and the apparent disparity between laboratory research and real-world inequality trends in the US.  In the process, we discover that people overestimate the effect luck has on individual incomes.  Furthermore, a separate part of the experiment reveals that people tend to overestimate the influence of luck on their own incomes, with those who earned more attributing a higher percentage to luck.  Combining these two key findings, we propose a simpler alternative to existing theoretical models that takes into account people's incorrect perception of luck's impact.  In this proposed model, people care more about reducing the effect of luck and, since they misunderstand its impact, they actually aim to reduce the observed, not the actual, difference it makes.  We utilize this new model to investigate its own predictions and those derived from the parametric variants, as well as its policy implications.  We also examine the conditions under which the diverse responses from our diverse subject pool can be represented by a single representative model.  In doing so, we identify key model features that produce the observed results and propose a new framework that integrates the distinct components of the existing models.  We argue that the most successful models should be those that not only accurately capture the distribution of subject responses but also produce plausible predictions in the context of the data collected.  We test this framework by validating the models against the data and assessing their own performance as well as that of the models that produced them.  We also introduce a new method for cross-validation that is applicable to a broader range of data and can handle diverse response distributions.  Ultimately, we validate our proposed model by comparing its predictions to those of the existing models and validating its own predictions.  We then apply this new model to explore its own predictions and the conditions under which the diverse responses from our diverse subject pool can be represented by a single representative model.  We identify key model features that produce the observed results and propose a new framework that integrates the distinct components of the existing models, producing a simpler alternative that takes into account people's incorrect perception of luck's impact.

We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. To achieve this, we develop a method that involves two components: first, a sampling strategy is employed to significantly reduce the large number of potential hyperedges; second, a hyperedge classifier with two optimized variants is designed to identify candidate hyperedges based on their structural properties in the graph projection. Our experiments validate the efficacy of our approach and its extensions, with impressive results that outperform baseline methods by a significant margin in accuracy, particularly on difficult datasets. Our implementation and data are freely available for download.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. The results demonstrate that our method not only outperforms current offline methods but also learned behaviors from our model generalizes effectively to new team settings. Moreover, an increased diversity of individual trajectories actually enhances the effectiveness of our model. In quantum computing, generating the same outcome from different input states is crucial for error-free operations. This concept is reflected in the principle of compositional fault tolerance, which states that generating the same outcome (whether classical or quantum) from diverse input states is necessary and sufficient for achieving error-free operations. While this principle holds true for individual gates, it does not apply to multi-qubit operations like the CNOT gate. Our research reveals that compositional fault tolerance can be achieved with a minimal number of single-qubit gates, providing a fundamental quantum lower bound. Furthermore, in the context of quantum error correction, using multi-qubit gates significantly improves fault tolerance, with a linear scaling of improvement. This finding is demonstrated through applications to CNOT-based quantum error correction codes and simulations of noisy quantum experiments. Our method of achieving compositional fault tolerance can be applied to any sequence of quantum operations, providing a general framework for improving the fault tolerance of quantum error correction. We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track the further development of these nuclear star clusters as the universe evolves. Our study reveals that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of most massive galaxies and that a significant portion of these remnants will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshift. In fact, our predictions indicate that roughly 20% to 50% of these mergers occur within the mass range of 10,000 to 500,000 M, a finding that could be used to guide observations of nuclear star clusters, particularly when searching for binary black holes formed from Population III binary remnants. Furthermore, our model anticipates that if such binary black holes have a total mass exceeding 60M, then they will be visible from a distance of at least 100 M. Additionally, we anticipate that the detection rates for these binary black holes in future gravitational wave experiments will depend on factors such as telescope sensitivity and targets for observations. When considering more sensitive detectors and a broader search scope, this percentage could increase to 20% to 50% in later decades. Lastly, our predictions also indicate that if nuclear star clusters are observable, then about 1% to 5% of Population III binary remnants will have contributed to the creation of heavy elements within nuclear star clusters through merging binary black holes or neutron stars. The primary objective of the Gravitational wave high-energy Electromagnetic Counterpart All-sky Monitor (GECAM) is to observe various Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRB) that arise from the merger of compact binary stars or the collapse of massive stars, which can also generate gravitational waves. To ensure the performance of GECAM's Gamma-Ray Detectors (GRDs) and test its onboard triggering and localization software before launch, a portable device that simulates Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) has been developed using a grid controlled X-ray tube and direct digital synthesis technology. This portable GRB simulator, which modulates an X-ray flux powered by up to 20 kV, demonstrates its capability of generating high-energy bursts. Before its launch in December 2020, both GECAM satellites were tested using this simulator, which produced short and long GRBs that were detected and analyzed by the onboard GECAM/GRDs. The results showed a strong consistency between the observed data and the programmed simulation functions, indicating excellent performance of the GRDs and the GRB simulator. The successful development of this simulator has not only enabled the pre-launch testing of GECAM/GRDs, but has also provided a valuable reference for the development of GRB simulators for other space missions. The capability of this simulator to generate various types of GRBs has also been validated through in-flight observations of the Large Area Telescope on the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope, which collects about 4 Tbytes of data every day and can detect over 10,000 Gamma-Ray events daily. The successful development of this simulator has significantly contributed to the pre-launch and in-flight performance validation of GECAM/GRDs, and has ensured the optimal functioning of the GECAM satellites during their operation in orbit. The experience gained in developing this simulator has also provided valuable insights for the development of other particle accelerators and X-ray generators that could be used in medical treatment. The development of this simulator has also sparked interest in the community and has led to the publication of two papers, one on the generation of gamma-rays and the production of the simulator, and the other on the in-flight validation of the simulator against in-flight data of the Fermi satellite. The successful development of this simulator has several implications and has the potential to contribute to various scientific research projects in the future.

We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major advancement of our approach, the method also achieves conservative and symmetric results with regards to pressure. This methodology's effectiveness is demonstrated through the execution of numerous test cases across both two and three-dimensional settings. Our numerical data shows our method's ability to accurately replicate the behaviour of both continuous and discrete fracture networks. Our approach's performance is also comparable to existing literature. This paper's novel contributions include the introduction of a mixed finite element approach for blocking fractures, as well as the implementation of a novel iterative method for solving the Schur complement. The latter method exhibits greater efficiency, particularly for larger-scale discrete fracture network cases. This paper also provides an exploration of the method's applicability to multiphase flow and general non-Newtonian fluid types. However, the latter two specifications are yet to be fully converged and thus are advised against for production use. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis. We create a set of scenarios that allow us to examine the performance of different computational approaches in estimating Bayes factors, and then investigate factors that influence the accuracy of these estimates. We find that even when true values are accurately simulated, Bayes factor estimates can be quite variable. We also find that these estimates are often biased in the context of frequentist hypothesis testing. Additionally, the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates can be affected by the choice of prior distribution, data characteristics, and the use of Markov chain Monte Carlo methods. Our findings highlight the importance of evaluating the methodological approaches used to analyze data and the potential limitations of Bayes factor estimates in cognitive science. We also discuss potential solutions to mitigate these issues and improve the reliability of Bayes factor estimates. Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use. Additionally, an evaluation is performed on a subset of the data employing a reliability index suited for categorical data. The obtained results demonstrate significant variations in prediction frequencies across semantically defined categories, revealing the prevalence of certain indicators in certain contexts. For instance, instance classifiers are substantially more likely to be predicted than other discourse classifiers. The constructed dataset aids in exploring the intricate connections between discourse indicators and semiotic relations and may contribute to the development of models capable of analyzing these complex relationships. By comparing our measurements to theoretical predictions, specifically from the Mott-Seitz model, we estimated that a significant barrier prevents the center from returning to its ground state quickly, and that this barrier is influenced by the presence of a nearby electron.  Additionally, our research showed that even in a perfect, ideal environment, a substantial reduction in the rate of radiative decay occurs due to the presence of a nearby electron, and that this phenomenon could potentially enable the development of highly sensitive sensors. It is intriguing to consider the implications of this method for the training of modern neural networks that consist of multiple layers. Despite this, the algorithm provides valuable insights into the nature of deep neural networks and raises important questions about their fundamental design. Using field-theoretic methods, researchers studied a spin model on the triangular lattice, where the SU(3) representation was placed on each site, mimicking an antiferromagnetic Heisenberg spin model with p-box symmetry. Taking a large-p limit, they found the model reduces to a relativistic sigma model in three-dimensional space, described by the SU(3)/U(1)^2 manifold. Due to a non-trivial homotopy, this model possesses distinct magnetic vortices, or skyrmions, that monopole instantons can create and annihilate. Upon analyzing the Wess-Zumino term, researchers found the Berry phase associated with these monopoles causes interference, constraining possible Lagrangian perturbations by monopole operators, resulting in a subset of relevant perturbations having the same form as those seen in the SU(2) model. Researchers also investigated the phase transition driven by a Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, studying DM-monopole anti-monopole pairs that develop from the sigma model's Wess-Zumino term. This results in a phase transition's free energy being minimized at a non-trivial DM field when considering the SU(3) representation, similar to the SU(2) model. However, when considering the SU(3) representation, researchers found the phase transition is first-order. This is because the DM field becomes pinned when the DM interaction's strength exceeds a certain threshold, which happens because of the inter-monopole interaction being influenced by the target space manifold. This leads to the phase transition's order parameter failing to become continuous. This pinning effect is anticipated to be observable in other relativistic field theories. Researchers also studied the phase transition's disorder phase by performing Monte Carlo simulations, obtaining disorder phase samples and comparing them to the clean phase. This revealed the disorder phase exhibiting the same universal characteristics as the clean phase, which is distinct from the SU(2) model. Additionally, researchers studied the phase transition's free energy in the disorder phase, finding it follows an exponential decay. This indicates the phase transition's disorder phase having a finite free energy barrier. This barrier is associated with the disorder phase's monopole anti-monopole pairs being unstable, and is governed by the same universal exponent as the clean phase. This exponential decay is anticipated to be observable in other relativistic field theories. The distinction between orderly and chaotic behavior within complex networks of interdependent oscillators corresponds to varying functional states found in numerous applications, including active brain states and stable electrical grids. Researchers have lately shown substantial interest in explosive synchronization phenomena which enable sudden shifts between these states due to their rapid and drastic nature. Although previous studies have highlighted key attributes of complex systems capable of explosive synchronization, these analyses were primarily undertaken on a case-by-case basis. This work establishes an exact standard for identifying explosive synchronization within coupled oscillator ensembles by determining the critical relationship between disorder in their internal workings and structure. This breakthrough brings us closer to understanding the intricacies of complex systems responsible for abrupt transitions and dual stability in both living organisms and man-made systems. Furthermore, this research reveals how internal fluctuations can trigger a drastic change when paired with the ability for a system to explosively synchronize. This happens because the starting conditions necessary for a system to explosively synchronize are met by the same parameters that initiate internal fluctuations. This, in turn, facilitates a sudden shift between two stable states existent within a system and leads to the observation of "hysteresis". This phenomenon is showcased through the study of active brain states and the exploitation of this new standard for constructing simple models capable of dual stability. This is achieved by applying the principles of explosive synchronization and hysteresis in a multi-frequency network where different frequency components correspond to distinct functional states. This work also highlights the potential for the exploitation of hysteresis in complex systems responsible for the exchange of information through different communication pathways, notably the human brain. We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. To achieve these results, we analyze a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, providing a critical connection, and also establish an independent result regarding the convexity of geodesic balls under the Riemannian quotient geometry. This could be possible if these particles once controlled the universe's energy density and led to a transition to a matter-dominated period before decaying in time for Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis to occur. Our experiments examine how the geometric structure of force-free rigid swimmers interacts with different fluid properties: Newtonian and viscoelastic (specifically Boger fluids).  By changing the swimmer body and its helical tail, our study reveals that viscoelastic effects provide additional propulsion benefits, except when the swimmer has a large cross-sectional area, where friction dominates and viscoelastic effects become minimal.  Interestingly, in viscoelastic fluids, the geometry of the swimmer that benefits most varies significantly, unlike in Newtonian fluids where the benefits are greatest for swimmers with medium sizes in the transverse direction.  Moreover, our findings suggest that viscoelastic forces provide additional propulsion up to 30% more than Newtonian forces for certain swimmer geometries.  We also develop a non-dimensionalization that allows us to compare our results with theoretical models and consider how these models can be applied to various swimmer designs.  Our study provides a comprehensive exploration of the interplay between viscoelastic forces, swimmer geometry, and propulsion mechanisms.  We identify the conditions in which elastic forces provide additional propulsion and highlight the complex relationship between the dimensions of force-free swimmers and their performance in viscoelastic fluids.  We propose that our non-dimensionalization framework can be a useful tool for analyzing and predicting the behavior of elastic forces on swimmer motion.  We also suggest that our results may be used in conjunction with multi-objective optimization techniques to design highly efficient swimmers in viscoelastic fluids.  Our study has the potential to contribute to the development of self-propelled elastic swimmers that can navigate various viscoelastic fluids efficiently.  We anticipate that our research will stimulate further theoretical and experimental investigations of force-free swimmers in complex fluids and encourage the exploration of novel swimmer designs.  We hope that our study will also pave the way for a deeper understanding of how viscoelastic forces influence swimmer motion and how this knowledge can be applied to different swimmer geometries.  We believe that our research has the potential to contribute to the broader field of swimmer research and could have significant implications for the development of self-propelled elastic swimmers in viscoelastic fluids.  We propose that our results may be used in conjunction with theoretical models that describe the elastic forces provided by viscoelastic fluids and how these forces interact with swimmer motion.  We suggest that our findings could be applied to different swimmer designs with various geometric structures and that our research can provide a foundation for the development of more efficient swimmers.

We employed co-evolutionary genetic algorithms in a range of Cournot models to replicate players' learning behavior and assess their capacity for convergence to a Nash Equilibrium. Introducing "social-learning" variations of two algorithms led to successful attainment of Nash Equilibrium, unlike "individual learning" counterparts which consistently failed to converge to the desired outcome. Utilizing simulation outcomes with a specific approach as well as general statistical analysis, our results showed that "social" learning versions resulted in an ergodic Markov Chain, characterized by frequent occurrence of states leading to NE play in the stationary distribution. In contrast, "individual learning" failed to reach the NE state in our simulations, exhibited significantly greater distance from the desired NE state, required substantially longer time to reach the NE state, and displayed reduced robustness. Ultimately, our findings confirmed that the majority of games reached a Nash Equilibrium when players used the "social" learning algorithms. Full results are presented using aggregate data and detailed analysis of specific game scenarios. Furthermore, we explored the effect of precision in the social learning algorithms, applied the same analysis to a game with a strictly dominant NE, extending our investigation to a model of dynamic oligopoly using a continuous-time approach. Our results showed that "social learning" led to the attainment of the strictly dominant NE and resulted in the NE being reached in the majority of games. Additionally, we utilized a co-evolutionary genetic algorithm to replicate the log-files produced by the repetitive game simulations, achieving matching frequency of NE play. Lastly, we utilized a continuous-time approach for an oligopoly model and derived a system of differential equations whose equilibrium points represented the pure strategy NE. A "social learning" variation of the evolutionary algorithm was applied to reach the NE in a Cournot duopoly model. Our results showed that this variation resulted in the majority of games being played at the NE, leading to the strict domination of one firm over the other. We extended our investigation to an n-firm Cournot competition model. wherein existing vulnerability information can be utilized to enhance knowledge 
and predictive analytics for risk mitigation. By structuring security 
knowledge as an ontology, anomaly detection and threat assessment become 
more feasible, along with other security operations. Nevertheless, 
traditional methods of enriching ontologies based on natural language 
processing and machine learning are hampered by issues in extracting contextual, 
domain-specific information from text. Therefore, sequential Deep Learning 
models, capable of navigating through the semantic structures in language and 
identifying crucial security features, are needed to enhance the effectiveness 
of their approaches. Furthermore, incorporating external knowledge could 
significantly improve their performance. In order to demonstrate the applicability 
of such methods in processing natural language for cybersecurity purposes, a 
framework has been devised which integrates a pre-trained language model, 
pre-extracted lexical and syntactic features, and a domain-specific ontology. 
The utilization of this combined set of features leads to a notable improvement 
in the enrichment of security knowledge when compared to applying the model on 
its own. Additionally, incorporating a smaller set of highly relevant ontological 
axioms also results in a further enhancement of this performance, which serves as 
an indication of the capacity of Deep Learning models to extract both the 
contextual information present in large language datasets and the nuanced, 
domain-specific information present in security ontologies. A thorough evaluation 
of multiple Deep Learning models, along with a detailed analysis of the impact 
of incorporating external knowledge, reveals that the incorporation of a 
small set of highly relevant axioms can lead to a significant improvement in 
their performance, which in turn results in an enriched ontology with a high 
degree of semantic coherence. Nevertheless, it has also been observed that 
the incorporation of all available axioms does not necessarily result in a 
more coherent ontology, which could be attributed to the presence of cycles

its enhanced effectiveness. Lastly, the incorporation of axioms spanning 5

vulnerabilities, which serves as an indication of the potential of this 
approach to address the renowned data skew issue prevalent in cybersecurity.

The Ising model falls within the domain of equilibrium statistical mechanics, in contrast, the voter model represents a system out of equilibrium. Our analysis focuses on an opinion formation model, a hybrid of Ising and voter agents, with concentrations of $p$ and $1-p$. Notably, even though detailed balance is violated for $p<1$, it has been shown that on a fully connected graph the stationary state average magnetization for any $p>0$ follows the same equation as for the pure Ising model ($p=1$). This behavior is further confirmed by numerical simulations; however, the observed equivalence with the pure Ising model is limited to magnetization. While susceptibility diverges at the same temperature as magnetization, its values vary according to the concentration of Ising agents $p$. Simulations conducted on a random graph also reveal that even a minimal proportion of Ising agents can trigger ferromagnetic ordering. Moreover, the onset of ferromagnetism is delayed by the presence of Ising agents in the concentration equilibrium solution. These findings have significant implications for opinion formation dynamics and may be applicable to other systems comprising diverse interacting components. Lastly, the inclusion of an external field accelerates the approach to the ferromagnetic state, regardless of the structure of the graph, and the effect is particularly pronounced when the system is largely composed of voter agents. This acceleration results from the enhanced ability of Ising agents to withstand the field's influence, thus serving as a key adaptation for withstanding environmental stress in these systems. Further research is necessary to explore the dynamic dynamics of these systems and the possible stationary state loops that may exist. The COVID19 virus is spread through contaminated droplets expelled by infected individuals when they cough, sneeze, speak or breathe. Understanding how these virus-carrying droplets behave under changing environmental conditions is essential to tracking the infection's spread. To investigate this, we examine the movement of evaporating droplets influenced by gravity and varying weather, observing how they change in size until either settling on the ground or breaking down into small particles that can linger in the air. Our analysis reveals significant impacts of humidity and temperature on evaporation, with large droplets falling due to gravity's dominance despite evaporative losses and smaller droplets suspended in the air due to diffusive forces. The size of intermediate droplets is highly dependent on weather conditions and is critical to infection spread, underscoring the need for physical distancing and making face masks essential. Additionally, our model highlights the importance of considering gravity in descriptions of evaporation and suggests that improving air circulation alone may not effectively mitigate the spread of the infection. Lastly, we use our model to evaluate the benefits of face masks, finding they can reduce the spread of infection when interacting with others and highlight the importance of protecting healthcare workers from large droplets containing the virus. Our findings provide a theoretical basis for evaluating infection control strategies and guiding further research in the physics of the pandemic. Finally, we propose conducting field experiments to observe and compare the behavior of evaporating droplets in different settings. By understanding and visualizing these processes, we can create more accurate computer simulations and inform data-driven policies to combat the spread of the infection. Consequently, our study offers a framework for exploring the complex interactions between the physical behavior of virus-carrying droplets and the environment, thereby contributing to the development of effective strategies to contain the pandemic. Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model choices, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and the inherent stochastic nature of optimization itself. Despite some recent efforts to quantify uncertainty within NNs, no overarching framework effectively addresses uncertainty quantification even in relatively simple cases such as function approximation. Moreover, very little research has focused on solving partial differential equations and mapping infinite-dimensional functions using NNs. In this work, a unified framework is established that tackles uncertainty quantification in various NN architectures solving various PDE systems, infinite-dimensional function mappings, and a few related problems. Several numerical experiments demonstrate the efficacy of this approach. Source code is available online at the specified link. Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems require ensuring the reliability of their underlying hardware, shielding them against faulty memory caused by hardware errors. Following the successful use of activation clipping, we have developed a prototype to demonstrate that range restriction can serve as a trustworthy error detection and prevention method for classifier CNNs, specifically against common memory malfunctions in a binary hardware platform. We also explore different input pre-processing techniques that can enhance the reliability of these systems. Experimental results show that our proposed method can accurately identify and prevent a range of error types, including data corruption, missing values, and overflow, without decreasing the network's classification accuracy. We have open-sourced our prototype and related data to facilitate further research in this area. In the long term, we expect this to contribute to the development of more dependable deep learning technologies capable of operating in a wider range of physically imperfect environments. For this particular study, we have created a reliable binary image recognition system that can operate with approximately 96% accuracy when subjected to hardware errors. However, this approach detects a limited subset of errors caused by the binary hardware platform we used and might not be suitable for systems that can cause errors due to overflows that result from the accumulation of multiple memory malfunctions. In such cases, a more sophisticated approach that handles multiple memory updates simultaneously would be necessary. This early exploration of reliable deep learning in the face of hardware errors has several potential avenues for further research, including the identification of activation functions that can provide more robust error detection, the creation of error models that can cover a broader spectrum of error types, and the development of error detection methods that can operate across multiple layers of the network. This could ultimately pave the way for the creation of dependable computer vision systems capable of operating in a wide range of physically imperfect environments. The European Central Bank's definition of clearing or netting has far-reaching effects on a nation's economy, affecting how businesses affect each other's operations. Essentially, netting represents a different method of transactional interaction. By combining transactions that cancel each other out, netting reduces the number of transactions required. In financial terms, this simplification speeds up payment processing and lowers costs. In the context of pandemic-related economic disruptions, the speed at which payments are processed becomes crucial. In this study, the model used to measure the speed of payment processing is applied to a realistic scenario. In doing so, the advantages of netting are quantified and illustrated through a series of graphs. The results show that processing payments using netting can accelerate payment clearance by a factor of up to 5.5, also yielding a more efficient payment arrangement. Notably, this arrangement is achieved by combining the resources of multiple payment providers, each with their own processing capabilities, thus leading to a significant reduction in payment clearance times. This finding has implications for the development of payment systems, suggesting that systems based on netting may require different system designs, one that accommodates payment cancellation, and could benefit from multi-payment processor connectivity. Lastly, this research offers a theoretical framework for examining the effects of netting in financial transactions and provides a practical application to pandemic-related economic challenges. In doing so, it highlights the need for further exploration of payment system design in the context of netting. The proposed model can be applied to analyze payment systems, and its simplicity allows for the derivation of results that illustrate the benefits of netting. The model's flexibility also enables the examination of various payment systems, including those involving the combination of payment cancellation and the involvement of multiple payment providers. The study on peer-to-peer payment systems serves as an example of this versatility. The results produced are relevant to the current global financial landscape, characterized by widespread use of digital payments and the emergence of new payment technologies like blockchain, also commonly known as distributed ledgers. The growth of these technologies has given rise to new payment systems, such as decentralized payment systems, that operate outside the traditional central bank framework. The characteristics of these new payment systems differ significantly from those used in the existing model, leading to questions about their suitability for netting and whether they could benefit from multi-payment provider connectivity. The model used in this study raises further questions about the optimal design for payment systems based on netting and whether system design should consider payment cancellation and the involvement of multiple payment providers. We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our framework relies on three key connections - monolingual clustering, bilingual linking, and space construction - that can be viewed as clustering, dimensionality reduction, and data imputation tasks. We make significant contributions by developing novel clustering and space construction methods that yield a more coherent and consistent semantic space. Our approach also facilitates the efficient use of limited data. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method by adapting monolingual models to a test set without direct supervision and achieving better results than the current state-of-the-art approaches. Our technique effectively leverages knowledge from source languages to improve performance on target languages with limited data, showcasing the benefits of a multilingual common semantic space. Our code is available at https://github.com/awadalla/mono-multilingual-semantic-space.git.

The MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset has significantly accelerated the study of dialogue state tracking, yet contains considerable annotation errors that significantly impede the robust training of models. The recent releases of refined datasets, MultiWOZ 2.0 'fix', also introduce a new challenge where they utilize a single model's outputs to correct the original versions, potentially being confined to a single paradigm. To address these limitations, we develop a framework named ASSIST, seeking to automatically scaffold state corrections based on both data refinements and corrections from diverse models. The proposed framework successfully mitigates the negative influences of annotation errors and enhances the accuracy of dialogue state tracking. The evaluations using both the corrected MultiWOZ 2.0 'fix' and a real-world customer service dataset demonstrate the capabilities of this approach, where it achieves an overall joint goal accuracy rate of 56.16% on the MultiWOZ 2.0 'fix' dataset and a state tracking F1 score of 51.57% on the real-world dataset. In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to understanding the spread of crime in Cape Town to the Santiago riots. By incorporating local data and implementing a susceptible-infected-removed style model with spatial movement, our simulation seeks to replicate the observed geographic distribution of rioting activity across Santiago. The model's ability to mimic this pattern depends heavily on the defined spatial interaction parameters, which can be inferred using Bayesian methods. However, given the limitations of the Markov Chain Monte Carlo method for complex cases, we employed the Augmented Simulation Monte Carlo method to estimate these key parameters, which essentially involves using the best model to make predictions and comparing them to actual data in order to gauge the performance. The results indicate a strong likelihood for the model to replicate the observed distribution of riots across different Santiago neighborhoods, and the estimated parameters reveal a significant impact of spatial proximity on the spread of rioting activity, as well as its rapid dissemination. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of the model's components highlights the effect of including infrastructure damage in the model and the variation of rioting activity across different socioeconomic Santiago districts. Lastly, the discussion includes potential applications and suggestions for refining the model by integrating additional factors and examining the implications for epidemic disease spread. The code and data used for this analysis are available at  https://github.com/edgarcampos/Santiago-riots-model. By comparing observed and predicted data for a set of 21 galaxies at a specific wavelength, we assess the reliability of star formation rate predictions made by the Prospector framework. Using a line that is less affected by dust at this wavelength, we find that the predictions are accurate within expected measurement errors and are relatively consistent, although the choice of stellar model affects the outcome. Furthermore, even if the predictions for other spectral features are inaccurate, we find that the Prospector-derived star formation rates are generally accurate. Additionally, we consider how observing the $\lambda$2.16 $\mu$m Brackett-$\gamma$ line might be used to constrain the model's predictions and as an indicator of star formation rates in future near-infrared spectroscopy missions like JWST. With optimal signal processing and detection limits, we estimate that detecting the Brackett-$\gamma$ line would be capable of accurately predicting star formation rates at least 0.5 dex more reliably than without it. With optimised signal processing and desired sensitivity levels, detection limits could be as low as $10^{8}$ $L_{\odot}$. As a result, observing the Brackett-$\gamma$ line in combination with other data can enhance the accuracy of star formation rate predictions and may provide an alternative method of measuring galaxy interactions if the line can be measured in sufficiently low-star-formation-rate galaxies.

We are studying a critical boundary that involves breaking down real polynomials into the sum of squares of other real polynomials, specifically those that don't equal zero. This specific boundary overlaps with another critical boundary that involves nonnegative polynomials and is characterized by polynomials that become zero at at least one point. Our focus lies on a separate part of the boundary that involves positive polynomials and we have already successfully identified the full version of this boundary for very simple examples and a key part of a more general version of this boundary for specific types of polynomials. However, identifying the full version of this boundary for all types of polynomials remains a challenge. To approach this challenge, we are exploring ways to apply nonnegative matrices that have positive determinants to create new sums of squares representations. This method allows us to break down rational functions into the sum of squares of other rational functions. This strategy enables us to prove a very important theorem that can be used to break down an extensive variety of real rational functions into the sum of squares of other real rational functions. Additionally, this method allows us to break down an even broader variety of real rational functions into the sum of squares of other real rational functions. This breakthrough leads to a major advancement in identifying the full version of this boundary for all types of polynomials. In high-scale theories involving extra neutrino states, the standard low-energy matrix used to describe neutrino interactions may be invalid. We reevaluate how much is currently known about individual components of this matrix, making no assumption about its unitarity. We establish two fundamental sets of experimental limitations - direct plus inherent constraints, and indirect ones. We examine the effects of each set on the possible deviation of neutrino behavior from expected unitarity. We also provide a clearer understanding of predictions related to flux and cross-sections, taking into consideration any contamination from new physics affecting hadronic measurements. We focus on the currently operating FASER$\nu$ experiment to show how certain neutrino experiments can provide unitarity evidence, either by confirming the expected cross-section or by identifying systematic errors. This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets to determine inclusion relationships. We have already proven the method's correctness and now present a practical algorithm utilizing a generalized Brzozowski algebraic derivative in combination with a Brzozowski-Joshi like algorithm, suitable for infinite character sets. This algorithm employs a novel Char2Der operator to compute derivatives, enabling the efficient solution of the containment problem. We have implemented this algorithm and tested its effectiveness using a variety of input scenarios. Our results demonstrate the algorithm's capability to efficiently tackle complex containment queries, even when character sets are highly extensive. Additionally, we have established an open-source tool, named RegEx Containment Checker (RCC), to demonstrate the algorithm's practical applications. RCC can be used as a standalone program or integrated with emerging regular expression development environments, offering a valuable asset for both researchers and industry professionals working with regular expressions. Finally, we have explored the algorithm's adaptability to other algebraic theories by reapplying the Brzozowski-Joshi like algorithm to other varieties of regular expressions, highlighting its versatility as a general containment assessment method. This research has significant implications for the study of containment problems and may pave the way for further advancements in other algebraic theories. Lastly, we have launched RCC with customizable extensions for user-defined regular expression operators, broadening its use and making it available at https://github.com/aliakbaros/RegEx-Containment-Checker. We look forward to exploring new applications of this research with RCC. Despite the algorithm's computational complexity of O(n^2 * m^2) for containment assessment in the context of Brzozowski's algebraic theory with 'n' states and'm' characters, it efficiently handles extensive character sets due to its Char2Der operator. This operator determines derivatives in O(m) time, which is a significant improvement over previous derivative-based algorithms that used Brzozowski's original method with a computational complexity of O(n). We have also demonstrated the algorithm's ability to handle complex containment queries with multiple operators and extensive character sets, demonstrating its effectiveness and practicality. We look forward to exploring new algebraic theories and applications with RCC. We believe this research addresses a long-standing open issue in the field of containment problems and paves the way for the extension of this research to other algebraic theories

Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO ones, offer the potential to provide pose information without the need to craft custom algorithms. Presently, the majority of VIO models are trained and utilized in mission-critical applications, the tendency to incorporate them into embedded systems' code has started to rise. Nevertheless, the limited capacity of these embedded systems' processors poses challenges for implementing VIO models. To overcome this difficulty, this paper reviews and assesses various processing architectures for VIO models on embedded systems, including benchmarks that compare various implementations' performance. To further contribute to this topic, an experimental evaluation of an embedded system executing a VIO model in real-time on an Ouster OS1-64 laser range finder and a high-resolution camera is conducted, with results indicating that the system fails to estimate its pose accurately in real-time when utilizing the sensor with a high resolution. To tackle this challenge, possible solutions such as decreasing the model's resolution, employing low-complexity VIO models and incorporating additional sensors like inertial sensors with higher precision are proposed. The outcomes of evaluating one of these possible solutions, an inertial-visual odometry system that uses a low-complexity VIO model and a more precise inertial sensor with the same camera, demonstrate that the system can accurately estimate its pose in real-time. The code and dataset associated with this comparative study have been made publicly accessible. 

This comparative review and the novel results it includes offer a basis for evaluating and assessing the performance of VIO models on embedded systems, also providing the community with an opportunity to build upon and contribute to this topic. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on electric field measurements, where the goal is to recover missing information on an inaccessible boundary segment using data from the accessible part of a confined domain. A non-iterative approach to solving the problem is examined and different hybrid mathematical formulations are introduced. Key aspects, such as stability, convergence and smoothness of solutions are demonstrated through rigorous analysis. Edge finite elements are employed to discretize the problem. Computational results, covering two- and three-dimensional cases and accounting for noisy input data, showcase the method's effectiveness. All implementations utilize the deal.II finite element platform. The technique's ability to handle complex configurations and its robust performance in solving large-scale problems are also highlighted. The code is openly accessible on GitLab. The results provided offer further proof of the method's validity and worth, making it a viable alternative to other approaches like the electric compact operator approach or the boundary integral format. The project's open-source nature and its successful performance in complex scenarios also set the stage for its potential adaptation to other similar problems. The code can be found at https://gitlab.praefect.at/hybrid_methods_for_maxwell_equations/-/snippets/79442. The researchers invite the public to try the code and contribute to the project. The code has been successfully built with GCC, Clang, Intel and PGI compilers on Linux and Windows compilers. The project's results have been verified to work with computing resources from several European research infrastructure providers. This paper delves into the vertex operator algebra structure of the parafermion type, in association with highest weight modules for integrable representations of the superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$, a simple affine Lie superalgebra. We establish the underlying generators of this algebra in detail. We also verify the existence of a quantum field, as well as its associated vertex operator algebra properties, including the central extension of the Lie algebra of symplectic automorphisms and the extended Kac-Moody algebra structure. Notably, this verifies that this parafermion algebra is isomorphic to the $A_1^{(1)}$-engagement of the highest weight module of type $A_1^{(1)*}$ for $osp(1|2n)$. Our methods employ the Frenkel-Lepowsky-Yao quantum field construction, combined with the Feigin-Lukashevich pseudo-vacuum approach. As a result, we demonstrate the algebraic expression of a specific combination of fields, as well as the associated screening operators and their commutators. These operators play a crucial role in the Beilinson-Bernstein realization theorem for irreducible highest weight modules of integrable representations of $osp(1|2n)$. These operators also enable the construction of extended vertex operator algebras, associated with highest weight modules of type $osp(1|2n)^*$. These vertex operator algebras possess central charge $c = (n+1)^2$, and their extended Kac-Moody algebra structure includes a non-trivial extended lattice part. This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student to excel in a different task than the teachers from which it draws information. To effectively handle FedSA, we implemented a custom technique where the student model selectively gathers knowledge from the FedSA platform by sending tailored sampling requests to the available teachers. To validate the FedSA model, we conducted comprehensive experiments and found it to be a highly efficient and adaptable solution. Moreover, our approach outperformed alternative strategies in both low and high client data settings. To facilitate further research, we made the code and data available at https://github.com/hub-hadoop-fs/FedSA-Challenge. Our study and associated findings have been published on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.04242. Despite achieving remarkable results with the FedSA approach, there remain concerns about its scalability, security risks associated with data exchange, and the potential for model poisoning attacks. To address these issues, we outlined potential solutions and suggested directions for related research communities. As a concrete example, we explored the application of FedSA in a real-world scenario involving the development of a medical diagnosis system. This initiative could give rise to innovative solutions that tackle the challenges of data isolation and facilitate collaborative machine learning practices. To participate in the FedSA challenge, interested parties are invited to utilize the provided code and data resources. As the first step, the FedSA platform expects potential contributors to upload pre-trained neural network models available at https://fedsa.hub.hedu. In response, the FedSA team will provide the results of a thorough security check on these models, followed by which the FedSA platform will conduct various evaluation tests to assess their performance. In return, the FedSA platform will rank these models in order of their effectiveness and offer the top-scoring ones a chance to participate in the student model training process.
